input: Which California band, whose debut album Adrenaline appeared in 1995, has been referred to as "the Radiohead of metal"?

notes.note_text: Adrenaline is the debut studio album by Deftones, released on October 3, 1995, by Maverick Records. Produced mainly by Terry Date, with Ross Robinson handling the hidden track "Fist." The band formed in 1988 in Sacramento, with Stephen Carpenter, Abe Cunningham, and Chino Moreno as founding members. They recruited Dominic Garcia as bassist and later Chi Cheng. The album features tracks like "7 Words" and "Bored," with music videos and a feature in the film *Law Abiding Citizen*. It received praise for its innovative sound, blending alternative metal, post-hardcore, and nu metal. Adrenaline was certified gold in 1999 and platinum in 2008, selling over 1 million copies. The album's personnel includes Chino Moreno (vocals), Stephen Carpenter (guitar), Chi Cheng (bass, vocals), Abe Cunningham (drums), and producers Terry Date and Ross Robinson. The track "Fist" is misspelled as "First" on some digital editions.

Neurosis released their ninth studio album, *Given to the Rising*, on June 5, 2007. The album is available in standard jewel case, limited-edition digipak, and double LP formats with the same track list. *Decibel Magazine* ranked it as the 76th-best metal album of the decade. A DVD documentary from Neurot Records is also available. The artwork, designed by Josh Graham, combines photos from Heroes Square in Budapest and drawings inspired by the location. Steve Von Till and Josh Graham independently considered using Heroes Square for the artwork. The album is described as more aggressive and heavier than Neurosis's recent work, marking their heaviest record since *Times Of Grace* (1999). It received critical acclaim, with Pitchfork's D. Shawn Bosler calling it "their best album in a decade" and AllMusic's Thom Jurek praising it as "one of the high moments in a career filled with them." Personnel include Scott Kelly (vocals, guitar), Dave Edwardson (bass, backing vocals), Jason Roeder (drums, percussion), Steve Von Till (guitar, vocals), and Noah Landis (keyboards, synthesizers, effects, backing vocals).

"Agent 51 released the punk rock album *Just Keep Runnin'* in 2000 on their own label, Suburban Hooligans Records. It was re-released in 2001 by Adeline Records with additional tracks. The album is their second and expanded their sound to include classic rock and heavy metal influences. It deepened the band's secret agent mythos, with liner notes detailing comic book-style origins. The band members are portrayed as rogue secret agents with psychic, cybernetic, and alien-enhanced abilities fighting 'The Agency,' a government organization seeking to control Earth's population via satellites. Agent 51's mission is to expose The Agency disguised as a rock band. The album includes tracks like 'C.I.A.F.B.I.' and 'Psychic Spies' addressing this theme. The track listing includes 20 songs, with Greg Schneider and Sean Scura on bass vocals. Chris Armes and Greg Hewitt handled art design and illustration."

Against All Will is an American rock band from Los Angeles, formed in 2007 by Jimmy Allen, with original members Mizzy Pacheco (vocals) and Mark "Moke" Bistany (drums). The band's debut album, *A Rhyme & Reason*, was released in 2009 and included tracks "All About You" and "The Drug I Need," which reached the national rock radio top 50 in 2010. In March 2011, Phillip Gonyea replaced Steve "Boomstick" Wilson on drums. Current members include Jimmy Allen (lead guitar), Jeff Current (vocals), Cello Dias (bass), and Phillip Gonyea (drums). Former members include Mizzy Pacheco, Mark "Moke" Bistany, and Steve "Boomstick" Wilson. The band's discography includes one extended play and ten singles, with plans for a full-length album in 2013.

Ryan Ferguson is an indie rock guitarist and singer-songwriter born around 1975. He was formerly part of the Southern California band No Knife. In 2004, he contributed the acoustic track "Wait for Me There" to the compilation album *San Diego Is Burning*. His solo debut, the EP *Three, Four*, was released in July 2005 and won a San Diego Music Award for "Best Pop Record" that year. It was also noted by critic Chris Nixon as one of the best releases of the year for San Diego musicians. The track "Suddenly" from *Three, Four* was featured in *The Sims 2*. Ferguson later released the full-length album *Only Trying to Help* in 2007. His influences include Jellyfish and Wire, and his style has been described as "power pop" by critic Kevin Bronson. Ferguson's discography includes *Three, Four EP* (2005) on Jr Varsity Records and *Only Trying to Help* (2007) on Better Looking Records.

Deftones, formed in 1988 in Sacramento, California, by Chino Moreno, Stephen Carpenter, Abe Cunningham, and Dominic Garcia. The lineup stabilized in 1993 with Chi Cheng as bassist. Frank Delgado joined in 1999. They released nine albums, including "Adrenaline" (1995), "Around the Fur" (1997), "White Pony" (2000), "Deftones" (2003), "Saturday Night Wrist" (2006), "Diamond Eyes" (2010), "Koi No Yokan" (2012), "Gore" (2016), and "Ohms" (2020). Chi Cheng died in 2013 after a 2008 car accident. Sergio Vega replaced him in 2009 but left in 2021. The band sold over 10 million albums worldwide. "White Pony" achieved platinum status and won a Grammy. Deftones' style includes alternative metal, art rock, experimental rock, and more. Influences include Faith No More, the Cure, and others. F-Minus was an American hardcore punk band formed in 1995 in Huntington Beach, California, by Jen Johnson and Brad Logan. The band disbanded in 2004. Their final album was recorded by Steve Albini. They covered bands like Antidote, Black Randy and the Metro Squad, 7 Seconds, Negative Approach, and Agnostic Front. Final lineup included Brad Logan (vocals, guitar), Erica Daking (vocals, guitar), Joe Steinbrick (bass), and Adam Zuckert (drums). Former members included Jen Johnson (vocals, bass), Sarah Lee (guitar), Chris Lagerborg (drums), John Guerra (drums), and JP Otto (drums). Their discography includes albums like *Self Titled LP/CD* (1999), *Suburban Blight LP/CD* (2001), and *Wake Up Screaming LP/CD* (2003). They released various EPs and compilations, including *Voice of Treason Cassette* (1996) and *Give Em' The Boot Volume 1 CD* (1997). Brad Logan now runs Blacknoise Records and is

Agent 51 is a rock band from Poway, California. Their album *The Red & the Black* was released in 2003 by Surfdog Records and was their third album. It won "best punk album" at the 2003 San Diego Music Awards. The album marked a shift from punk rock to classic rock and heavy metal influences, with bands like AC/DC, Motörhead, and Def Leppard. The band also moved away from their secret agent theme, stopping the black suit uniform and UFO-related songs. The album's track listing includes 13 songs, all written by Chris Armes. Personnel include Chris Armes (guitar, vocals), Eric "E-Rock" Davis (guitar, vocals), Sean Scura (bass, vocals), and Michael "Mikey L" Levinson (drums). The album was recorded at 4th Street Recording and mastered by Tom Baker. It was the band's last before a 2005 reunion and no further albums were released.

Cream City is the debut album by the American funk/soul band Aalon, released in 1977 and produced by Jerry Goldstein. It reached number 45 on the R&B albums chart in the US. The group disbanded after the album's release. The album was reissued on CD by Thump Records in the mid-1990s and has developed a cult following. The track listing includes "Cream City," "Rock and Roll Gangster," "Midnight Man," "Summer Love," "Steven Baine's Electric Train," "Lonely Princess," "Magic Night," and "Jungle Desire." Aalon Butler is credited as the primary songwriter for most tracks, with Jerry Goldstein and Juan Luis Cabaza also contributing. The band members include Aalon Butler (guitars, vocals), Luis Cabaza (keyboards), Luther Rabb (bass), Ron Hammond (drums), with additional personnel Al Roberts (bass), Alvin Taylor (drums), and Barbara Benney, Freddy Pool, Paula Bellamy (backing vocals on "Cream City").

Noah Georgeson is an American musician, producer, engineer, mixer, and solo recording artist. His debut album, *Find Shelter*, was released by Plain Recordings on November 28, 2006. Born in San Anselmo, California, he moved to Nevada City, California at age three. Georgeson earned a Bachelor of Arts in composition from San Francisco State University in 2001. With a recommendation from Terry Riley, he attended Mills College, obtaining a Master of Fine Arts in 2003. At Mills, he studied with Fred Frith, Pauline Oliveros, and Alvin Curran. He gained popularity as a member of the San Francisco band The Pleased, alongside Joanna Newsom, for whom he produced the debut album *The Milk-Eyed Mender*. He has been nominated for Grammy Awards, Latin Grammy Awards, and Emmy Awards.

notes.note_text: The Pit River Bridge, officially known as the Veterans of Foreign Wars Memorial Bridge, is a double-deck, deck truss bridge over Shasta Lake in Shasta County, California. Built in 1942 as part of the Shasta Dam and Shasta Lake reservoir system, it replaced the Lower Pit River Bridge due to rising water levels. The bridge spans 3,588 feet (1,094 m) on the upper deck (Interstate 5) and 2,754 feet (839 m) on the lower deck (Union Pacific Railroad). It stands 500 feet (150 m) above the old Pit River bed, making it the highest double-deck bridge in the U.S., though it is now only 40 feet (12 m) above Shasta Lake when full. The bridge is the halfway point of Interstate 5. Originally signed as U.S. Route 99, it was used by the Coast Starlight passenger train line operated by Amtrak. The bridge was featured in the 1954 Pulitzer Prize for Photography-winning photo "Rescue on Pit River Bridge" by Virginia Schau.

Atherton Bridge is a historic iron truss bridge in Lancaster, Massachusetts, spanning the South Branch of the Nashua River. Built by J. H. Cofrode & Co. of Philadelphia in 1870, it was the first iron bridge in the town. Added to the National Register of Historic Places in 1979, it was formerly used for Bolton Road but was closed to vehicular traffic in 1975 and bypassed by a modern highway in the 1980s. Pedestrian access ended in April 2020 after flood damage. The bridge is 72 feet long, 18.5 feet wide, with eight panels, resting on granite abutments. It features iron compression posts, diagonal tension rods, double end posts with adjustable turnbuckles, channeled castings, and patented Phoenix columns. It does not use Simeon S. Post's patented joints. The bridge was documented in 1979 by Jet Lowe and in 1990 as part of the Massachusetts Historic Bridge Project. It is a rare example of a hybrid pony truss similar to Simeon S. Post's 19th-century design. Named after James Ath

Walnut Street Bridge (Chattanooga), built in 1890, is a 2,376-foot-long Pennsylvania through truss bridge connecting Chattanooga, Tennessee's downtown with North Chattanooga. It was the first non-military highway bridge across the Tennessee River. Chief engineer was Edwin Thacher; superstructure by Smith Bridge Company, substructure by Neeley, Smith, and Company. Stone contractor was William Andrew Slayton, a former Union officer. The bridge connected predominantly white Chattanooga with the black workforce in Hill City, annexed in 1912. Two men were lynched on the bridge: Alfred Blount (1893) and Ed Johnson (1906), with Johnson's case leading to United States v. Shipp. Closed to motor vehicles in 1978, it was restored as a pedestrian walkway, added to the National Register in 1990. The bridge hosts events like Wine over Water, Riverbend Festival, Seven Bridges Marathon, and Ironman.

Nashua River, 37.5 miles long, is a tributary of the Merrimack River in Massachusetts and New Hampshire. It forms at the confluence of the North and South Nashua Rivers in eastern Worcester County, Massachusetts, and flows north-northeast to join the Merrimack at Nashua, New Hampshire. The North Nashua River rises west of Fitchburg and flows southeast past Fitchburg to join the South Nashua River, which is the main stem. The river's name comes from an Algonkian word meaning "beautiful river with a pebbly bottom." It was heavily polluted in the late 18th to early 19th century due to paper mills and dyes. Marion Stoddart led a restoration campaign in the mid-1960s, resulting in eight treatment plants and a conservation buffer. In 2013, 27 miles of the Nashua River were designated a National Wild and Scenic River. The watershed covers 538 square miles, with 454 in Massachusetts and 74 in New Hampshire. Major tributaries include the Stillwater, Quinapoxet, Squannacook, Nissitissit,

The Colorado River Bridge at Bastrop is a 1,285-foot-long bridge with three identical Parker through truss spans, each 192 feet, supported by concrete piers. It crosses the Colorado River as part of Loop 150 in Bastrop, Texas. The bridge is one of the earliest surviving Parker truss bridges in Texas. The first bridge at the site was built 1889–1890 for $45,000, replacing ferries used since the 1830s. The current bridge, originally a toll bridge, was completed in 1923, opened in January 1924, and cost $167,500. It was partially funded by Bastrop County bonds and federal funds. Ownership passed to the state during the Great Depression. In the 1990s, a wider concrete beam bridge was built alongside it. The truss bridge was transferred to the City of Bastrop and became a pedestrian walkway, used for events like "Art on the Bridge." It was listed in the National Register of Historic Places on July 19, 1990.

The Miami Bridge, also known as the McDaniel Memorial Bridge, is a concrete girder bridge that replaced a cantilever through truss bridge over the Missouri River at Miami, Missouri, between Saline County and Carroll County. Built in 1939, it carries Route 41. The original bridge had a main cantilever span of 474.7 feet and two anchor spans of 415 feet each, totaling 1304.7 feet. It included 11 approach spans, with a total bridge length of 2,071.9 feet and a deck width of 23.0 feet. The Federal Administration of Public Works, with Sverdrup and Parcel as consulting engineers and Massman Construction Company as contractor, built the bridge. The original plans included a wooden toll building with a cast iron stove. The bridge was deemed eligible for the National Register of Historic Places in 1992. Missouri Department of Transportation decided to demolish the superstructure and build a new bridge using the existing piers and abutments, with closure scheduled for October 5, 2009.

- **Monocacy River Railroad Bridge and Viaduct**: 326-foot open deck steel girder bridge with two main spans over the river and two viaduct sections over the floodplain, south of Walkersville, Maryland.  
- **Original Construction**: Built by Frederick and Pennsylvania Line Railroad Company (F&PL) from 1871–1872; original structure was a Bollman suspension truss with wrought iron and cast iron components.  
- **Rebuilds**: Rebuilt by Pennsylvania Railroad in 1900–1905 as an open deck riveted iron plate under girder bridge; rebuilt again in 1927 with deeper steel girders.  
- **Damage and Rebuilding**: Two 85-foot river spans washed out by Hurricane Agnes (1972); rebuilt in 1995 by the State of Maryland using concrete.  
- **Ownership**: Purchased by Maryland in 1982; maintained by Maryland Transit Administration (MTA) since 2001.  
- **Current Status**: In active rail service as of 2016, operated by Walkersville Southern RR.

The Port Mann Bridge in British Columbia, Canada, is a 10-lane cable-stayed bridge that opened in 2012, replacing the original steel arch bridge built in 1964. The original bridge, spanning the Fraser River between Coquitlam and Surrey, was 2,093 m long with a main span of 366 m. It was the longest arch bridge in Canada and third-longest in the world. The new bridge, 2.02 km long and 65 m wide, became the world's widest long-span bridge in 2012. The old bridge was demolished from 2012 to 2015 using reverse construction. The replacement project cost $2.46 billion, with tolls removed in 2017. The bridge faced issues like ice and slush accumulation, leading to closures. It carries 10 lanes of traffic and includes space for light rail.

The Columbia River Bridge, also known as the Bridgeport Bridge, is located in Bridgeport, Washington. Built in 1950, it spans the Columbia River and is composed of three spans. The bridge carries Washington State Route 17 on a 26-foot-wide roadway with two 3-foot sidewalks. The center span is 300 feet, with 250-foot end spans. The north approach span is 70 feet, and the south approach span is 100 feet. The bridge was designed and built by the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers as part of the Chief Joseph Dam project. It played a significant role in the dam's construction, as no bridge existed in the area prior. Construction on the dam began in 1945 and was completed in 1955, except for the powerplant. The bridge was added to the National Register of Historic Places on May 31, 1995.

- **Maiden Lane Bridge**: A railroad bridge across the Hudson River between Albany and Rensselaer County, New York.  
- **Design**: Designed by Kellogg, Clark & Co.  
- **Ownership**: Built and owned by the Hudson River Bridge Company, jointly owned by the New York Central and Hudson River Railroad Company (3/4) and the Boston and Albany Railroad Company (1/4).  
- **Alternative Name**: "South Bridge"; contrasted with the "North Bridge" (Livingston Avenue Bridge).  
- **Construction**: Authorized on May 10, 1869; began in May 1870; first train crossed on December 28, 1871.  
- **Structure**: Four 185.5-foot fixed spans, one 274-foot draw span, seven 73-foot spans over the Albany Basin, one 110-foot span over Quay Street, and one 63-foot span over Maiden Lane.  
- **Reconstruction**: Partial reconstruction in 1899 by Pencoyd Bridge Company, completed by January 3, 1900.

input: Who was the last monarch of England to be overthrown before The English General Election, 1690?

notes.note_text: The 1689 English general election, held in January 1689, elected the Convention Parliament following the Glorious Revolution. 513 Members of Parliament were returned across 53 counties and 217 boroughs in England and Wales, with most returning two members. Only 69 seats were contested, with the rest unopposed. Six boroughs had double returns, five of which were voided, leading to by-elections. Partisan alignment is identified by historians, with 174 Whigs, 151 Tories, and around 190 uncommitted members. Later estimates suggest 232 Tories and 319 Whigs (including Court Tories), with no uncommitted, or 254 Whigs, 221 Tories, and 38 uncommitted. The election marked the beginning of the Convention Parliament (1689).

The 1695 English general election was the first under the Triennial Act of 1694, requiring parliamentary dissolution every three years. This act intensified partisan rivalry between Whigs and Tories. The election was relatively quiet, focusing on local issues. The Whig junto gained a narrow majority in most contested constituencies, with 85 constituencies contested, representing 31% of the total. Party allegiances were uncertain, and many MPs' loyalties were unknown. The new Whig government faced challenges, as backbench 'country' Whigs grew alienated and sometimes cooperated with Tories. The election results were seen as genuinely representative of the voting population. The constituencies in England and Wales remained consistent, while Scottish members were co-opted in 1707. The election is part of the 3rd Parliament of King William III.

The 1690 English general election followed the dissolution of the Convention Parliament after the Glorious Revolution. It saw continued partisan conflicts, with the Tories gaining significant ground against the Whigs, particularly in contested counties and boroughs. The Whigs were viewed as a threat to the Church of England. William of Orange formed a coalition government with non-partisan figures, led nominally by the Marquess of Carnarvon. The Tories, with greater numbers in the House of Commons, secured more government positions. Contests occurred in 103 constituencies, 38% of the total. Party strengths are based on estimates by the History of Parliament, though precise counts are uncertain due to lack of division lists. The constituencies in England and Wales remained unchanged, while Scottish members were co-opted in 1707.

The March 1679 English general election led to the formation of the Habeas Corpus Parliament, which enacted the Habeas Corpus Act in May 1679. The Parliament was dissolved on 12 July 1679 while in recess. During this time, the Exclusion Bill, which aimed to exclude the King's younger brother from the throne, faced debate. 218 members supported the bill, 137 opposed it, and 167 members did not attend, making their stance on the Exclusion Bill unknown. The Habeas Corpus Act was a significant legislative achievement of the Parliament, reinforcing the ancient prerogative writ of Habeas Corpus. The election and subsequent parliamentary actions were part of the broader political tensions surrounding the succession to the throne.

The 1685 English general election elected the Loyal Parliament under James II, the first use of "Whig" and "Tory" as political groupings. 513 MPs were returned across 53 counties and 217 boroughs, with 100 seats from contested elections and others unopposed. 99 boroughs received new charters to reduce Whig influence, leading to a decline in Whig county seats from ~60 in 1681 to 8. Tories had a majority in both houses. Of 525 MPs, 468 were estimated as Tories, 57 as Whigs, with up to 30% inactive. Most MPs were inexperienced, over half new to Parliament, and many were High Church Anglicans, government officials, or military officers. Two minors, Peter Legh (15) and Thomas Windsor (16), were elected. The election significantly altered Parliament's demographic and political composition, with many MPs losing seats in 1689.

The October 1679 English general election resulted in a majority of members supporting the Exclusion Bill. This parliament, known as the Exclusion Bill Parliament, did not assemble until 21 October 1680. It was dissolved on 18 January 1681, three months after its assembly. The election and subsequent parliament were significant in the context of the Exclusion Bill, which aimed to exclude James, Duke of York, from the line of succession due to his Catholic faith. The parliament's short duration and focus on the Exclusion Bill highlight its pivotal role in the political landscape of late 17th-century England.

The 1661 English general election resulted in a Parliament dominated by members supporting Charles II of England. This Parliament is known as the Cavalier Parliament, as many elected MPs were former Cavaliers or the sons of Cavaliers. The election marked a shift in political power, with a majority favoring Charles II. During the tenure of the Cavalier Parliament, there was notable movement between Cavaliers and Roundheads, indicating some level of political realignment. The passage references a list of MPs elected in 1661, though the specific names are not provided. The key entities include Charles II, the Cavalier Parliament, and the political factions of Cavaliers and Roundheads. The event occurred in 1661, and the Parliament was characterized by its alignment with the monarchy and its internal political dynamics.

The Glorious Revolution (1688–1689) involved the deposition of James II of England, Ireland, and Scotland and his replacement by his daughter Mary II and her husband William III of Orange. James, a Catholic, faced opposition due to his policies and the birth of his Catholic son, James Francis Edward. The revolution was triggered by the birth of the male heir and the acquittal of seven bishops. William, supported by English politicians and religious leaders, invaded England in November 1688, leading to James's exile. The revolution resulted in the Bill of Rights 1689, establishing parliamentary sovereignty and limiting royal power. The Dutch Republic played a key role, with William's invasion supported by the States General. The revolution had significant impacts on Ireland, Scotland, and the Anglo-Dutch alliance, shaping the future of constitutional monarchy in England.

Samuel Manetoali (born 24 January 1969) is a member of the National Parliament of the Solomon Islands, representing the Gao/Bugotu constituency in Isabel Province. He attended Lepi Primary School and King George Sixth National School in Honiara for secondary education. He earned an LLB from the University of Papua New Guinea and unspecified qualifications from the University of Tasmania and University of South Australia. Prior to politics, he worked in the Public Solicitors Office, as a private lawyer, and as a legal adviser to the Isabel Provincial Government. He first entered parliament in the 2006 general election, was re-elected in 2010, and served as Minister of Police, National Security and Correctional Services until May 2009. He later became Minister for Lands, Survey, and Housing, then Minister for Tourism and Culture under Prime Minister Danny Philip. Re-elected as an independent in 2014 and 2019 for the Kadere Party.

The 1681 English general election resulted in the formation of the Oxford Parliament, the last parliament of Charles II. The parliament met from 21 March 1681 to 28 March 1681, sitting for one week. It was referred to as the Oxford Parliament. The election returned members to this parliament. Party strengths are approximate, as many MPs' allegiances were unknown. The event is historically noted as the final general election under Charles II. No specific numbers of MPs or party affiliations are provided in the text. The location of the parliament is not specified, but it is implied to be in Oxford, given the name. The election marks a significant point in the political history of England during the late 17th century.

input: What lake in Australia is named after a Scottish Knight?

notes.note_text: William Wallace (c. 1270 – 23 August 1305) was a Scottish knight and leader in the First War of Scottish Independence. He defeated an English army at the Battle of Stirling Bridge (11 September 1297) with Andrew Moray. Appointed Guardian of Scotland, he was defeated at Falkirk (1298) and captured in Robroyston (5 August 1305), later executed by Edward I of England. Wallace's family origins are uncertain; his father may have been Alan Wallace or Sir Malcolm of Elderslie. He is the subject of Blind Harry's poem, literary works, and the film Braveheart. Wallace's military career began with the killing of William de Heselrig (May 1297) and led to the formation of the Council of Twelve. He was knighted at Kirk o' the Forest (Selkirk) in late 1297. After Falkirk, he resigned as Guardian to Robert the Bruce. Wallace's execution involved being hanged, drawn, and quartered. His legacy includes the Wallace Monument and cultural references in literature and film.

William Wallace (died 1305) was a Scottish knight, landowner, and leader during the Wars of Scottish Independence. The passage lists multiple individuals with the name William Wallace across different regions and professions. Notable entries include Willie Wallace (born 1940), a Scottish footballer; William Wallace (footballer, born 1893), an English footballer; William Wallace of Failford (d. 1616), a Scottish courtier; and William Vincent Wallace (1812–1865), an Irish composer. Other entries include William Wallace (philosopher) (1844–1897), William Wallace (Scottish composer) (1860–1940), and William Wallace (Jesuit) (1863–1922). American entries include William Wallace Lincoln (1850–1862), son of Abraham Lincoln; William A. A. Wallace (1817–1899), a Texas Ranger captain; and William H. Wallace (1811–1879), the first territorial governor of Idaho. Canadian and New Zealand entries are also listed, along with a South

Sir William Keith of Galston (died 1337) was a Scottish knight who fought in the Wars of Scottish Independence. He was the son of Robert de Keith and grandson of John de Keith, King's Marischal. He fought alongside Thomas Randolph, Earl of Moray, and James Douglas, Lord of Douglas, in the capture of Berwick in 1318. After Robert I of Scotland's death in 1329, Keith accompanied James Douglas on a crusade, surviving the siege of Teba. He returned to Scotland with Douglas's bones and Robert I's heart, which were buried at Melrose Abbey and St Bride Kirk, respectively. Keith was involved in the 1333 Berwick campaign, captured Richard Talbot in 1334, and died during the Siege of Stirling Castle in 1337. He had a daughter, Jonetta Keith, who married David Hamilton of Cadzow and Alexander Stewart of Darnley.

Lake Wallace is a freshwater lake located in Edenhope, Wimmera region, Victoria, Australia. It is named after William Wallace. In 1866, Australian cricketer Tom Wills trained a team of Aborigines on the lake's banks. The team played throughout Victoria and New South Wales. Several members of this team formed the Aboriginal team that toured England in 1868. The lake's location is in Victoria, Australia. The key entities are Lake Wallace, Edenhope, Wimmera region, Victoria, Australia, William Wallace, Tom Wills, and England. The key dates are 1866 and 1868. The relations include the naming of the lake, training of the team, and the team's tour of England.

Sir David de Inchmartin (died 4 August 1306) was a Scottish knight and supporter of Robert the Bruce during the War of Scottish Independence. He was the son of John de Inchmartin and held lands in Inchmartine (now Inchture), Perth and Kinross. He participated in the Battle of Methven on 19 June 1306, where he was captured by English forces under Aymer de Valence, Earl of Pembroke. Despite orders from Edward I of England, the Earl of Pembroke did not execute the prisoners summarily. David was later executed by hanging on 4 August 1306 at Newcastle-upon-Tyne. His execution was part of the English campaign against Bruce's supporters.

Sir John de Seton (d. 4 August 1306) was a knight involved in the War of Scottish Independence, supporting Robert de Brus. He held lands in England and Scotland. Son of Sir John de Seton of Skelton, Cumberland and Erminia Lascelles, he had brothers Christopher and Humphrey de Seton. His family served the Bruces in Yorkshire, Cumberland, and Scotland. John performed fealty to King Edward I of England at Berwick on 28 August 1296. He was present on 10 February 1306 when Sir John Comyn, Lord of Badenoch, was stabbed by Robert de Brus in Greyfriars Church, Dumfries. A letter of excommunication named Robert de Brus, Earl of Carrick, and three knights, including Sir Christopher Seton and his brother John, as murderers. John was captured after the fall of Tibbers Castle in 1306, executed by hanging and drawing at Newcastle-upon-Tyne on 4 August 1306. His lands in Cumnock, Ayrshire were given to Roger, son of Finlay, in a charter from Robert de Brus.

Sir William Oliphant (died after 1313) was a Scottish knight and Governor of Stirling Castle during the Wars of Scottish Independence. He fought at the Battle of Dunbar in 1296, was captured and imprisoned in Devizes Castle, then released on 8 September 1297. He later served in King Edward I's army but later switched allegiance to the English. He became Governor of Stirling Castle, where he held out against Edward's forces until 20 July 1304. After surrendering, he was imprisoned in the Tower of London. Released in 1308, he served King Edward II. By 1309, he was at Stirling Castle. In 1312, he commanded Perth, which fell to Robert the Bruce in a siege. Oliphant was captured and sent in chains to the western Isles, where he died in captivity. John Barbour noted that Robert ordered executions only for those who could not be captured, suggesting Oliphant's survival indicated he was not executed.

Sir Bernard de Monte Alto (de Mowat) was a Scottish knight who participated in the War of Scottish Independence as a supporter of Robert de Brus. He was the son of Roger de Monte Alto, Sheriff of Cromarty, and the younger brother of William de Monte Alto. Bernard fought alongside Robert the Bruce at the Battle of Methven on 19 June 1306. He was captured by English forces led by Aymer de Valence, Earl of Pembroke. Bernard was executed by being drawn and hanged at Newcastle-upon-Tyne on 4 August 1306. His execution was for bearing arms against King Edward I of England in support of Robert de Brus, and for killing Roger de Tany, the king's valet, in Selkirk Forest.

Sir Reginald Crawford (died 17 February 1307) was a Scottish knight involved in the Wars of Scottish Independence. Appointed Sheriff of Ayr in 1296 by the English administration, he participated in a deal in June 1297 where he and other Scots nobles were released by the English to fight against Andrew Moray. This may indicate his involvement in the revolt of early 1297 that ended in the capitulation at Irvine. He later became a supporter of Robert the Bruce and was captured during the Battle of Loch Ryan in February 1307. He was executed by hanging in Carlisle, England. There is uncertainty regarding his relation to Ronald Crawford, who was hanged at the Barns of Ayr, with this connection being surrounded by legend.

Sir David de Brechin (died 1320) was a Scottish knight who fought in the Wars of Scottish Independence. He was the son of Sir William de Brechin and Elena Comyn, daughter of Alexander Comyn, Earl of Buchan. He was a ward of Sir John de Callendar in 1292. Brechin fought in the Earl of Surrey's army at the Battle of Dunbar and was granted lands previously owned by Alan Durward. He appears on the 1296 Ragman Rolls for Forfarshire. He was present at the swearing in of Robert the Bruce as Guardian of Scotland and later returned to English service, homaging Edward I at the Siege of Stirling Castle. He was wounded at Lochmaben Castle in 1301. He appended his seal to the Declaration of Arbroath in 1320. At the Black Parliament in August 1320, he was found complicit in a conspiracy to depose the king and was executed. He married Margaret de Bonkyll by 1304 and had issue. He also married Margaret Ramsay.

input: Which is a shrub, Mimosa or Cryptocoryne?

notes.note_text: Mimosa is a genus of about 590 species in the legume family Fabaceae, known for its sensitive leaves. Two notable species are Mimosa pudica, a touch-me-not plant native to South America, and Mimosa tenuiflora, used in ayahuasca brews. The genus has undergone taxonomic changes, leading to over 3,000 names, with some species now classified in other genera like Albizia and Acacia. Mimosa pudica's leaves close when touched or exposed to heat, and experiments by Jean-Jacques d'Ortous de Mairan in 1729 provided evidence of biological clocks. Mimosa flowers have ten or fewer stamens, and the genus contains heptanoic acid. Species listed include Mimosa pudica L., Mimosa tenuiflora (Willd.) Poir., and others. Some species are invasive in areas like Hawaii.

Mimosa somnians, commonly known as dormideira, is a woody shrub in the Fabaceae family, native to the Caribbean, Central America, and South America. It has minuscule thorns on its stems and exhibits rapid leaf movement in response to touch, similar to Mimosa pudica. Its leaves are bipinnate with more than four subbranchlets originating from multiple points. Leaflets are 4–5 mm long, and flowers form pink balls. It propagates by seeds. Varieties include f. viscida, subsp. longipes, subsp. viscida, and var. aquatica, deminuta, diminuta, glandulosa, lasiocarpa, leptocaulis, longipes, lupulina, possensis, somnians, velascoensis, and viscida. In Guyana, it is used to calm irritable children by washing. The whole plant contains approximately 0.029% tryptamine and 0.029% methyltryptamine.

Mimosa turneri, known as the desert mimosa, is a perennial shrub native to the Southern United States, particularly Texas. It grows 3.5 to 10 feet (1.1 to 3.0 m) tall and produces pink flowers. It is considered a weed due to its invasive growth in moist soils. The plant is localized on limestone soil at elevations between 2200 and 4000 feet above sea level. It is deciduous and highly heat-tolerant. Originally a contained species, it became invasive in Florida, Texas, and Mexico. It thrives in high alkalinity soils. The leaves are bipinnate, with 12-25 leaflets each, measuring 9-12 mm in length and 1.5 mm in width. Flowers are globe-like clusters with stamens equal to or double the number of petals, and anthers are small with sessile ovaries. The plant is used as livestock feed, fuel, construction material, and for living fences.

Mimosa aculeaticarpa, commonly known as the catclaw mimosa or wait-a-minute bush, is a woody shrub in the Fabaceae family. It is endemic to upland regions of Mexico and the Southwestern United States, specifically Arizona, New Mexico, and Texas. The plant grows to about one metre tall, with hairy twigs and backward-pointing spines. Its alternate, bi-pinnate leaves have small oblong leaflets, and its flowers are white or pale pink, clustered in globular heads. The fruits are flat pods up to four centimetres long, splitting open when ripe, with recurved prickles on the edges. It is found in oak, oak-pine, and evergreen woodlands, pinyon-juniper woodlands, and shrub-steppe communities. It grows on mesas, rocky slopes, and gravel deposits. The plant is fire-tolerant and sprouts after bushfires. In west Texas, redberry juniper acts as a nurse plant, providing shade and leaf litter for seedling establishment. Seeds are dispersed by cattle through dung.

Mimosa invisa is a leguminous woody shrub or vine native to South America. It includes two subspecies, each with two varieties. The species is considered noxious and invasive in much of the United States. The subspecies are Mimosa invisa invisa and Mimosa invisa spiciflora. Mimosa invisa invisa has two varieties: var. invisa, native to Brazil and Paraguay, and var. macrostachya, also native to Brazil and Paraguay. Mimosa invisa spiciflora has two varieties: var. spiciflora, native to northern South America, and var. tovarensis, native to Venezuela. The subspecies and varieties are named with taxonomic authorities: Barneby and Bentham.

Mimosa rubicaulis is a shrub in the family Fabaceae, subfamily Mimosoideae. It is bipinnately compound, with leaves having 8–12 pairs of pinnae, each with 16–20 pairs of pinnules. It flowers from June to September, producing pink spherical flower heads 1–1.5 cm across, which fade to white. Leaves are double-compound, 8–15 cm long, with thorny rachis and 3–2 pairs of side-stalks, each with 6–15 pairs of tiny oblong leaflets 4–8 mm. Pods are thin, flat, curved, 8–13 cm long, 1 cm wide, breaking into 4–10 rectangular single-seeded units. It is found in the Himalayas, from Afghanistan to Bhutan, at altitudes 300–1900 m, preferring forest edges and field/garden boundaries. Used for hedges, its wood is suitable for tent pegs and gunpowder charcoal. Roots and leaves have medicinal uses. Unlike Mimosa pudica, it has more than two prickly leaflet pairs.

Mimosa hamata, also known as Alāy shrub in Hindi, is a species of flowering shrub belonging to the family Fabaceae. It is native to the countries of India and Pakistan. The plant is noted for its use as animal feed. No specific dates, numbers, or additional details about its characteristics, distribution, or other uses are provided in this source. Cryptocoryne is a genus of aquatic plants in the Araceae family, native to tropical regions of India, Southeast Asia, and New Guinea. It is commonly called "crypts" or "water trumpets" due to its spadix and spathe inflorescence. The genus was first described in 1779 as Arum spirale by Retzius and formally in 1828 by Fischer. Cryptocoryne species exhibit convolute vernation, distinguishing them from Lagenandra, which has involute vernation. Some species, like C. beckettii, are hardy aquarium plants, while others are endangered. Crypt melt, a phenomenon where plants lose all leaves, can be caused by rapid environmental changes or nitrate buildup. The genus includes over 100 species, with notable examples like C. wendtii and C. ciliata. Many species are found in peat bogs or on limestone, with varying water and pH requirements. Cultivation dates back to the late 18th century, with increased popularity in the 1960s.

Mimosa tenuiflora, also known as Mimosa hostilis, is a perennial tree or shrub native to northeastern Brazil and found in southern Mexico, El Salvador, Honduras, Panama, Colombia, and Venezuela. It grows up to 8 m tall, with finely pinnate leaves and white fragrant flowers. The tree produces brittle fruits with 4–6 seeds each. It is used medicinally for tooth pain, coughs, and wound healing, and its bark is used as a dye and in leather production. The tree has high tannin content (16%) and is used for fuel wood, construction, and charcoal. It is an entheogen used in the Jurema Cult, containing DMT (1–1.7% in root bark). It is also used in clandestine DMT production. The plant fixes nitrogen, aids soil erosion control, and provides forage for animals. It thrives in USDA Zone 9 or higher. Seeds germinate best at 25°C, with scarification improving germination. The tree is a pioneer species that conditions soil after ecological disturbances.

Mimosa texana, also known as the Texas mimosa, Texas catclaw, or Wherry mimosa, is a shrub in the Fabaceae family. It is endemic to upland regions of Mexico and Texas. Previously classified as Mimosa biuncifera, it was reclassified in 1986 by Rupert C. Barneby, who split the species into Mimosa aculeaticarpa var. biuncifera and Mimosa texana. The plant grows in alkaline soils, specifically in Zapata and Starr counties in Texas, as well as in Mexico. It thrives on caliche and gravelly hillsides. Mimosa texana is a deciduous shrub, up to two metres tall, with slender, zigzag, dark-coloured twigs covered in backward-pointing prickles. Its alternate, bi-pinnate leaves have medium-sized leaflets. The species produces globular, creamy-white flowers in spring, which are intensely fragrant and attract insects. The seed pods are brick red, flattened, and have prickly edges.

notes.note_text: CeCe Peniston's song "Finally" was released in September 1991 as her debut single. It peaked at number five on the US Billboard Hot 100 in January 1992 and spent two weeks at number one on the Billboard Hot Dance Club Play chart in late 1991. Don Coleman (May 4, 1928 – January 30, 2017) was an American football player and teacher. Born in Ponca City, Oklahoma, he moved to Flint, Michigan. He played high school football at Flint Central High School, becoming the first Black swimmer at Royal Oak High School. Coleman played college football at Michigan State University (1949–1951), where he was the first African-American All-American and had his jersey number (78) retired. He was the first African-American on Michigan State's coaching staff (1968) and later became a teacher and administrator at Flint Central High School and Michigan State University. Coleman was inducted into the College Football Hall of Fame in 1975 and received numerous honors, including the Michigan State Hall of Fame and the Michigan Hall of Fame Legends Award. He served in the U.S. Army during the Korean War and was drafted by the Chicago Cardinals but chose teaching over professional football. Coleman died at age 88.

notes.note_text: August Hirt (28 April 1898 – 2 June 1945) was a Swiss-German anatomist and SS-Hauptsturmführer who served as chairman at the Reich University in Strasbourg during WWII. He conducted mustard gas experiments on Natzweiler-Struthof inmates and led the murder of 86 people for a Jewish skull collection. Hirt was involved with the Ahnenerbe, proposing to collect Jewish skeletons for racial research. He directed the selection of 115 inmates at Auschwitz, 86 of whom were sent to Natzweiler-Struthof and gassed in August 1943. Their bodies were to be used for anatomical specimens but the project was abandoned in 1944. Hirt fled to Tübingen in 1944 and committed suicide in 1945. His war crimes were tried in absentia in 1953. Posthumously, the identities of 86 victims were identified, and memorials were placed in Strasbourg. Hirt's records, including Auschwitz tattoo numbers and medical documents, are in the US National Archives.

African-American bookstores, also called black bookstores, are owned and operated by African Americans. They often specialize in works by and about African Americans. The first documented African-American bookstore was established by David Ruggles in 1834. Young's Book Exchange was the first in Harlem. Lewis Michaux's African National Memorial Bookstore in Harlem operated from the early 1930s to the mid-1970s and served as a meeting place for activists like Malcolm X. The Black Power movement used these bookstores to promote ideology in the 1960s-70s. By the 1990s, media like Black Enterprise began to cover them. The number of African-American bookstores dropped from over 250 to just over 70 by the 2010s. Prominent current bookstores include Marcus Books in Oakland, Everyone's Place in Baltimore, Hakim's Bookstore in Philadelphia, Eso Won Books in Los Angeles, and Sankofa in Washington, D.C. Online bookstores include AALBC.com (founded 1998), Mahogany Books, and Hue-Man Bookstore.

**Black Power Movement Notes:**

The Black Power movement emerged in the U.S. as a counterculture within the civil rights movement, reacting against its moderate tendencies. It emphasized self-sufficiency and safety in redlined neighborhoods. Key figures include Stokely Carmichael (Kwame Ture) and Willie Ricks, who first used the term "Black Power" in 1966. The Black Panther Party (BPP), founded in 1966 by Huey P. Newton and Bobby Seale, became a cornerstone, influenced by pan-Africanism, black nationalism, and socialism. The movement escalated in the late 1960s, with the BPP using open-carry laws and documenting police brutality. The FBI's COINTELPRO targeted the BPP, leading to arrests and internal conflicts. The movement declined in the 1980s, with the BPP disbanding and the Black Liberation Army (BLA) becoming less active. The Australian Black Power movement was influenced by American activists, particularly in Sydney, Brisbane, and Melbourne. The legacy includes groups like the Black Radical Congress and the New Black Panther Party.

Born in Roxbury, Boston, Donaldson had a troubled childhood, including parental abandonment and substance abuse. He joined the Nation of Islam, changed his name to Hakim Jamal, and became a spokesman for Black Power. After Malcolm X's death, Jamal co-founded the US Organization with Maulana Karenga, but later left to establish the Malcolm X Foundation. He had relationships with Jean Seberg, Diana Athill, and Gale Benson. Benson was murdered in 1972 by Michael X. Jamal was killed in 1973 in Boston, with the murder attributed to a factional dispute. His autobiography was published in 1972.

He was born in Corinth, Mississippi, moved to Kentucky, and later lived in Indiana, Pittsburgh, Minneapolis, and Memphis. Knight married Sonia Sanchez (1968–1970) and Mary McAnally (1972–1977). His works include *Belly Song and Other Poems* (1973), *Born of a Woman* (1980), and *The Essential Etheridge Knight* (1986). He earned a bachelor’s degree in 1990 and taught at several universities. Rainbow Coalition (Fred Hampton) was founded April 4, 1969 in Chicago, Illinois by Fred Hampton of the Black Panther Party, William "Preacherman" Fesperman of the Young Patriots Organization, and José Cha Cha Jiménez of the Young Lords. The coalition included groups like the Lincoln Park Poor People's Coalition, Students for a Democratic Society, Brown Berets, American Indian Movement, and Red Guard Party. It focused on fighting poverty, corruption, racism, police brutality, and substandard housing. The coalition collapsed due to harassment by law enforcement, including the murder of Hampton. The Rainbow Coalition concept influenced later multicultural coalitions, including Reverend Jesse Jackson's Rainbow/PUSH and Barack Obama's political career. Fred Hampton and Jimenez were arrested in February 1969 for protesting welfare office mistreatment. The coalition also brokered treaties to end crime and gang violence. Chicago's segregation and Mayor Richard J. Daley's policies contributed to the coalition's formation.

Maulana Ndabezitha Karenga (born Ronald McKinley Everett, July 14, 1941) is an American activist, author, and professor of Africana studies. He created Kwanzaa in 1966, a pan-African holiday inspired by African "first fruit" traditions. Karenga was active in the Black Power movement, co-founding the US Organization in 1966, which later clashed with the Black Panther Party. In 1971, he was convicted of felony assault, torture, and false imprisonment, receiving a one-to-ten-year sentence. He was paroled in 1975. Karenga holds two doctorates: Political Science (1976) and Social Ethics (1994). He chairs the Africana Studies Department at California State University, Long Beach. Kwanzaa's seven principles, known as Nguzo Saba, include unity, self-determination, collective work, cooperative economics, purpose, creativity, and faith. Karenga authored several books, including "Introduction to Black Studies" and "Maat, the moral ideal in ancient Egypt."

Press TV, an Iranian state-owned news network, was launched on 2 July 2007 in Tehran. It aims to counter Western media by presenting an Iranian perspective, particularly on Middle Eastern affairs. Beckwith is known for works on abortion, including *Defending Life* (2007) and *Politically Correct Death* (1993). He returned to Catholicism in 2007, writing *Return to Rome* (2009). He has held academic positions at UNLV, Whittier College, Trinity International University, Princeton, Notre Dame, and the University of Colorado. Street punk is an urban working class-based subgenre of punk rock, emerging as a rebellion against the artistic pretensions of first-wave British punk. It developed from Oi! and hardcore punk, with the Exploited being a key band in defining its aesthetic. Street punk features flamboyant appearances, multi-colored hair, tattoos, and political slogans. It is characterized by single-note guitar lines, communal vocals, and lyrics addressing fighting, inner-city issues, and politics. The 1990s and 2000s saw a revival with bands like the Casualties, whose 2004 album *On the Front Line* peaked at number 8 on the Independent Albums chart. UK 82, also known as second wave punk, influenced street punk with its aggressive sound and themes of nuclear holocaust and unemployment. Key UK 82 bands include the Exploited, Discharge, and GBH. D-beat, a subgenre of street punk, developed from Discharge and is associated with anti-war and anarchist messages.

It is a form of Japanese erotica and prostitution request involving copious amounts of lubricant referred to as "lotion" in Japanese. Lotion can be used by rubbing it on another person, during sexual intercourse in a pool or bath filled with lotion, or by pouring it over participants during sex. Lotion is available in concentrated form, with a one-gallon concentrate yielding 6-10 gallons of lotion (J-Lube Lotion Concentrate). The main component in most lotion is polyacrylate. notes.note_text: Gary L. Bennett (born January 17, 1940) is an American scientist and engineer specializing in aerospace and energy. Bennett managed NASA's Advanced Space Power Systems program and was involved in the Pluto Fast Flyby (New Horizons) and TIMED missions. He directed safety and nuclear operations for radioisotope power sources on Galileo, Ulysses, Cassini, and New Horizons. He also worked on the NERVA program and at Idaho National Laboratory. Planetary protection aims to prevent biological contamination of celestial bodies and Earth. It includes forward (Earth to space) and back (space to Earth) contamination. The Outer Space Treaty (1967) and COSPAR guidelines form its legal and operational basis. COSPAR categorizes missions into five groups (I-V), with increasing sterilization requirements. Mars special regions require sterilization to Category IVc. The Coleman–Sagan equation calculates contamination probability, targeting less than 1/10,000 per mission. Containment and quarantine are required for restricted Category V sample returns. Decontamination methods include heat, hydrogen peroxide, and radiation. Challenges include impact prevention and debates over planetary protection necessity. The 2010 COSPAR workshop proposed extending protection to non-biological aspects and creating "Planetary Parks." The 2018 National Academies report urged broader planetary protection strategies.

Transit in astronomy refers to a celestial body passing between a larger body and an observer, appearing smaller. It differs from occultations where the nearer object appears larger. In the Solar System, Mercury and Venus transit the Sun, while Earth transits the Sun from Mars. Notable events include Mercury transiting the Sun from Venus on 27 June 1586. The Cassini–Huygens probe observed Venus transiting the Sun on 21 December 2012, and Curiosity observed Mercury transiting the Sun on 3 June 2014. The transit method detects exoplanets by measuring light curve dips. The probability equation is P_transit = (R_star + R_planet)/a. Hot Jupiters and red dwarf stars are favorable for detection. Contacts during transit include first to fourth contacts and greatest transit. Missions like HATNet, KELT, Kepler, and TESS use transit photometry. HATNet has northern and southern telescopes, KELT detects 1% flux dips, Kepler operated until 2018, and TESS launched in 2018 to survey the sky.

Roche limit: A distance in celestial mechanics where tidal forces from a primary body exceed a satellite's self-gravitation, causing disintegration. Named after Édouard Roche, calculated in 1848. Applies to satellites disintegrating due to tidal forces from their primary. Inside the Roche limit, material disperses; outside, it coalesces. The limit depends on the primary's radius and density ratio with the satellite. For rigid satellites, the Roche limit is $ d = R_M \left(2 \frac{\rho_M}{\rho_m}\right)^{1/3} $ or $ d = R_m \left(2 \frac{M_M}{M_m}\right)^{1/3} $. For fluid satellites, an approximate formula is $ d \approx 2.44R \left(\frac{\rho_M}{\rho_m}\right)^{1/3} $. Comet Shoemaker–Levy 9 fragmented within Jupiter's Roche limit in 1992, later impacting Jupiter in 1994. Exceptions to planetary rings within Roche limit include Saturn's E-Ring and Phoebe ring.

Ulysses was a joint ESA-NASA spacecraft launched in 1990 on a mission to study the Sun at all latitudes. It used a gravity assist from Jupiter to achieve an 80° orbital inclination. The spacecraft, originally named Odysseus, was renamed Ulysses in honor of Homer's hero and Dante's character. It was launched on October 6, 1990, aboard the Space Shuttle Discovery. Ulysses studied the Sun's polar regions from 1994–1995, and again in 2007–2008. It also studied comets, including Hyakutake (1996), McNaught-Hartley (2004), and McNaught (2007). The mission ended on June 30, 2009, due to power and communication failures. Ulysses had a mass of 371 kg and used a radioisotope thermoelectric generator (RTG) for power.
