She joined the Royal Shakespeare Company in 1957 and made her Broadway debut in 1966. She was nominated for four Tony Awards. She co-created the TV series "Upstairs, Downstairs" and "The House of Elliot." She wrote the screenplay for "Mrs. Dalloway" (1997). She was appointed CBE in 1990 and DBE in 2001. She was married to Julian Glover (1957–1966) and Bill Shepherd (1978–2016). She was diagnosed with breast cancer in 1995 and recovered. She authored an autobiography, "Will She Do?" and received honorary degrees from Oxford and City University London.

Sons and Lovers is a 1981 BBC television serial based on D. H. Lawrence's 1913 book of the same name. The serial was adapted by Trevor Griffiths and directed by Stuart Burge. It featured Eileen Atkins, Tom Bell, Karl Johnson, Lynn Dearth, and Leonie Mellinger. Originally broadcast as seven episodes, it was later aired in the United States by PBS's Masterpiece Theatre in 1982. In 1981, Griffiths expressed his motivation for adapting the work, highlighting Lawrence's celebration of dignity in working-class culture and critique of industrial societies. He noted the relevance of the themes in the context of high unemployment, mentioning over three million unemployed people at the time.

Jessica Swale (born 27 February 1982) is a British playwright, theatre director, and screenwriter. Her first play, *Blue Stockings*, premiered at Shakespeare's Globe in 2013. *Nell Gwynn* (2015) won the Olivier Award for Best New Comedy in 2016 after transferring to the West End. She directed *Summerland* (2020), a feature film. Swale studied drama at the University of Exeter and the Royal Central School of Speech and Drama. She worked with Max Stafford-Clark at Out of Joint Theatre Company and co-founded Red Handed Theatre Company. She directed plays at Shakespeare's Globe, including *Bedlam* (2010), and adapted works like *Sense and Sensibility* and *Far from the Madding Crowd*. Swale also wrote drama games books and is an associate artist with Youth Bridge Global. She lives in South London with photographer Michael Wharley.

Alex Michael Jennings (born 10 May 1957) is an English actor known for stage, screen, and television work. He won three Olivier Awards: Best Comedy Performance (1988) for *Too Clever by Half*, Best Actor (1996) for *Peer Gynt*, and Best Actor in a Musical (2003) for *My Fair Lady*. He portrayed Prince Charles in *The Queen* (2006) and Edward VIII in *The Crown* (2016–2017). Jennings trained at the Bristol Old Vic Theatre School and studied English and Theatre at the University of Warwick. His film roles include *The Wings of the Dove* (1997), *Babel* (2006), *Belle* (2013), and *Mangrove* (2020). He has appeared in TV series like *Victoria* (2016–2019) and *A Very English Scandal* (2018). Jennings has worked extensively with the Royal Shakespeare Company and National Theatre, and has recorded audiobooks for BBC Radio 4.

Sarah Solemani (born 4 September 1982) is an English actress, writer, and activist. She starred in the BAFTA-winning sitcom *Him & Her* and played Miranda in *Bridget Jones's Baby*, earning an Evening Standard Best Actress nomination. She also appeared in *Bad Education* and *The Wrong Mans*. 

Born in London's Camden Borough, she attended Henrietta Barnett School and studied Social and Political Sciences at New Hall, Cambridge. She joined the Footlights and performed in West End and National Theatre productions. Solemani wrote plays, including *The Cost of Things* (2010) and *The Baron* (2011), and adapted Jo Bloom's *Ridley Road* (2021). 

She wrote and starred in *Aphrodite Fry* (2013) and co-wrote *Chivalry* (2022). She contributed to publications like *The Guardian* and *Harper's Bazaar*. She won the Royal Television Society award for *Him & Her* (2011) and was named a Broadcast Hot Shot (2012). 

Solemani is an activist against the criminalisation of sex

Frances de la Tour (born 30 July 1944 in Bovingdon, Hertfordshire) is an English actress. She is known for her role as Miss Ruth Jones in the sitcom *Rising Damp* (1974–1978) and for playing Madame Olympe Maxime in *Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire* (2005). She won a Tony Award for Best Featured Actress in a Play for *The History Boys* (2006) and three Olivier Awards. She was born to Moyra and Charles de la Tour, with French, Greek, and Irish ancestry. She is the sister of actor Andy de la Tour and was married to playwright Tom Kempinski. She has a son and daughter. De la Tour performed in *The History Boys* on stage and film, and in *Peace Mom* (2005). She appeared in *Vicious* (2013–2016) and *Outlander* (2016). She is a socialist and was a member of the Workers' Revolutionary Party in the 1970s.

input: What is the name of this suburb within the Central Coast Council local government area, where Tessa, of Microwave Jenny, grew up?

notes.note_text: Avoca Beach is a coastal suburb in New South Wales, Australia, part of the Central Coast region, approximately 95 km north of Sydney. It is known for surfing, tourism, and has a variety of amenities including restaurants, a post office, and a historic cinema. Located 17 km east-southeast of Gosford, it is bordered by Bulbararing Lagoon, Saltwater Creek, and the ocean. Originally inhabited by the Darkinjung and Awabakal people, the area was granted to John Moore in 1830, with official deeds in 1839. Residential development began in the 20th century, making it a popular retreat. The 2016 census recorded a population of 4,584, with a median age of 41 and median weekly income of $764. The median house price in 2020 was $1,150,000. Politically, it falls under the Division of Robertson federally and the electorate of Terrigal state-wise.

Hamlyn Terrace is a suburb located in the Central Coast region of New South Wales, Australia. It falls under the Central Coast Council local government area. Previously, the suburb was part of Warnervale and is now part of the Warnervale development precinct. The suburb is divided between two governmental wards within Central Coast Council: the northern portion is in the Budgiewoi ward, while the remainder is in the Wyong ward. The passage does not mention specific dates or numerical data. The key entities are Hamlyn Terrace, New South Wales, Central Coast Council, Warnervale, Budgiewoi ward, and Wyong ward. The relationships include administrative divisions and historical affiliations.

Woy Woy Bay is a suburb in the Central Coast region of New South Wales, Australia, under the Central Coast Council. Most of the area is part of Brisbane Water National Park, with a small community including a community hall, public reserve, and wharf. The suburb is popular with boaters on weekends. The main road is Taylor Street.

Notable residents include John Della Bosca (born 1956), a former New South Wales Legislative Council member (1999–2010), and Belinda Neal (born 1963), a former Australian House of Representatives member (2007–2010), and former New South Wales Legislative Council and Gosford City Council member (1994–1998).

Phegans Bay is a suburb located in the Central Coast Council local government area of New South Wales, Australia. It is situated on the Central Coast. The suburb is 6 kilometres (4 miles) west of Woy Woy. Phegans Bay is positioned between Brisbane Water National Park and Woy Woy Inlet. The passage provides geographical and administrative details about Phegans Bay, including its proximity to other locations and its local government jurisdiction. No dates or additional historical information are mentioned in the source material. The notes capture the key entities, locations, and relationships as presented in the passage.

Umina Beach is a suburb in New South Wales, located 85 km north of Sydney and 111 km south of Newcastle. It is part of the Central Coast Council and known as "The Peninsula," including towns like Woy Woy and Ettalong Beach. The main street, West Street, has retail stores like Coles, Woolworths, and Bunnings. Umina Beach has two sections: Umina Beach (southwest) and Ocean Beach (northeast), both with Surf Life Saving Clubs. The area is geographically on the north side of Broken Bay, influenced by Hawkesbury Sandstone formations. The name "Umina" comes from an Aboriginal word meaning "Place of sleep." European contact began in 1788. Umina Public School (1956) and Brisbane Water Secondary College serve the area. The Peninsula Chamber of Commerce represents the town centre. Umina Beach celebrated its 100th anniversary in 2014. Notable residents include Belinda Emmett, Mark Geyer, and James Harrison OAM.

Shelly Beach is a coastal suburb in the Central Coast region of New South Wales, Australia. It is located east of Tuggerah Lake, bordering the Pacific Ocean south of The Entrance. It falls under the Central Coast Council local government area. The suburb is 66 km south of Newcastle and 93 km north of Sydney. Shelly Beach is known as one of the most popular surfing beaches on the Central Coast. The Shelly Beach Golf Club, previously known as Tuggerah Lakes Gold Club, is an 18-hole golf course established in 1930, located at the eastern end of Shelly Beach Road. It moved to its current location in 1954. Notable local entities include the Shelly Beach Surf Club and the Shelly Beach Fossils soccer club. Red Bus Services operates routes 11, 12, 21, 22, and 23 through Shelly Beach, with Bus 21 running from The Entrance North to Gosford. Notable people include Nikki Garrett (golfer) and Banjo Paterson (poet). Accommodation options include Shelly Beach Cabins, Bluewater Resort, and Sun Valley Tourist Park.

Magenta is a coastal location in the Central Coast region of New South Wales, Australia, part of the Central Coast Council local government area. It contains a significant portion of Wyrrabalong National Park. Magenta was gazetted as a suburb in 1991. Previously, it was used for rutile mining and as a garbage tip for The Entrance. Wilfred Barrett Drive, named after a Wyong Shire President, runs through Magenta from south to north, connecting The Entrance and Toukley. The road was designated part of the Central Coast Highway in 2006. Magenta Shores is a golf resort with an 18-hole course, private housing, and a resort facility.

Gorokan is a suburb in the Central Coast region of New South Wales, Australia, part of the Central Coast Council local government area. The name "Gorokan" means "The Morning Dawn" in the Awabakal language. The area has two schools: Gorokan Public School and Gorokan High School. Electricity was introduced as part of a £42,000 reticulation program under the Brisbane Water County Council. Gorokan is located on Lake Tuggerah and has been a holiday destination since at least 1923, when the Quoy family purchased land and built holiday homes. In 1956, the Gedling family (Gordon and Margaret Gedling) constructed a holiday house on the waterfront.

Kulnura is a suburb in the Central Coast region of New South Wales, Australia, located north of Mangrove Mountain along George Downes Drive. Named in 1914 by early pioneers, its population is approximately 600. The area relies on fruit and cattle industries, with many residents commuting to Gosford, Wyong, and Sydney. Kulnura features Mangrove Creek Dam, the largest catchment area on the Central Coast, with a capacity of 190,000 ML. It also hosts the Mangrove Mountain Bottlers Pty Ltd, which bottles still water. The Paintball Place, open to those over 16, is another attraction. Kulnura extends from Bloodtree Road to Great Northern Road, encompassing the Mangrove Creek reservoir. Key locations include the Kulnura General Store-café, Kulnura Public School at 9 Williams Road, and the Bloodtree Festival, held annually at Kulnura Oval for the past five years.

Microwave Jenny is an Australian pop/folk/jazz duet consisting of Tessa Nuku (vocals) and Brendon Boney (guitar, vocals). Both have Indigenous backgrounds; Brendon was born in Wagga Wagga, and Tessa was born in Ulladulla, New South Wales, later moving to Umina Beach. Brendon voiced Willie in the film Bran Nue Dae and has a solo project called The Magpie Swoop. The duo, married with a daughter, performs live in acoustic, trio, quartet, or full band formats. They perform at festivals like Bluesfest and Woodford Folk Festival and supported Thirsty Merc in 2011. Influences include James Taylor, Janis Ian, Bill Withers, and Van Morrison. They received the 2009 Peter Garrett Breakthrough Grant and Brendon won an APRA award in 2011. They were nominated for a Deadly Award in 2009. Their discography includes two EPs: "Summer" and "Crazy, Crazy Things," with tracks listed.

input: Who won more awards, Brothers Quay or Jake Kasdan?

notes.note_text:
**Bad Teacher (2011)**  
- **Director:** Jake Kasdan  
- **Screenplay:** Lee Eisenberg and Gene Stupnitsky  
- **Studio:** Columbia Pictures  
- **Release Date:** June 24, 2011 (U.S.)  
- **Cast:** Cameron Diaz, Justin Timberlake, Lucy Punch, John Michael Higgins, Jason Segel  
- **Plot:** Elizabeth Halsey, a lazy middle school teacher in Chicago, reforms after her fiancé dumps her. She attempts to raise money for breast enlargement by manipulating students and parents. She steals state test answers, leading to her arrest, but reforms by the end.  
- **Box Office:** $216.2 million worldwide, $100.3 million in the U.S. and Canada.  
- **Critical Response:** Rotten Tomatoes (45% approval), Metacritic (47/100).  
- **Accolades:** DVD/Blu-ray release on October 18, 2011.  
- **Sequel/TV:** Sony developed a sequel (no deal with Diaz) and a TV series (3 episodes aired, canceled in 2014).

"Pilot" is the first episode of the first season of *New Girl*, written by Elizabeth Meriwether and directed by Jake Kasdan. It premiered on Fox in the United States on September 20, 2011, drawing 10.1 million viewers (4.7 rating) and surpassing the lead-in show *Glee*'s 8.9 million viewers (5.4 rating). The episode features Jess Day, who moves in with three roommates—Nick, Schmidt, and Coach—after a breakup. Jess attempts to seduce her ex-boyfriend Spencer but fails, leading to her emotional turmoil. The episode includes a scene where Jess strips in a cab and tries a striptease with pillows. The production notes mention Zooey Deschanel's comments about her character resembling her younger self. Jake Kasdan was nominated for a Primetime Emmy Award for Outstanding Directing for a Comedy Series for this episode.

"The Piano Tuner of Earthquakes" is a 2005 animated drama film by the Brothers Quay. It is their second feature-length film and their first in over ten years. The film features Amira Casar, Gottfried John, Assumpta Serna, and Cesar Sarachu. The plot follows Malvina van Stille, a 19th-century opera singer murdered on-stage by Dr. Emmanuel Droz. She is reanimated and forced to perform in a grim production recreating her abduction. Piano tuner Felisberto activates seven automata to prepare for the performance. Malvina, now amnesiac, is drawn to Felisberto due to his resemblance to her former fiancé Adolfo. The film is listed in the "List of stop-motion films." External links include Metacritic, Rotten Tomatoes, MovieScore Media, IMDb, and AllMovie. A review by Jeannette Catsoulis appeared in The New York Times on 17 November 2006.

Sex Tape is a 2014 American sex comedy film directed by Jake Kasdan and distributed by Sony Pictures Releasing. It was written by Jason Segel, Nicholas Stoller, and Kate Angelo and stars Segel, Cameron Diaz, Rob Corddry, Ellie Kemper, and Rob Lowe. The film follows a married couple, Jay and Annie Hargrove, who make a sex tape but lose it, leading to a frantic search. The film was produced by Columbia Pictures and released on July 18, 2014. It grossed $126.1 million worldwide against a $40 million budget. It received generally negative reviews. The film was shot in Newton, Massachusetts, with Hank's house located in Weston. It was rejected by India's CBFC initially but was accepted after changes and released on August 29, 2014. The film opened in 2,457 theaters in North America, earning $14.6 million in its opening weekend.

Jake Kasdan (born October 28, 1974) is an American filmmaker and actor. He directed Walk Hard (2007), Bad Teacher (2011), Sex Tape (2014), Jumanji: Welcome to the Jungle (2017), and Jumanji: The Next Level (2019). He was born in Detroit, Michigan, to Meg Goldman and Lawrence Kasdan, and has a younger brother, Jon Kasdan. Kasdan directed seven theatrical films and worked on TV shows like Freaks and Geeks and Undeclared. He was nominated for a Golden Globe for Walk Hard (2007). He signed with 20th Century Fox Television in 2012 and directed The Grinder (2015 pilot). In 2019, he reupped with 20th Century Fox. He is married to Inara George, and they have three children, including twins. He is attached to direct Calico Joe and served as an executive producer for XYZ (ABC pilot).

Stephen and Timothy Quay, known as the Brothers Quay, are American stop-motion animators born on June 17, 1947. They moved to England in 1969 to study at the Royal College of Art. They formed Koninck Studios in 1980. Their works are influenced by Polish animators Walerian Borowczyk and Jan Lenica, writers like Franz Kafka and Bruno Schulz, and composers such as Leoš Janáček and Leszek Jankowski. Notable films include "Street of Crocodiles" (1986) and "Institute Benjamenta" (1995). They received the 1998 Drama Desk Award for Outstanding Set Design. Their films often feature puppets made of organic and inorganic materials, with minimal dialogue and reliance on music scores. They have created music videos for artists like Peter Gabriel and Michael Penn. The Quay Brothers have exhibited their work internationally and were featured in a 2015 retrospective at MoMA. They have also worked on stage designs for productions by Richard Jones.

Speechless is an American sitcom that aired on ABC from September 21, 2016, to April 12, 2019. Created by Scott Silveri, it was greenlit on May 13, 2016, and premiered in the fall of 2016. The series follows the DiMeo family, including JJ, a teenager with cerebral palsy. The show was canceled on May 10, 2019, after three seasons due to low ratings. It received positive critical reviews, with a 98% rating on Rotten Tomatoes. Main cast includes Minnie Driver, John Ross Bowie, Micah Fowler, and Cedric Yarbrough. The show was praised for its authentic portrayal of a family with a disabled teenager. It aired on Tuesdays at 9:30 P.M. EST initially, then moved to Fridays at 8:30 P.M. EST for its third season. The final season had around 2.3 million live viewers.

**Notes:**

*Walk Hard: The Dewey Cox Story* (2007) is a comedy film directed by Jake Kasdan and written by Kasdan and Judd Apatow. It stars John C. Reilly as Dewey Cox, a fictional rock and roll star. The film parodies biopics like *Ray* (2004) and *Walk the Line* (2005), referencing musicians such as Ray Charles, Johnny Cash, Roy Orbison, and others. It was released on December 21, 2007, and grossed $20 million against a $35 million budget. It received positive reviews, with a 74% approval rating on Rotten Tomatoes. John C. Reilly was nominated for a Golden Globe. The film's soundtrack includes songs by Dan Bern, Mike Viola, and others, with "Beautiful Ride" as the final song. Dewey Cox is portrayed as dying in 2007, with a post-credits scene showing him in 2002. The film became a cult classic.

Weird Loners is an American sitcom created by Michael J. Weithorn, ordered straight-to-series by Fox in 2014. The 6-episode first season premiered on March 31, 2015, and was canceled by Fox on May 11, 2015. The series was executive produced by Weithorn and Jake Kasdan. Kevin Reilly, the network president who ordered the series in 2013, was fired months later. The show follows four individuals in Queens, New York, who form an unlikely bond after being thrust into each other's lives. Caryn Goldfarb (Becki Newton) is a dental hygienist who calls off her engagement. Stosh Lewandowski (Zachary Knighton) moves in with his cousin Eric (Nate Torrence) after losing his job. Zara Sandhu (Meera Rohit Kumbhani) befriends Eric. The show received mixed reviews, with Rotten Tomatoes giving it 44% based on 25 critics. Neil Genzlinger of The New York Times gave a positive review, while Gwen Ihnat of The A.V. Club gave it a "B+" rating.

input: What stagecoach robber did Frederick John Fulton prosecute?

notes.note_text: John Fulton (1803–1853) was a Scottish instrument maker and self-taught astronomer, originally a cobbler. He built three orrerys in his workshop in Fenwick, now demolished. His third orrery, completed in 1833, is on display in Glasgow's Kelvingrove Art Gallery and Museum. It measures 1000mm x 3000mm x 3000mm, has 175 wheels, and over 200 moving parts. It was awarded a silver medal by the Society of Arts and was purchased by Glasgow in 1869. A local story claims he used his grandmother’s candlesticks for the first orrery. He was appointed instrument maker to King William IV and later retired to Fenwick, where he is buried in Fenwick Kirk graveyard. His father was a cobbler and library member in Fenwick. The John Fulton Memorial Hall in Fenwick, a Category C listed building, was previously the Guthrie Memorial Free Church and opened in 1920 after fundraising in 1919.

Davie Fulton (Edmund Davie Fulton), born March 10, 1916, in Kamloops, British Columbia, was a Canadian politician and judge. He served in World War II with the Seaforth Highlanders, later becoming a platoon and company commander. His brother, John "Moose" Fulton, was in the Royal Canadian Air Force and went missing in action in 1942; Kamloops honored him with the Moose Squadron in 1943 and named its airport Fulton Field in 1944. After the war, Fulton was brought into politics by the Conservatives and won a seat in the House of Commons in 1945. He introduced legislation to ban crime comics in 1949. He served as Minister of Justice (1957–1963) and Minister of Public Works (1962). He later became a justice on the British Columbia Supreme Court (1973–1981) and a commissioner on the International Joint Commission (1986–1992). He was made an Officer of the Order of Canada in 1992 and died on May 22, 2000,

Harry Head (died 1881), known as Harry the Kid, was a cattle rustler and stagecoach robber. On March 15, 1881, he and three companions—Bill Leonard, Jim Crane, and Luther King—robbed a Wells Fargo stagecoach near Contention City, Arizona Territory. The stagecoach carried $26,000 and eight passengers. During the robbery, Bob Paul, the guard, was killed, and passenger Pete Roerig was also killed. There was speculation that Doc Holliday was involved, but he claimed an alibi and was later released. After the robbery, Paul and Wyatt Earp offered a $2,000 reward for information. Head and Leonard were eventually killed in Eureka, New Mexico, during a robbery. Luther King was arrested but escaped. Crane and others later hunted the Haslett brothers.

The Dillinger Escape Plan (DEP) was an American metalcore band from Morris Plains, New Jersey, formed in early 1997. Originally named Arcane, the band included Dimitri Minakakis (vocals), Ben Weinman (lead guitar), Derek Brantley (rhythm guitar), Adam Doll (bass, keyboards), and Chris Pennie (drums, keyboards). Brantley left after two shows, and the band recorded their debut EP as a four-piece. In 2000, Liam Wilson replaced Doll, and in 2001, Greg Puciato replaced Minakakis. Weinman was the only constant member. The band disbanded in December 2017 after releasing their sixth album, Dissociation. Key lineup changes included Benoit, Love, Tuttle, and Antreassian. Notable events include Doll's spinal injury in 1998, Weinman's temporary departure in 2006, and Pennie's departure to join Coheed and Cambria in 2007. The band's final tour ended with three shows in December 2017, featuring guest appearances by former members and Mike Patton.

Buck English (born Lawrence Buchanen English, 1855 – January 15, 1915) was an American Old West outlaw and stagecoach robber in Lake County, California. He earned the nickname "Buck" and was known for his rash and boastful nature. Born in Oregon, he became involved in criminal activities at a young age, including robbing a stagecoach in Lower Lake at 22. He targeted Wells Fargo strongboxes and operated near Middletown and Lower Lake. Buck engaged in duels, including one with Captain Good, and shot and killed a man in a skating rink. After serving time at San Quentin (1882), he returned to Middletown and continued his criminal activities. Captured on May 7, 1895, he was severely wounded but survived. He was involved in cattle rustling and other crimes. Buck died in San Francisco in 1915 of natural causes, unlike his brothers who died violently.

Bill Miner (Ezra Allen Miner), born December 27, 1846, in Vevay Township, Michigan, was an American bandit known as the "Grey Fox" or "Gentleman Bandit." He committed stagecoach robberies and popularized the phrase "Hands up!" Miner was arrested multiple times, including in California and British Columbia. He was involved in the 1904 Silverdale train robbery in British Columbia, though not conclusively linked. He was captured in 1907 near Kamloops after a failed robbery, convicted, and imprisoned. He escaped in 1907 and later robbed in the U.S. He died in 1913 in Georgia from gastritis. Miner's legacy includes the Keg Steakhouse & Bar's Billy Miner Pie, a mural in Kamloops, the Billy Miner Pub in Maple Ridge, and the 1982 film "The Grey Fox." He is buried in Milledgeville, Georgia, with a corrected headstone. Mount Miner in Princeton, BC, and Billy's Restaurant in Princeton are named after him. A Red Ale titled "Hands Up!" was brewed by Tin Whistle Brewing Co. in 2014.

"The Grey Fox" is a 1982 Canadian biographical Western film directed by Phillip Borsos and written by John Hunter. Based on the true story of Bill Miner, an American stagecoach robber who committed his first Canadian train robbery on 10 September 1904. The film stars Richard Farnsworth as Miner, with supporting roles by Jackie Burroughs, Ken Pogue, Wayne Robson, Gary Reineke, and Timothy Webber. The film was shot in British Columbia and Washington, with locations including Fort Steele and the British Columbia Railway. It was funded by 696 investors at $5,000 each, had a budget of $3,480,000, and cost $4,500,000 to make. Released in Toronto on 16 December 1982, it grossed over $6 million. Nominated for thirteen Genie Awards in 1983, winning seven, including Best Picture and Best Director. The film was restored in 4K and re-released in April 2020. It was designated a "masterwork" by the Audio-Visual Preservation Trust of Canada.

Douglas Squire Irving Burrows CBE (Civil) MBE (Military) (7 August 1915 – 10 December 1982) was an Australian stock broker, businessman, and philanthropist. He co-founded the Children's Medical Research Foundation and served as Chairman of the Management Committee from 1970. From 1970 until his death, he was President of the Royal Alexandra Hospital for Children. Born in Sydney, he was educated at Newington College and rowed in the 1st IV. He enlisted in the Australian Army in 1939, serving in North Africa, Greece, and New Guinea. He was made an MBE in 1946. He married Valma Ashcroft in 1942; they had three children. Valma was appointed to the Royal Alexandra Hospital for Children board in 1973. Burrows was made a CBE in 1979 and the Douglas Burrows Chair of Paediatrics and Child Health was established in 1983 in his honor.

John Fulton "Jack" Folinsbee (1892–1972) was an American painter known for his impressionist scenes of New Hope, Pennsylvania, and Lambertville, New Jersey. Born in Buffalo, New York, he contracted polio at 14, leaving him wheelchair-bound. He studied with Jonas Lie, Birge Harrison, and John Carlson, and later with Frank Vincent DuMond. He married Ruth Baldwin in 1914 and moved to New Hope in 1916, where he painted landscapes and marine scenes. He was a founding member of Phillips' Mill and the Bucks County Playhouse. His work includes "Winter Nocturne" (1926) and "Zero Morning" (1970). He won numerous awards, including the 1952 Palmer Marine Prize for "Off Seguin (Ellingwood Rock)." He taught Peter G. Cook, his son-in-law, and was a member of the National Academy of Design and the American Academy of Arts and Letters. His works are in major museums, and his legacy is documented in Kirsten M. Jensen's biography.

Frederick John Fulton, KC (December 8, 1862 – July 25, 1936) was a British-born Canadian lawyer and politician. He practiced law in Kamloops, British Columbia. He served in the British Columbia Legislative Assembly from 1900 to 1909, holding cabinet roles including President of the Executive Council, Minister of Education, Provincial Secretary, Attorney General, and Chief Commissioner of Lands and Works. As Attorney General, he prosecuted and convicted Bill Miner. He was elected to the House of Commons of Canada in 1917 as a Unionist under Prime Minister Borden and served until 1920. In 1906, he married Winnifred M. Davie, daughter of Hon. A.E.B. Davie. They had four sons, including Davie Fulton, a Kamloops lawyer, provincial and federal politician, and judge.

input: When was the plaintiff in the 1892 Barbed Wire Patent Case born?

notes.note_text: Cheval de frise is a defensive obstacle, originally from ancient China, used as anti-cavalry and anti-ship barriers. It consists of a frame with spikes. The term "cheval de frise" translates to "Frisian horse" in French, referencing the Frisian people's use of cavalry. The concept was adopted in Europe during the Middle Ages and became common in medieval fortifications. During the American Civil War, Confederates used it more than Union forces. In World War I, it was used to plug gaps in barbed wire, and in World War II, in jungle fighting. The American Revolutionary War saw its use by Thaddeus Kosciuszko and Robert Erskine to block British ships on the Delaware and Hudson Rivers. A cheval de frise was recovered from the Delaware River in 2007. A promontory in the UK is named Chevaux de Frise Point.

Jacob Haish (March 9, 1826 – February 19, 1926) was an inventor of barbed wire, known for his "S-barb" design, which was patented in August 1875. He was born in Baden, Germany, and immigrated to the U.S. in 1835, settling in Illinois in 1845. He married Sophie Ann Brown in 1847 and moved to DeKalb in 1853, where he worked as a carpenter and architect. Haish's barbed wire competed with other manufacturers in DeKalb, Illinois. He patented three styles of barbed fencing by June 1874. His patent was challenged in court, and the U.S. Supreme Court ruled against him in 1895. In 1893, DeKalb established a public library, which later received a $150,000 gift from Haish in his will, leading to the creation of the Haish Memorial Library in 1926. The library moved locations twice, first to the city hall and then to the DeKalb Daily Chronicle building in 19

Concertina wire, also known as Dannert wire, is a type of barbed wire or razor wire formed in large coils that can be expanded like a concertina. It is used in military and non-military settings, including prisons, detention camps, and borders. During World War I, soldiers created concertina wire from ordinary barbed wire, and today it is factory-made. Concertina wire was developed further by German Horst Dannert in the 1930s, resulting in self-supporting wire that required no vertical posts. Dannert wire was imported into Britain before World War II and was sometimes made with low manganese steel, known as "Yellow Dannert." Triple concertina wire is a barrier made of three concertina sections joined by twists of wire. Concertina wire is sometimes mistakenly called "Constantine" wire, a term that originated from a misunderstanding of the word "concertina." Razor wire, sometimes called Constantine wire, consists of a single wire with periodic teeth.

Wire obstacles are defensive structures made from barbed wire, barbed tape, or concertina wire, used to slow down or channel enemy forces. They were first used by the Union Army during the Battle of Fort Sanders in the American Civil War. The Royal Danish Army used wire fences during the Second Schleswig War. Wire obstacles gained prominence during the Second Boer War and reached their peak in World War I, where they were used to funnel troops into killing zones. Some entanglements were tens of meters thick and several meters deep. During World War I, wire obstacles were often combined with machine guns and mines. In the Korean War, elaborate wire obstacles were used, and they continue to be used on the Korean Demilitarized Zone. Modern wire obstacles are usually simple and temporary. Tanks and armored vehicles can flatten wire obstacles, but they may become entangled. Anti-personnel and anti-tank mines, tripwires, and other methods can enhance the effectiveness of wire obstacles.

- **Case**: Barbed Wire Patent Case, 143 U.S. 275 (1892)  
- **Parties**: Joseph Glidden (plaintiff), USPTO  
- **Inventor**: Lucian Smith (original inventor in 1867)  
- **Glidden's Invention**: Improved barbed wire with a method to hold barbs in place (1874)  
- **Patent Claim**: A twisted fence wire with transverse spur wire bent and clamped by another wire strand.  
- **USPTO Decision**: Denied Glidden's patent, stating lack of novelty.  
- **Supreme Court**: Reversed the decision, ruling in favor of Glidden.  
- **Reasoning**: Glidden's invention was deemed novel enough and significantly improved the product.  
- **Dissent**: Justice Field argued no true novelty existed.  
- **Significance**: Established first-to-file and scope of novelty in patent law.  
- **Outcome**: Glidden gained exclusive rights, founded Barb Fence Company in Dekalb, Illinois, and became wealthy.

Joseph F. Glidden House, located in DeKalb, Illinois, was built in 1861 and designed by Jacob Haish. It is a French Colonial style home with elements of Greek Revival architecture. The house was added to the National Register of Historic Places in 1973. The barn, significant in Glidden's invention of barbed wire, was added to the Register in 2002. The Glidden House and barn are part of the Joseph F. Glidden Homestead and Historical Center. The house features a fieldstone foundation, original front porch, and a basement where Glidden experimented with barbed wire. The barn, constructed around 1871, is two stories high and made of soft brick. The property also includes the remains of a windmill foundation. Glidden's barbed wire, called "The Winner," revolutionized westward settlement. The house underwent restoration in 2006, and a fundraising drive aimed to expand the site into a museum.

The Devils Rope Barbed Wire Museum is located in McLean, Texas, United States. It was officially opened in 1991 and focuses on barbed wire and its history. The museum is housed in a converted brassiere factory. It features exhibits on barbed wire, fencing tools, and ranching heritage. It holds the largest collection of published material on barbed wire. The museum includes collections from private wire collectors across the U.S., a reference library with extensive patent information, a Dust Bowl exhibit, salesman samples, warfare wire, and artifacts related to the Texas portion of Historic Route 66. The museum is dedicated to the history of barbed wire and its cultural and historical significance.

The Kansas Barbed Wire Museum is located in La Crosse, Kansas, and is known as the “Barbed Wire Capital of the World.” It displays over 2,000 forms of barbed wire and its history. Established in 1970 in a storefront on Main Street, downtown La Crosse. By 1990, a new building was constructed adjacent to the Post Rock Museum and Rush County Historical Museum in Grass Park. In 2004, an addition was built to house the Antique Barbed Wire Society and the Larry Greer Research Center. The Antique Barbed Wire Society is an international organization focused on collecting, preserving, and interpreting barbed wire history. The Larry Greer Research Center contains publications and patents related to barbed wire. The museum's address is 120 W. 1st Street, La Crosse, KS 67548.

Joseph Farwell Glidden (1813–1906) was an American businessman and farmer, inventor of modern barbed wire. He patented his design on November 24, 1874, called "The Winner." He and Isaac L. Ellwood formed the Barb Fence Company in DeKalb, Illinois, which later became American Steel and Wire. Glidden won a legal battle in 1892, but his patent expired that year. He earned $1,000,000 in royalties. He donated 63 acres for Northern Illinois State Normal School (now Northern Illinois University) in 1898. He also established the Frying Pan Ranch in Texas in 1881, which was later deeded to his son-in-law, William Henry Bush. Glidden married Clarissa Foster (1837), who died in 1846; then Lucinda Warne (1851), who died in 1895. He had a daughter, Elva Frances, who died in 1906. The town of Glidden, Iowa, is named after him.

"Hanging on the Old Barbed Wire" is a British World War I war song (Roud 9618). It sarcastically describes soldiers not in the combat zone and ends with the battalion "hanging on the old barbed wire," referencing the barbed wire fence separating front-line trenches from no man's land. Soldiers who went over the top were often shot and caught in the wire. The song's final two lines are consistent across versions, with variations in other lines, such as "if you want to find the privates" and a verse mentioning a colonel on leave. The song has been covered by Chumbawamba (1988, 2003), 1914 (2018), Maruta Kommand (2000), and appears in John Roberts and Tony Barrand's "Great War Trilogy" on the 1992 album "A Present from the Gentlemen." It was unpopular with officers due to its perceived negative impact on morale.

Greg Gianforte (born April 17, 1961) is an American businessman, politician, and software engineer serving as Montana's 25th governor since 2021. He previously served as a U.S. Representative from Montana's at-large district (2017–2021). Gianforte co-founded RightNow Technologies, acquired by Oracle in 2011 for $1.5 billion. He was convicted of misdemeanor assault in 2017 after body-slamming journalist Ben Jacobs during a campaign event. He was fined, ordered to community service, and anger management therapy. Ryan Zinke (born November 1, 1961) is an American politician and businessman who served as the U.S. Representative for Montana's 1st congressional district since 2023. He was appointed U.S. Secretary of the Interior by President Donald Trump in 2017, serving until 2019 due to ethical scandals. Zinke, a former Navy SEAL, supported military action against ISIS and opposed the Affordable Care Act and environmental regulations. As Secretary, he opened federal lands for resource extraction and faced investigations over misuse of taxpayer funds, including a $200,000 flagpole expense. He resigned in 2019 amid misconduct allegations. Zinke's career includes roles in the Montana Senate (2009–2013) and the U.S. House (2015–2017). He ran for Congress in 2022 and won, representing Montana's 1st district. Zinke's tenure as Secretary involved reducing national monuments, rescinding a lead bullet ban, and facing controversies over travel expenses and political donations. He later joined a cryptocurrency firm and ran for re-election in 2022.

Kevin Aguiar is an American politician born on September 7, 1972. He represented the 7th Bristol district in the Massachusetts House of Representatives. Aguiar was first elected in a 2008 special election following Robert Correia's resignation to become Mayor of Fall River, Massachusetts. From 2002 to 2009, he served as a member of the Fall School Committee. In the 2012 Democratic primary, Aguiar was defeated by challenger Alan Silvia, who succeeded him.

Mike Aguirre (born 1949), City Attorney of San Diego from 2004 to 2008. He ran for mayor in 2013 but lost to Kevin Faulconer. Aguirre's father was of Spanish and Mexican descent; mother of Mexican descent. Served as Assistant U.S. Attorney, then assistant counsel to the U.S. Senate's Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations. Focused on securities fraud in private practice. In 1990, filed a successful federal voting rights lawsuit against San Diego's redistricting. Defended UFW in 1993, lost trial but case overturned on appeal. In 1996, challenged a San Diego-Chargers stadium contract, leading to renegotiation in 1998. Addressed San Diego's pension crisis as City Attorney, reducing unfunded liabilities. Represented Ruth Hendricks in San Onofre nuclear plant settlement challenges.

He served in various parliamentary roles until 2001, when he left politics to become headmaster of Summer Fields School, effective September 2010. She served on the European Economic and Social Committee. She studied a BSc in government, politics, and modern history at Brunel University and an MA in education from the Open University. She was a member of Barnet London Borough Council (2006–2010). She was a member of the Committee on Women's Rights and Gender Equality, the Committee on the Environment, Public Health and Food Safety, and a substitute on the Special Committee on Organised Crime, Corruption and Money Laundering. She opposed the EU financial transaction tax and Iceland's EU accession due to the Icesave dispute. She married Zacharias Yannakoudakis in 1983 and has three children. The family resides in Barnet.

He was accused of allowing an Arab businessman to pay for his Paris hotel stay during his time as Minister of State for Defence Procurement. Aitken was ordained as an Anglican priest in 2019. DNA testing in 1999 confirmed he was the biological father of Petrina Khashoggi. Aitken's paternity was questioned, with claims he was the child of Prince Bernhard of the Netherlands and Penelope Aitken. He wrote several books, including "Pride and Perjury" and "Nazarbayev

Christine Hamilton (née Holman), born 10 November 1949, is an English media personality and author. She is married to Neil Hamilton, a former Conservative MP for Tatton. The couple became prominent UKIP supporters; Neil ran for a local council seat in 2014 and was on UKIP's National Executive Committee in 2011. They worked together as MPs' secretaries, with Christine serving Neil after their 1983 marriage. Neil was involved in the Cash-for-questions affair and later faced a libel case against Mohamed Al-Fayed, leading to his bankruptcy. Gyles Daubeney Brandreth (born 8 March 1948) is an English broadcaster, writer, and former Conservative MP for Chester (1992–1997). He proposed the Marriage Act 1994. Known for his humorous jumpers, he co-founded Gyles & George knitwear with George Hostler. He has appeared on BBC and Channel 4 shows, including Countdown, The One Show, and QI. Brandreth wrote books on Scrabble, words, and royal families, including "Philip and Elizabeth: Portrait of a Marriage" (2004) and "Charles and Camilla: Portrait of a Love Affair" (2005). The baronetcy passed to his second and only surviving son, Clive Bossom, who became the 2nd Baronet. Bruce Bossom, Clive's son, is the 3rd Baronet. notes.note_text: "You're the Apple of My Eye" is a 1956 song written by Otis Blackwell, initially recorded by The Four Lovers, a precursor to The Four Seasons. The group, consisting of Frankie Valli, Nick and Tommy DeVito, and Hank Majewski, was signed to RCA Victor after an executive saw their performance. The single, released in May 1956, reached #62 on the Billboard Hot 100 and earned an Ed Sullivan Show appearance. It was a last-minute substitution for "Don't Be Cruel," which Elvis Presley later recorded. The Four Lovers' other 1956 single, "Honey Love"/"Please Don't Leave Me," included covers of R&B hits. The group's only chart success was "Apple of My Eye," which was re-recorded by The Four Seasons in 1962. The Four Lovers disbanded in 1957 but later became The Four Seasons in 1961. The song is featured in the musical "Jersey Boys."

"Dawn (Go Away)" is a song written by Bob Gaudio and Sandy Linzer, recorded by The Four Seasons in November 1963. It reached No. 3 on the Billboard Hot 100 on February 29, 1964, and was the 25th biggest hit of 1964. The song was released in January 1964 by Philips Records, a subsidiary of Mercury Records. The Four Seasons were involved in a royalty dispute with Vee-Jay Records, which was settled in 1965. The single version had a two-line introduction and was never recorded in true stereo. Early stereo releases were rechanneled, while later versions, including those from the Edizione d'Oro album, featured different takes. The mono version with the introduction was 2 minutes 45 seconds, while the stereo version was 2 minutes 30 seconds. "Dawn (Go Away)" was the only Philips single by The Four Seasons without the "featuring the 'sound' of Frankie Valli" credit.

"Watch the Flowers Grow" is a song composed by L. Russell Brown and Raymond Bloodworth, popularized by The Four Seasons in 1967. It was released after The Beach Boys' Pet Sounds and The Beatles' Sgt. Pepper's Lonely Hearts Club Band. The single peaked at #30 on the Billboard Hot 100. The Four Seasons' music was losing favor with the public; their next single, a cover of "Will You Love Me Tomorrow," reached #24, their last Top 40 hit until "Who Loves You" in 1975. Billboard described the song as a "timely, easy-beat ballad" and one of the group's "most unusual entries." Cash Box called it "gently pulsing, melodic, romp." L. Russell Brown went on to compose (or co-compose) several hit records in the 1970s, including tracks recorded by Dawn featuring Tony Orlando.

Gloaming (1915–1932) was a New Zealand-based Thoroughbred racehorse with 67 race starts, 57 wins (including 39 Principal Races), and 9 seconds. He set the Australasian record of 19 successive wins (jointly with Desert Gold, Black Caviar, and Winx) and still holds the 45-second four-furlong record. Owned by George D. Greenwood, he was trained in New Zealand and raced from age three to nine. Gloaming defeated champions like Desert Gold, Beauford, and The Hawk. He won major races in Australia and New Zealand, including the AJC Australian Derby, New Zealand Derby Stakes, and multiple Challenge Stakes. He was sold as a yearling in 1916 for 230 guineas. Gloaming was inbred 3x3 to Sterling and sired by The Welkin. He was inducted into the New Zealand Racing Hall of Fame and honored with the Gloaming Stakes. Died on 5 May 1932.

Donna Summer's *Four Seasons of Love*, released October 11, 1976, is her fourth studio album and third consecutive gold-certified album in the US. It peaked at #29 on the Billboard 200 and had all tracks reach #1 on the disco chart. The concept album tells a love story through the four seasons, with tracks "Spring Affair," "Summer Fever," "Autumn Changes," and "Winter Melody," plus a reprise of "Spring Affair." The album included a pull-out 1977 calendar with seasonal photos of Summer. It was distributed by Casablanca Records in the U.S. and Atlantic Records in West Germany. Edited versions of "Spring Affair" and "Winter Melody" were released, with the latter reaching the UK Top 30. The album features Donna Summer on lead vocals, with contributions from Thor Baldursson, Keith Forsey, Nick Woodland, Les Hurdle, Dino Solera, Geoff Bastow, and backing vocals by Madeline Bell, Sue & Sunny. It was mixed by Giorgio Moroder and engineered by Jürgen Koppers.

The Wonder Who? was a pseudonym used by The Four Seasons for four singles from 1965 to 1967. The group, originally known as The Four Lovers, evolved from 1956-1960, with Frankie Valli using pseudonyms like Frankie Tyler. The Four Seasons achieved national success starting in 1960, with "Sherry" launching their hit streak. The Wonder Who? singles were produced by Bob Crewe, including "Don't Think Twice" (No. 12), "On the Good Ship Lollipop" (No. 87), "The Lonesome Road" (No. 89), and "Peanuts" (unsuccessful). The name was used to avoid conflicts with existing releases. The group continued releasing singles under different names until 1975. Key members include Frankie Valli, Tommy DeVito, Bob Gaudio, Nick Massi, and Joe Long. The Wonder Who? singles were included on Four Seasons albums but not acknowledged in their original releases.

Donna Summer (Donna Adrian Gaines), born December 31, 1948, in Boston, Massachusetts, died May 17, 2012, in Naples, Florida, from lung cancer. She was an American singer and songwriter known as the "Queen of Disco." She had 32 Billboard Hot 100 singles, including 14 top 10s and four number ones. She was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in 2013. Summer's career spanned from the 1970s to the 2010s, with hits like "Love to Love You Baby," "Last Dance," and "MacArthur Park." She married Helmuth Sommer (1973-1976) and Bruce Sudano (1980-1989). She had three daughters: Mimi, Brooklyn, and Amanda. Summer's last Hot 100 hit was "I Will Go with You (Con te partirò)" in 1999. She sold over 100 million records worldwide and won five Grammy Awards.

Ivanov choreographed The Nutcracker in 1892 due to Petipa's illness, though some dispute his role. He also worked on Swan Lake in 1895. Adam Cooper (born 22 July 1971, Tooting, London) is an English actor, choreographer, dancer, and theatre director. He trained at the Jean Winkler School of Dance and ArtsEd, joining the Royal Ballet in 1989. He became a Principal Dancer in 1994 and left in 1997 to freelance. Cooper choreographed and starred in Matthew Bourne's "Swan Lake," creating the Swan/Stranger role, which earned him awards including the 1999 Astaire Award. Cooper has performed in films and TV, such as "The Soldier's Tale" (2010) and "Swan Lake" (1998). The Nutcracker (1993 film) is a Christmas musical film based on Peter Martins's stage production, directed by Emile Ardolino, and released by Warner Bros. on November 24, 1993, four days after Ardolino's death. It stars Darci Kistler, Damian Woetzel, Kyra Nichols, Bart Robinson Cook, Macaulay Culkin, Jessica Lynn Cohen, Wendy Whelan, Margaret Tracey, Gen Horiuchi, Tom Gold, and the New York City Ballet. George Balanchine's 1954 production of *The Nutcracker* became the most famous stage version in the U.S., premiering at City Center, New York. It uses the plot from Alexandre Dumas, père's adaptation of E.T.A. Hoffmann's tale. Willam Christensen's 1944 San Francisco Ballet production first introduced the complete work to the U.S. The ballet features children in leading roles, with Marie and the Nutcracker/Prince not participating in the Final Waltz. The 1958 Playhouse 90 telecast, narrated by June Lockhart, changed Marie's name to Clara. The 1993 film version, directed by Emile Ardolino, starred Macaulay Culkin and was poorly received. The complete Balanchine version was broadcast on PBS in 2011. Balanchine added an entr'acte from *The Sleeping Beauty* and repositioned the *Dance of the Sugar Plum Fairy*. Darci Kistler (born June 4, 1964) is an American ballerina and the youngest principal dancer in the New York City Ballet (NYCB) at 17. She trained at Mary Lynn's Ballet Arts and the School of American Ballet (SAB), where she met George Balanchine. Kistler joined NYCB's corps de ballet in 1980, became a soloist in 1981, and principal in 1982. She performed signature roles like Balanchine's *Jewels* (Diamonds), *Agon*, *Prodigal Son*, and *Symphony in C*. She danced the Sugarplum Fairy in the 1993 film version of *The Nutcracker*. Kistler retired from NYCB in 2010 after a farewell performance. She married Peter Martins, NYCB's balletmaster-in-chief, in 1991, and they have a daughter, Talicia Tove Martins. Gwen Verdon (1925–2000) was an American actress and dancer who won four Tony Awards. Born in Culver City, California, she had a career spanning Broadway, film, and television. She originated roles in "Damn Yankees," "Sweet Charity," and "Chicago." Verdon married James Henaghan (1942–1947) and Bob Fosse (1960–1971), with whom she collaborated extensively. She was a key figure in Fosse's work, including "Cabaret" and "All That Jazz." Verdon also appeared in films like "The Cotton Club" and "Alice," and received Emmy nominations. She died of a heart attack in 2000 in Vermont. Verdon was inducted into the American Theater Hall of Fame (1981) and received the National Medal of Arts (1998). She was a mental health advocate and had a daughter, Nicole. The miniseries "Fosse/Verdon" (2019) portrays her relationship with Fosse.

Mansi Aggarwal is an Indian filmmaker, writer, producer, and choreographer. Born on 10 June 1984 in Delhi, she trained in Kathak and became a Visharad. She started her Bollywood career after being spotted by Anurag Kashyap, choreographing "Gulaal" and later "Dev D." She is known for choreographing the song "Bharat Mata ki Jai" from "Shanghai," which was nominated for Filmfare and Stardust awards. She also choreographed "Suno na Sangmarmar" from "Youngistaan." Mansi has worked with actors like Priyanka Chopra, Rajkumar Rao, and Emraan Hashmi. She has choreographed commercials for brands like Nykaa and Biba. She was published as the youngest choreographer in Femina. Mansi made her directorial debut with "The Handbag" in 2018, followed by "Raani," which was selected for international film festivals and released on Disney Hotstar and MX Player. She is married to cinematographer Arindam Bhattacharjee and runs Mansi Dance Creations.

The area is centered on Glastenbury Mountain and includes towns like Bennington, Woodford, Shaftsbury, and Somerset. Notable disappearances include Middie Rivers (1945), Paula Jean Welden (1946), James Tedford (1949), Paul Jepson (1950), and Frieda Langer (1950). Welden's case inspired Shirley Jackson's novel *Hangsaman*. Tedford's disappearance involved a bus journey with no trace found. Jepson was left unattended by his mother and later linked to Welden's legend. Langer fell into a stream and was found dead in 1951. The area is associated with folklore, including the "Bennington Monster." The Bennington Triangle has been featured in media like *William Shatner's Weird or What?*, *Lore*, *Most Terrifying Places in America*, and *My Favorite Murder*. Van Arkel–Ketelaar triangles, also known as bond triangles, are used to represent compounds with varying degrees of ionic, metallic, and covalent bonding. Anton Eduard van Arkel introduced the concept in 1941 by placing ionic, metallic, and covalent bonds at the corners of an equilateral triangle, suggesting intermediate species. In 1947, J. A. A. Ketelaar expanded on van Arkel's work by adding more compounds and refining the triangle's application. The triangle is used to analyze compounds based on electronegativity, with the x-axis representing the average electronegativity of two atoms and the y-axis showing the electronegativity difference. Compounds with equal electronegativity, like Cl2, are placed in the covalent corner, while those with large differences, like NaCl, are in the ionic corner. The triangle helps classify bonds as ionic, metallic, or covalent based on these parameters. D-elements cannot be analyzed due to their high electronegativity. The triangle is also used to assess the directionality of bonds.

Urban agriculture involves cultivating, processing, and distributing food in urban areas, including animal husbandry, aquaculture, and horticulture. It differs from peri-urban agriculture, which occurs in rural areas. Urban agriculture has historical roots in Mesopotamia (3500BC) and was used during wars and depressions, such as Detroit's Pingree's Potato Patches (1893) and Victory Gardens during WWI and WWII. The USDA defines a farm as producing $1,000 or more in agricultural products. Community gardens, like Seattle's P-Patch, and city farms, such as the Collingwood Children's Farm (1979), are key components. Urban agriculture improves food security, reduces transportation emissions, and can decontaminate soil through phytoremediation. It also addresses health inequalities and food justice, particularly in food deserts. The UN estimates over 800 million people grow food in cities. Urban farms can be on rooftops, as seen in New York and Singapore. Urban agriculture contributes to economic, social, and environmental benefits, including job creation and reduced carbon footprints.

- **Displacement activity** refers to behaviors that occur when an animal faces conflicting motivations or is prevented from performing a desired behavior. These activities, such as scratching or preening, often provide comfort.  
- **Examples** include birds pecking at grass when uncertain between attacking or fleeing, and hungry hens pacing or preening when food is blocked.  
- **Animal welfare** assessments use displacement activities as indicators of frustration or stress.  
- **Alfonso Troisi**, a psychiatrist and primatologist, proposed using displacement activities as non-invasive stress measures in primates and humans.  
- **History**: The concept originated in 1940 with Nikolaas Tinbergen and Adriaan Kortlandt, influenced by Konrad Lorenz's work on instincts.  
- **Early references** include J. M. Barrie's *The Little White Bird* (1902) and Julian Huxley's 1914 work.  
- The term has recently been adopted to describe **procrastination** as a form of displacement activity.

Race engineer: A motorsport team member who analyzes data to optimize vehicle and driver performance. Responsibilities include communication with data analysts, mechanics, and drivers; managing vehicle mechanics; organizing testing schedules; ensuring regulatory compliance; and handling media interactions. Requires academic degree in engineering or related field. Must have strong people skills and media skills. Role has grown in importance since adoption of on-board sensors for performance data collection. Evaluates vehicle performance via telemetry and driver feedback to adjust suspension, engine calibrations, aerodynamics, and other variables. Race engineers travel extensively during racing season, often internationally, and for testing/training off-season. See also: Automotive aerodynamics, Automotive engineering, Control theory, Mechanical engineering.

JAK Members Bank (JAK Medlemsbank) is a cooperative, member-owned financial institution based in Skövde, Sweden. Founded on the concept from Denmark in 1931, it operates under the principle of "Land Labour Capital" (Jord Arbete Kapital). With approximately 39,000 members as of December 2015, the bank's policies are determined by its members. It does not offer interest on savings and uses a "Saving Points" system for loans. Members must balance saving and spending points to ensure sustainability. JAK also offers loans without saving points. The Danish co-operative society Jord Arbejde Kapital was founded in 1931 during the Great Depression and inspired the Swedish JAK in 1965. The bank received a banking license in 1997 and is government-insured. JAK operates in Sweden, Denmark, Germany, Italy, and had an earlier attempt in Norway. Deposits are in SEK, and Swedish residency is required for loans.

Bridgewater Triangle is a 200 square mile area in southeastern Massachusetts, known for paranormal phenomena. The term was coined by cryptozoologist Loren Coleman in the 1970s. Key locations include Freetown-Fall River State Forest, Profile Rock, Solitude Stone, Bridgewater State University, Taunton State Hospital, and Hornbine School. Paranormal claims include UFOs, giant snakes, thunderbirds, Bigfoot, poltergeists, and shadow people. Cult activity, including animal mutilations, has been reported, particularly in Freetown and Fall River. Two notable incidents in 1998 involved a butchered cow and mutilated calves. Native American curses, specifically related to the lost wampum belt during King Philip's War, are part of local legends. Pukwudgie, Algonquian folklore creatures, are associated with the area. The area is also linked to Lovecraft Country.

Context-sensitive solutions (CSS) is a transportation approach emphasizing community and environmental considerations. Developed at the 1998 "Thinking Beyond the Pavement" conference, CSS prioritizes stakeholder input, safety, and harmony with the surrounding context. It contrasts with traditional methods focused solely on vehicular throughput. CSS involves multidisciplinary teams and continuous communication with stakeholders from project planning to maintenance. The Federal Highway Administration aimed for CSS integration in all state Departments of Transportation by September 2007. CSS promotes "target speed" based on community needs, balancing safety, social exchange, and environmental impact. It includes principles like preserving historic and natural resources, creating public spaces, and minimizing community disruption. CSS is linked to concepts like transit-oriented development and placemaking.

notes.note_text: Robert Burgess Aldrich (1918–1983) was an American film director, producer, and screenwriter. He directed notable films like Vera Cruz (1954), Kiss Me Deadly (1955), The Dirty Dozen (1967), and The Longest Yard (1974). Born in Cranston, Rhode Island, he was part of a wealthy family with political connections. He began his career at RKO Pictures as a production clerk and later worked as an assistant director under notable filmmakers. Aldrich's directorial style combined macho mise-en-scène and complex interpretations of genre tropes. He served as President of the Directors Guild of America and won the Robert B. Aldrich Achievement Award. His films influenced the French New Wave and were known for pushing cinematic boundaries. Aldrich died of kidney failure in 1983 and is buried in Forest Lawn Cemetery.

*Hush... Hush, Sweet Charlotte* (1964) is a psychological thriller directed by Robert Aldrich, starring Bette Davis, Olivia de Havilland, Joseph Cotten, Agnes Moorehead, and Mary Astor (her final film role). Based on Henry Farrell's short story "What Ever Happened to Cousin Charlotte?" and adapted by Farrell and Lukas Heller. The film follows Charlotte Hollis, a middle-aged Southern woman accused of murdering her lover John Mayhew decades earlier. After her home is threatened by demolition, she summons her cousin Miriam, leading to a series of bizarre events. The film was a critical success, earning seven Academy Award nominations. It was shot in Baton Rouge, Louisiana, with scenes at Houmas House plantation. The film's title song was a hit for Patti Page. Mary Astor's character is revealed to be the murderess from her youth. The film was released on DVD in 2005 and Blu-ray in 2016. Agnes Moorehead won the Golden Globe for Best Supporting Actress.

A Kiss for Corliss (retitled Almost a Bride) is a 1949 American comedy film directed by Richard Wallace, written by Howard Dimsdale, and starring David Niven and Shirley Temple. It is a sequel to the 1945 film Kiss and Tell. The film was released on November 25, 1949, by United Artists. It marks the final film for both Wallace and Temple. The story follows Playboy Kenneth Marquis, who is divorcing his third wife. Corliss, his attorney Harry Archer's daughter, is infatuated with Marquis. After Corliss feigns amnesia to cover up her late return from a raid at the Penguin Club, her parents believe she is in a relationship with Marquis. Marquis claims the diary entries are true, leading to a public engagement. The truth is revealed during a wedding rehearsal, resulting in a fight where Marquis is defeated. The cast includes Shirley Temple as Corliss Archer, David Niven as Kenneth Marquis, Tom Tully as Harry P. Archer, and others.

Vera Cruz is a 1954 American Western film directed by Robert Aldrich, starring Gary Cooper and Burt Lancaster. It was produced by Hecht-Lancaster Productions and released by United Artists on December 25, 1954. Set during the Franco-Mexican War, the film follows American mercenaries transporting gold to Veracruz. It features Denise Darcel, Sara Montiel, Cesar Romero, Ernest Borgnine, Charles Bronson, and Jack Elam. The film's amoral characters and cynical attitude influenced later Westerns, including The Magnificent Seven (1960) and Spaghetti Westerns by Sergio Leone. It was the first American film shot entirely in Mexico, using the SuperScope widescreen process. The film earned $5 million in North America and $9 million overall. It inspired critics to label it "the first Spaghetti Western." A sequel, There Really Was a Gold Mine, was planned but never made.

Enteng the Dragon is a 1988 Philippine comedy film directed by Romy Villaflor and written by Tony S. Mortel. It is a parody of Enter the Dragon. The story follows Enteng (Dolphy), a mobile food vendor in China Town known for his humor. Rowena (Dang Cecilio), a journalist, covers his story after her Editor-in-Chief deems him worthy of a human interest piece. Kuto (Vandolph), a young boy found in Enteng's food wagon, leads him to a shrine where his destiny as a vigilante is sealed. The film was produced by RVQ Productions, owned by Dolphy. It was released on July 14, 1988. Cast includes Dolphy, Vandolph, Dang Cecilio, Eddie Garcia, Monica Herrera, and others. No accolades are mentioned.

O Cangaceiro is a 1953 Brazilian adventure western film directed by Lima Barreto. It was shot in 1952 after some reluctance by Franco Zampari of Vera Cruz. The film was a national and international success, winning the Adventure Film Award at the 1953 Cannes Film Festival. It was released on January 20, 1953, and grossed ₢$30 million in 24 Brazilian theaters. It was distributed to over 80 countries. The film features Alberto Ruschel as Teodoro, Marisa Prado as Olívia, Milton Ribeiro as Galdino, Vanja Orico as Maria Clódia, and Adoniran Barbosa as Mané Mole. It started the "Nordestern" genre, blending cangaço with Western. The film was praised for its musical score and performances but criticized for its sociological inaccuracies and style borrowing from American films. It is considered Vera Cruz's "high point" and "most important production."

The film was shot in Boston, Atlanta, Los Angeles, Paris, and Berlin from September 2013 to June 2014. It premiered in London on November 10, 2014, and released in the U.S. on November 21, 2014. notes.note_text: Brett Allen Scallions (born December 21, 1971) is an American singer, best known as the original lead vocalist and rhythm guitarist for Fuel from 1993 to 2006 and again from 2010 to 2020. He was born in Brownsville, Tennessee, and attended Lambuth University on music and theater scholarships. Scallions joined Fuel after bassist Jeff Abercrombie saw him perform in Jackson, Tennessee. He also formed World Fire Brigade with Sean Danielsen and Eddie Wohl, releasing their debut album "Spreading My Wings" in 2012. Scallions left Fuel in 2006 due to the band becoming a "one-man band," but returned in 2010, reforming Fuel with Lonich, Schalk, and Brad Stewart. He left again in 2020 due to internal conflicts. Scallions is married to Abby Gennet, and they have two sons.

"Memo from Turner" is a 1970 solo single by Mick Jagger, featuring slide guitar by Ry Cooder, from the soundtrack of the film *Performance*, in which Jagger played the role of Turner. It was re-released in October 2007 on *The Very Best of Mick Jagger*. The song was ranked No. 92 on Rolling Stone's 100 Greatest Guitar Songs list. Three versions of the song were released: a slow version by Traffic, a 1968 Rolling Stones version, and the 1970 film version. The film version, recorded in Los Angeles, uses vocals from the Traffic version and features Ry Cooder on slide guitar. The song was used in *Goodfellas* (1990), incorrectly credited to the Rolling Stones. It has been covered by Dramarama, Diesel Park West, Deborah Harry, and Patty Palladin. The lyrics may reference *The Soft Machine* by William S. Burroughs.

Jagger–Richards is a songwriting partnership between Mick Jagger (born 1943) and Keith Richards (born 1943), founding members of the Rolling Stones. They are one of the most successful songwriting duos in history. Their collaboration was influenced by manager Andrew Loog Oldham, who encouraged them to write original material. Their first original song, "As Tears Go By," was written under pressure from Oldham. The duo also produced Rolling Stones albums under the pseudonym "The Glimmer Twins," starting with *It's Only Rock 'n' Roll* (1974). They shared production credits with other producers from *Undercover* (1983) onward. Some Jagger/Richards songs were released by other artists, such as Gene Pitney and George Bean. Notable songs include "Sympathy for the Devil," "Brown Sugar," and "Ruby Tuesday." Their songwriting credits were transferred to BMG on June 26, 2013. Rolling Stone ranked them as the sixth greatest songwriter of all time.

Mick Jagger, born 26 July 1943 in Dartford, is the lead vocalist of the Rolling Stones. He formed the band with Keith Richards, Brian Jones, and others in the early 1960s. Jagger and Richards are known for their successful songwriting partnership. He was knighted in 2003 for services to popular music. Jagger has released solo albums, including "She's the Boss" (1985) and "Goddess in the Doorway" (2001). He has been involved in film production through Jagged Films, producing "Enigma" (2001). Jagger has had multiple relationships, including marriages to Bianca Pérez-Mora Macias and Jerry Hall, and has eight children. He has been inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame (1989) and the UK Music Hall of Fame (2004). Jagger's career spans over six decades, with 13 UK and US No. 1 singles. He has been recognized for his influence on rock music and has been involved in various charitable and cultural activities.

"Disease" is the first single from Matchbox Twenty's third album, *More Than You Think You Are*, released on September 30, 2002. The song was co-written by Rob Thomas (lead singer of Matchbox Twenty) and Mick Jagger (frontman of The Rolling Stones). It peaked at number 29 on the US Billboard Hot 100. Thomas wrote "Disease" and another song, "Visions of Paradise," for Jagger's solo album *Goddess in the Doorway*. Jagger returned "Disease" to Thomas, stating it "sounds like you. It's your song." The music video, directed by Phil Harder, features a man roller skating through New York City, with scenes of the band performing at an outdoor roller-rink. Rob Thomas slides off the stage onto the dance floor during the third chorus. The video ends with the roller skater shutting off his boombox and heading home.

notes.note_text: Victor Diamond Mine, located in the James Bay Lowlands, 90 km west of Attawapiskat, Ontario, is De Beers' second Canadian diamond mine. Construction began in 2006, with production starting in 2008. The mine operated as an open-pit mine until 2019, with a 17-year project life. It processed 2.5 million tonnes of kimberlite annually, producing about 600,000 carats yearly. The mine's Impact Benefit Agreement (IBA) was ratified by the Attawapiskat First Nation in 2005. Royalties from the mine totaled $226 million by 2013–2014. De Beers paid $474.9 million into the Canadian economy in 2010. The mine employed 3,200 during construction and around 400 permanently. It also provided training and employment to Attawapiskat First Nation members. Environmental concerns were raised, and the project received ISO 14001 certification. The mine's operations impacted 5,000 hectares and involved 15 kimberlite pipes

Dry Fork Mine is a coal mine located 8 miles north of Gillette, Wyoming, in the Powder River Basin. It is an open pit mine using truck and shovel methods to extract low-sulfur, sub-bituminous coal. The mine supplies coal to the Dry Fork power station, constructed in 2011 adjacent to the mine. Owned and operated by Western Fuels Association, it had 330 million tons of reserves as of 2009, with a maximum production capacity of 15 million tons per year. Annual production has typically been in the 5.2 million ton range, with 5.2 million short tons produced in 2008. The mine shipped its first coal in 1990 to Western Fuels Association members. Coal quality averages 8,050-8,200 BTU/lb, 0.20-0.42% sulfur, 3.8-5.1% ash, and 1.50% sodium (of ash). Train loading uses a batch weigh bin system linked to a "weigh-in-motion" track scale. The rail loop's silo can hold 10,800 tons.

The Tundra Mine was a gold mine located in the Northwest Territories, Canada. It operated from 1962 to 1968, producing 104,476 troy ounces (3,249.6 kg) of gold from 187,714 tons of ore. The mine is associated with the Indian and Northern Affairs Canada, which has a project under the Northern Contaminants Program to remediate the site. This project is funded by the Canadian Federal Contaminated Sites Action Plan. The notes include the mine's name, location, operational dates, production figures, and the responsible government agency and its associated programs. No other sources are referenced.

The Franklin-Creighton Mine was a gold mine in Cherokee County, Georgia, located along the Etowah River near Ball Ground. It was initially called the Franklin Mine, started by Mrs. Mary G. Franklin in 1832 after she won a 40-acre lot in the Gold Lottery. By 1883, it became known as the Creighton Mine or Franklin-Creighton Mine. It was highly productive, yielding an estimated $1,000 per day in 1893, with total production after 1880 possibly reaching $1,000,000. The mine closed in 1913 due to a collapsed shaft causing flooding. As of 2022, three major structures remain: the stamping mill's concrete foundation (rebuilt into a pavilion), the Franklin residence and doctor's office, and the "Shingle House," which served as the mine's post office and general store.

Raspadskaya Coal Mine is located in Mezhdurechensk, Kemerovo Oblast, Russia. It is the largest coal and underground mine in Russia, opened in 1973 and completed in 1977. The mine includes MUK-96, Raspadskaya Koksovaya, Razrez Raspadsky, and Raspadskaya preparation plant. Total resources are 1,461 million tons, with 782 million tons in reserves (as of June 2006). By 31 March 2008, 22 million tons were produced. Reserves-to-production ratio is about 55 years. The mine produces 10% of Russia's coking coal and is owned by Raspadskaya OAO. In March 2001, a methane explosion killed four miners and injured six. The mine was closed for two weeks in 2008 due to safety violations. A collapse in January 2010 killed one worker. On 8 May 2010, an explosion killed 66 workers. In 2022, the mine released 87 metric tons of methane per hour

The Salmita Mine was a gold-producing operation in the Northwest Territories, Canada, active from 1983 to 1987. The deposit was first discovered in 1945, with underground exploration conducted between 1951 and 1952. It was reactivated for exploration by Giant Yellowknife Mines Limited in 1975 and began production in 1983. The mine utilized the old camp and milling plant of the abandoned Tundra Mine, located a few kilometers to the south. It produced 179,906 troy ounces (5,595.7 kg) of gold from the processing of 238,177 tons of ore. The area is currently owned by Seabridge Gold.

The Colomac Mine, a privately owned open-pit gold mine in the Northwest Territories, Canada, operated from 1990–1992 and 1994–1997. Operated by Neptune Resources Limited and later Royal Oak Mines Inc., both owned by Peggy Witte, the mine faced financial difficulties and bankruptcy due to low gold prices and high costs. The Canadian Federal Government acquired the mine and its environmental issues in 1999. Cleanup efforts, estimated at $70 million, included a $1.5 million security deposit and involved aboriginal businesses. In 2012, Nighthawk Gold Corporation acquired the mine's claims. The mine produced 16.7 Megagrams of gold, valued at $916 million. Cleanup included remediation procedures and a $19 million contract for final remediation, suspended in 2010 due to an accident. The site's cleanup and environmental monitoring continued until 2012.

Murowa diamond mine is located in Mazvihwa, south central Zimbabwe, approximately 40 km from Zvishavane. Owned and operated by Rio Tinto Group, which also owns Argyle diamond mine (Australia) and part of Diavik Diamond Mine (Canada). The mine combines open pit and underground construction. Construction costs are estimated at $61 million USD. Mine reserves are 19 million tonnes of ore with an ore grade of 0.9 carats (180 mg) per tonne. The deposit consists of three north-trending kimberlite pipes intrusive into Chivi suite granites of the Zimbabwe Craton, dated at 500 Ma. Diamond possibilities were first realized in 1997; two larger pipes deemed economically feasible. Construction completed in late 2004. Relocation of 926 people occurred. Limited mining began in 2004, full capacity expected by 2005, though delayed by permitting issues. Full-scale production processes 200,000 tonnes annually, potentially up to 1 million tonnes with further investment. Rio Tinto estimates average price of $65 USD per carat (325 $/g)

Negus Mine was a gold-producing mine located in Yellowknife, Northwest Territories, Canada. It operated from 1939 to 1952. During its operational period, it produced 255,807 troy ounces (7,956.5 kg) of gold from 490,808 tons of ore milled. In 1953, the underground workings of Negus Mine were acquired by the adjacent Con Mine. These workings were subsequently used for ventilation purposes by Con Mine until its closure in 2003. The mine's operations and subsequent transfer to Con Mine are key points of historical record. No other entities or events are mentioned in this source.

Start-rite is a brand of children's shoes founded in 1792 in Norwich, England, by James Smith. The company was renamed by his grandson, James Southall. It gained prominence in the 20th century with an iconic poster, "Children's shoes have far to go," displayed on the London Underground from 1947 to 1967. The poster's origin is controversial, with multiple artists attributed. Start-rite received a royal warrant from Queen Elizabeth II in 1955 to supply footwear for the royal family's children. A second royal warrant was granted in 1989 by the Prince of Wales, later withdrawn in 2003 due to UK production moving to India and Portugal. In 2016, Prince George was photographed wearing Start-rite shoes. The company ceased UK production in 2003, outsourcing to India and Portugal, and reversed a £600,000 annual loss to achieve a £1.5 million profit the following year. It introduced variable width fittings for children's shoes and had concession stores in Adams.

Nora Lewin is a fictional character on Law & Order, portrayed by Dianne Wiest from 2000 to 2002. As the first female New York County District Attorney in the show's history, she served as an interim DA appointed by the Governor under New York law. Lewin, a former law professor, faced political and legal challenges during her tenure, including a 2001 decision to pursue the death penalty for an 18-year-old murderer. She worked closely with Jack McCoy and Abbie Carmichael, later replacing Carmichael with Serena Southerlyn. Lewin left the role in September 2002, citing disillusionment and not seeking re-election. Located 22 miles north of Nashville, it lies along Interstate 65, State Highway 76, and US Highway 31W. Incorporated in 1971 under a Mayor and Aldermanic charter, its current mayor is John Corbitt. The town's name originated from a white house built by Richard Stone Wilks in 1829, which served as a stagecoach stop.
