Mount Kaukau is a 445m hill in Wellington, New Zealand, near Johnsonville, Khandallah, and Ngaio. Its original Māori name, Tarikākā, means "where the parrots rested." The summit has a 122m television transmitter mast, built in 1965, which was reduced by 18m in 2022. The hill is part of the Northern Skyline track and Khandallah Park, established in 1888. The park features native forest with birds like kererū and tūī. A World War II bunker from 1942 was rediscovered in 2017. The Kaukau Challenge, an annual event since 2006, involves a walk/run from Khandallah School to the summit. In 2011, snowfall allowed skiing and snowboarding down the hill. The hill's slopes were once covered in totara forest, with kākā parrots, now regenerating. Former analogue TV frequencies were used until 29 September 2013.

Traverse City, Michigan, is the county seat of Grand Traverse County and the second-largest city north of the Tri-Cities. Population was 15,678 in 2020. It is located at the head of Grand Traverse Bay, divided by the Old Mission Peninsula. Known for cherry production and viticulture, it hosts the National Cherry Festival. The city was incorporated as a village in 1881 and as a city in 1895. It has a warm-summer continental climate. The Traverse City State Hospital, established in 1885, closed in 1989 and was redeveloped. The city has a mayor-council government, with Richard Lewis as mayor. It is served by the Traverse Area District Library and has a population of 15,678 as of the 2020 census. The city has one superfund site, the Avenue E Groundwater Contamination Site. It is home to Northwestern Michigan College and has a growing technology industry. The city has a sister city, Tsuchiyama, Japan.

*The Life of Emile Zola* (1937) is a biographical film about 19th-century French author Émile Zola, directed by William Dieterle and starring Paul Muni. It was selected for preservation in the U.S. National Film Registry in 2000 for its cultural and historical significance. It is a remake of the 2002 Hong Kong-Thai-Singaporean film *The Eye*. The film features Aravind, Kazan Khan, Vijayan, and Abbas in supporting and cameo roles. The Wolf of Wall Street (2013) is a biographical crime film directed by Martin Scorsese, based on Jordan Belfort's memoir. It stars Leonardo DiCaprio as Belfort and Jonah Hill as Donnie Azoff. The film depicts Belfort's rise and fall in the stock market, including his firm Stratton Oakmont's fraudulent activities. It premiered in New York on December 17, 2013, and was released in the U.S. on December 25, 2013, as the first major film distributed digitally. It grossed $406.9 million worldwide. The term appears infrequently in sources until the Fourth Fitna (810s), when it was applied to Khurasanis supporting Caliph al-Amin against his brother al-Ma'mun. Bajkam rose to become amir al-umara under Caliph al-Radi in 938, consolidating power over the caliphs al-Radi and al-Muttaqi. He faced challenges from Muhammad ibn Ra'iq, the Baridis, and the Buyids but retained control until his death in 941. Bajkam was killed by Kurds during a hunting trip. Sa'id ibn Makhlad (died 889) was a senior official of the Abbasid Caliphate. Born a Nestorian Christian, he converted to Islam and served as a secretary in Baghdad. He rose to prominence during the regency of al-Muwaffaq over Caliph al-Mu'tamid (r. 870–892), acting as de facto vizier between 878 and 885. In 882, he was awarded the title Dhu'l-wizaratayn ("possessor of the two vizierates"), which appeared on coins. His fall from power in 885 was due to his brother Abdun's activities, who remained a Christian and sought concessions for Christians. Sa'id died in 889. - Created in the 6th century, it reached its peak under the Abbasid Caliphate, supplying water to Baghdad and serving as its breadbasket.  
- The canal was first developed in Parthian times, with large-scale construction under Sassanid ruler Khosrau I (r. 531–579), who established it as Bazidjan Khusraw.

- The canal was breached in 937/8 during Bajkam's revolt, leading to its abandonment for 14 years.

The purpose of claiming races includes quality classification, increasing betting, and providing liquidity to the market. Some horses rise above claiming races, while others remain in the claiming class.

The Miss Preakness Stakes is a Grade III Thoroughbred horse race for three-year-old fillies, held annually at Pimlico Race Course in Baltimore, Maryland on Black-Eyed Susan Stakes Day. The race covers six furlongs on dirt and offers a purse of $150,000. First run in 1986, it was graded in 2002. From 1986 to 2003, it was called the Miss Preakness Stakes; it was renamed in 2004 with sponsorship by Adena Stallions. Adena Springs, owned by Frank Stronach, sponsored the event from 2015 to 2019. The race's speed record is 1:07.70 set by Covfefe in 2019, with an 8.5-length margin. Chris McCarron has the most wins as a jockey (4), and D. Wayne Lukas and Todd Pletcher each have 3 wins as trainers. No owner has won more than once. Adena Springs' stallions include Ghostzapper, Macho Uno, and others. The 2017 winner

The Alysheba Stakes is a Grade II American Thoroughbred horse race for horses aged three and older, run over 1+1/16 miles on dirt. It is held annually in early May on Kentucky Oaks Day at Churchill Downs in Louisville, Kentucky, during the spring meeting. The race was added to Derby Week in 2004 as the sixth race on the undercard of the Kentucky Oaks day meeting, becoming the first stakes to join since 1997. The event is named after Alysheba, a 1987 Kentucky Derby winner and Hall of Fame inductee. The race received graded status in 2007 and was upgraded to Grade II in 2012. Successful Dan (2012) set the track record for the distance (1:41.04). Take Charge Indy (2013) holds the record for the largest margin (6 lengths). John Velazquez has the most wins by a jockey (3), and Todd Pletcher and Bob Baffert each have the most wins by a trainer (2).

The Jim McKay Turf Sprint is a Listed horse race for three-year-olds and up, held over five furlongs on turf at Pimlico Race Course in Baltimore, Maryland, during the third week of May as part of the Black-Eyed Susan Stakes undercard. It offers a $100,000 purse and is the lead-off leg of the MATCh Sprint Turf Division. The race was named after Jim McKay, a TV sports journalist (1921-2008), known for hosting ABC's Wide World of Sports. First run in 2006 as the Baltimore Breeders' Cup Turf Sprint, it has had various names, including the Baltimore City Turf Sprint (2007) and Old Mutual Turf Sprint (2008). The speed record is held by Hero's Reward (2007) in :55.90. Ben's Cat has the most wins (5), as does trainer King T. Leatherbury and owner The Jim Stable. Jockey Julian Pimentel has 3 wins.

Horse Racing is a 1980 equestrian video game released by Mattel Electronics for the Intellivision console. It features 8 fictional Thoroughbred horses at Rainbow Thoroughbred Stables, located at Plympton Downs, a fictional western Kentucky race track inspired by George Plimpton. The game includes 10 races with 4 horses per race, and players bet on win or exacta using a $750 bankroll. Horses are identified by colors, with buttons [1] to [8] assigned to PINK, RED, ORANGE, YELLOW, GREEN, BLUE, VIOLET, and WHITE. A BLACK horse, Black Maurauder, was removed from the original release and replaced by WHITE horse Snowy Guy. The game supports three track types: dry, turf, and muddy. It was also released by Sears for the Super Video Arcade. Horse Racing is included in the Intellivision Lives! collection.

input: Are Stanley Elkin and Anne Tyler from the same country?

notes.note_text: Noah's Compass is a 2009 novel by Anne Tyler, her 18th. It follows Liam Pennywell, a 60-year-old man in Baltimore who is widowed, divorced, and recently dismissed from his teaching job. After moving to a smaller apartment, he is assaulted by a burglar and loses his memory. He meets Eunice, a "rememberer" for an aging entrepreneur. Complications arise with his daughter Kitty moving in and his middle daughter Louise leaving his grandson Jonah with him. Eunice is married and does not want to let go of Liam. The burglar is arrested, and Liam reconciles with his eldest daughter Xanthe, ends his relationship with Eunice, and starts working as a zayde. The title references a conversation with his grandson about Noah's ark. Reviews include contributions from William Boot, Kathleen Byrne, Elizabeth Day, Kathryn Harrison, and Yvonne Zipp. See also 2009 in literature.

Stanley Lawrence Elkin (May 11, 1930 – May 31, 1995) was an American novelist, short story writer, and essayist. Born in Brooklyn, New York, to a Jewish family, he grew up in Chicago. He earned a bachelor's degree in English from the University of Illinois in 1952 and a Ph.D. in 1961. He served in the U.S. Army from 1955 to 1957 and taught at Washington University in St. Louis until his death. Elkin battled multiple sclerosis and signed the "Writers and Editors War Tax Protest" in 1968. He published ten novels, two novella volumes, two story collections, essays, and a screenplay. Notable works include *George Mills* (1982), *The MacGuffin* (1991), and *Mrs. Ted Bliss* (1995). He won the National Book Critics Circle Award in 1982 and 1995. Elkin died of a heart attack in St. Louis, and his manuscripts are archived at Washington University. He has a star on the St

Earthly Possessions is a 1977 novel by Anne Tyler, her seventh novel, following Celestial Navigation (1974) and Searching for Caleb (1976), and preceding Morgan's Passing, Dinner at the Homesick Restaurant, The Accidental Tourist, and Breathing Lessons. The story follows Charlotte Emory, a 35-year-old woman trapped in Clarion, Maryland, who attempts to escape her life but is kidnapped by Jake Simms, a prison escapee. Jake, who blames others for his chaotic actions, takes Charlotte to Florida, where he plans to "rescue" his pregnant girlfriend, Mindy Callender, from a home for wayward girls. The novel explores themes of escape, fate, and passive living. Reviews by John Leonard and John Updike highlight Tyler's talent and the novel's strengths and weaknesses. An adaptation titled Earthly Possessions (TV) was released in 1999, starring Susan Sarandon, Stephen Dorff, and Elisabeth Moss, with a romantic element added for the film.

"Searching for Caleb" is Anne Tyler's sixth novel, published by Alfred A. Knopf in 1975. The story centers on the Peck family, including Duncan Peck, his wife Justine, and her grandfather Daniel. Duncan is fascinated by randomness and frequently moves his family, while Justine, a fortune teller with memory issues, seeks adventure. Daniel seeks his lost brother from 1912. The narrative spans from the late 19th century to the mid-1970s, exploring themes of rebellion, acceptance, and self-discovery. Justine joins Daniel's quest, seeking personal identity. The novel received praise from Katha Pollitt in the New York Times (1976) and John Updike in The New Yorker (1976), highlighting its wit, detail, and emotional depth.

Anne Tyler (born October 25, 1941) is an American novelist, short story writer, and literary critic. She has published 24 novels, including "Dinner at the Homesick Restaurant" (1982), "The Accidental Tourist" (1985), and "Breathing Lessons" (1988). "Breathing Lessons" won the Pulitzer Prize in 1989. She has also won the Janet Heidinger Kafka Prize, the Ambassador Book Award, and the National Book Critics Circle Award. Tyler's twentieth novel, "A Spool of Blue Thread," was shortlisted for the Man Booker Prize in 2015, and "Redhead by the Side of the Road" was longlisted for the same award in 2020. She is recognized for her fully developed characters, "brilliantly imagined and absolutely accurate detail," and "rigorous and artful style." Tyler was born in Minneapolis, Minnesota, and grew up in a Quaker community in North Carolina. She attended Duke University and Columbia University. She married Taghi Modarressi in 1963, and they had two daughters. She resides in Baltimore, Maryland.

"Dinner at the Homesick Restaurant" is a 1982 novel by Anne Tyler, her ninth work. Set in Baltimore, Maryland, it was a 1983 finalist for the Pulitzer Prize, National Book Award, and PEN/Faulkner Award. The story follows siblings Cody, Ezra, and Jenny, whose father, Beck, abandons the family. Pearl, their mother, struggles to maintain normalcy. Cody is envious of Ezra, who becomes a restaurant owner. Ezra's restaurant, "Homesick Restaurant," symbolizes his desire to reunite the family. Jenny marries impulsively but finds stability in her third marriage. The novel explores how siblings experience shared events differently. At Pearl's funeral, Beck returns but leaves during a dinner conflict. Reviews by Benjamin DeMott, John Updike, and Margaret Manning praise the novel's depth and emotional impact.

Steven Nathan Zwicker (born June 4, 1943) is an American literary scholar and the Stanley Elkin Professor in the Humanities at Washington University in St. Louis. He specializes in Restoration-era English literature and politics. Zwicker was born in San Diego, California, and earned his BA from UCLA (1965), MA (1966), and PhD (1969) from Brown University, where he was a Woodrow Wilson Scholar. He has been a faculty member at Washington University since 1969. His notable works include *Dryden's Political Poetry: The Typology of King and Nation* (1972), *Politics and Language in Dryden's Poetry: The Arts of Disguise* (1984), and *Lines of Authority: Politics and English Literary Culture, 1649-1689* (1993). He has edited several volumes, including *Politics of Discourse* (1987), *The Cambridge Companion to English Literature, 1650-1740* (1998), and *The Cambridge Companion to John Dryden* (2004).

Gwyn Avenue–Bridge Street Historic District is a national historic district in Elkin, Surry County, North Carolina. It includes 124 contributing buildings and 1 contributing site, primarily built between 1891 and 1955. The district features examples of Queen Anne, Colonial Revival, and Bungalow / American Craftsman architecture. Notable buildings are the Elkin Presbyterian Church (built in 1937, 1944, 1950, 1955, 1961), First Baptist Church (1955, 1968), Alexander Martin Smith House (1893–1897, designed by George Franklin Barber), Gwyn-Chatham-Gwyn House (c. 1872, 1911, 1936), Richard Gwyn Smith House (c. 1918), and Mason Lillard House (c. 1910). The district was added to the National Register of Historic Places in 2007.

Mrs. Ted Bliss is a 1995 novel by Stanley Elkin, published by Hyperion Books. It follows Mrs. Dorothy Bliss, an 80-year-old Jewish woman living in a retirement community near Miami Beach, Florida. Born in Russia, she immigrated to the U.S. with her family, with her mother altering her age on legal documents. Her husband, Ted Bliss, ran a butcher shop in Chicago; they had three children, one of whom died of cancer. After his death, the couple moved to Florida. The novel, released posthumously on 7 September 1995, won the 1995 National Book Critics Circle Award in fiction. Elkin, who died on 31 May 1995, had previously won the same award for George Mills (1982). The story explores Mrs. Bliss's life, relationships, and eventual death during Hurricane Andrew.

George Mills is a 1982 novel by Stanley Elkin, published by E. P. Dutton. It is structured in five parts and spans over 1,000 years, covering the First Crusade, the Ottoman Empire, and present-day America. The novel explores the lives of successive generations of a family named George Mills, all of whom are aware of their fates but unable to change their circumstances. Elkin won the 1982 National Book Critics Circle Award for the novel. He mentioned it as one of his favorites and called it his "longest and most complexly organized work." The 43rd Mills encounters King George IV and later reaches America, where the present-day Mills cares for Judith Glazer in St. Louis. The novel was published on 25 October 1982. Elkin later noted that sections were adapted from William Faulkner's Absalom, Absalom! and that he realized his identity as a novelist.

notes.note_text: The passage lists various categories of board games. Single-player games include solo variants of titles like Arkham Horror and Agricola. Two-player abstract strategy games involve full game state visibility without random elements. Multi-player elimination games feature player removal before the end. European race games are multiplayer without elimination, suitable for mixed-age groups. Economics strategy games focus on scarce resources and strategy. Games of physical skill require coordination or dexterity. Children's games have simple rules and chance-based outcomes. Cooperative games require teamwork to win. Word games involve word construction for scoring. Gaming systems allow multiple games to be played. Notable references include Spiel des Jahres, Games 100, and lists of wargames, Japanese games, and publishers. External links include Board Game Geek and Boardgames.org.

This passage is a glossary of board game terms, explaining common terminology in alphabetical order. Key terms include "bear off," "capture," "gameboard," "piece," "space," and "turn." It defines terms like "custodian capture," "displacement capture," and "intervention capture," which describe different methods of capturing pieces in games. The glossary also covers game components such as "deck," "dice," and "equipment," and explains gameplay concepts like "engine-building" and "worker placement." It distinguishes between "in play" and "out of play" pieces, and defines terms like "handicap" and "odds." The passage also includes definitions for specific game types, such as "checkers," "chess," and "mancala." It notes that some games use modular boards and that certain pieces, like "meeples," represent players. The glossary references other resources like "List of board games" and "Glossary of chess."

Bear Games is a category of two-player abstract strategy board games with historical roots in the Roman Empire, played in regions such as Turkey, France, and Italy. The games typically feature three hunters and one bear on a patterned board, with the objective of the hunters to hem in and block the bear's movements. The bear aims to avoid capture, and an optional rule allows the bear to win if the hunters fail to stalemate it within a set number of moves (e.g., 40). 

Bear Games are closely related to Hare Games, where the roles are reversed, and the hares cannot move backward. Related games include Watermelon Chess, Sz'Kwa, Fox Games, Rimau-Rimau, Bagha-Chall, and Main Tapal Empat. The games use patterned boards, with initial positions varying by variant, and both players move one space per turn without capturing pieces.

BoardGameGeek (BGG) is an online forum and game database for board gaming hobbyists, founded in January 2000 by Scott Alden and Derk Solko. As of 10 March 2019, it had an Alexa rank of 1,745. BGG hosts an annual board game convention, BGG.CON, since 2005, with family-friendly Spring BGG.CON and BGG@Sea on cruises. It received the Diana Jones Award in 2010 and was inducted into the Origins Award Hall of Fame in 2020. The site also hosts RPG and video game sites, rpggeek.com and videogamegeek.com. Since 2006, BGG annually awards the Golden Geek Award for best new board games, with categories expanded in 2020 to include "Game of the Year, Light", "Medium", and "Heavy". RPG and video game awards were introduced in 2014 but discontinued after 2017.

David Parlett (born 18 May 1939 in London) is a games scholar, historian, and translator from South London. He is the president of the British Skat Association. Born to Sidney Thomas Parlett and Eleanor May Parlett, he has three brothers. Educated at Battersea Grammar School and University College of Wales, Aberystwyth, he holds a BA in Modern Languages. Parlett is married to Barbara and has a son and daughter. He is a Quaker. His notable works include *The Oxford History of Board Games*, *The Oxford Guide to Card Games*, and *The Penguin Book of Card Games*. He invented numerous games, including *Hare and Tortoise* (1973), which won Spiel des Jahres in 1979. Parlett has created over 70 card games and several board games, such as *Around the World in 80 Days* (2016) and *Chicken Out!* (2017). His publications cover card games, board games, languages, and other subjects.

Yut (also called yut nori, nyout, yoot, cheok-sa, sa-hui) is a traditional Korean board game played during Korean New Year. It originated as early as the Three Kingdoms period (57 BCE – 668 CE). The game uses a board with 29 stations, yut-sticks (jang-jak yut and bam yut), and tokens called mal. The sticks are cast to determine movement, with combinations like do (1), gae (2), geol (3), yut (4), and mo (5). Yut and mo allow for extra casts. The game is played between teams, with the goal of bringing all tokens home. Special rules include the Seoul, Busan, and back rules. The board's stations are linked to Korean cosmology, symbolizing heaven and earth. Yut is a social game, often played during Seollal, and has cultural significance in Korean tradition. The game is also used for fortune-telling in the Dongguksesigi.

Francis Tresham (1936–23 October 2019) was a British board game designer who created games since the early 1970s. He founded Hartland Trefoil in 1971, known for the Civilization board game, which was sold to MicroProse in 1997. Tresham introduced the concept of a technology tree in board games, influencing both board and computer games. He was managing director of Tresham Games, producing 18xx-style games. Inducted into the UK Games Expo Hall of Fame in 2013. His notable board games include 1825, 1829, 1829 Mainline, 1830, 1853, Civilization, Revolution: The Dutch Revolt 1568–1648, Shocks & Scares, Spanish Main, and The Game of Ancient Kingdoms. Some of his games inspired Sid Meier's computer games like Railroad Tycoon.

Days of Wonder is a board game publisher founded in 2002 by Mark Kaufmann, Eric Hautemont, and Yann Corno. It was acquired by Asmodee Group in 2014. The company distributes games to 25 countries and publishes games in English, Dutch, French, German, Russian, and Greek. It specializes in German-style board games and has expanded into online games. 

Key games include "Gang of Four" (2002), "Ticket to Ride" (2004, designed by Alan R. Moon), which won Spiel des Jahres in 2004 and had a digital version in 2006. "Shadows Over Camelot" was named Best Fantasy Game at Spiel des Jahres 2006. "Smallworld" received three awards in 2009. The company's games have been recognized with various awards, including "Best Game of the Year" and "Best Family Game" from the Dice Tower Gaming Awards.

Tsuro is a tile-based board game designed by Tom McMurchie, originally published by WizKids and now by Calliope Games. It is for 2-8 players, played on a 6x6 grid with 35 standard path tiles and one Dragon tile. Players place tiles and move pieces along paths, with elimination occurring if a path ends at the board edge. The game has themed editions like Tsuro of the Seas and Asteroid Escape. The name derives from the Japanese word "tsūro" meaning "route." The game was patented in 1979, with the Weismans publishing it as Tsuro in 2005. Calliope Games, founded by Ray Wehrs in 2011, now publishes Tsuro. Variants include a German edition (2007) and Tsuro: Phoenix Rising (2019). A Luxury Limited Edition was announced for 2022. The Dragon tile is used when there are three or more players.

Robert Charles Bell (1917–2002) was a Canadian-born British consultant plastic surgeon and author of board game books. He moved to England in 1928 and was educated at Haileybury College and St Bartholomew's Hospital. Bell's major work, *Board and Table Games From Many Civilizations*, won the Premier Award at the Doctors' Hobbies Exhibition. He categorized board games into four main types and contributed to David Parlett's *The Oxford History of Board Games*. His publications include *Tangram Teasers*, *Discovering Old Board Games*, and *Oriental Games*. Bell also wrote on coin collecting and Tyneside pottery. His works were published by Oxford University Press, Shire Publications, and Dover. Much of his collection is at the University of Durham. He collaborated with various authors on books like *Potteries of Tyneside* and *Board Games Round the World*.

notes.note_text: Primary Care Behavioral Health (PCBH) is a model integrating mental health services into primary care. It aims to improve overall health by addressing psychiatric comorbidities, which affect about half of primary care patients. Behavioral health consultants (BHCs) work alongside primary care providers (PCPs) to enhance care for mental health issues. BHCs provide brief interventions (15–30 minutes) and support for conditions like depression, anxiety, and substance abuse. The model improves communication between providers and patients, with referral completion rates around 80–90%. Research shows PCBH improves outcomes, medication adherence, and patient satisfaction. The model is supported in settings like Veterans Affairs Medical Centers and federally qualified health centers (FQHCs). Challenges include funding barriers, lack of trained mental health workers, and policy issues like same-day billing restrictions in Medicaid. The PCBH model has roots in the 1960s with Kaiser Permanente and was further developed through studies like the Hawaii Medicaid Project.

Fredric Rieders (July 9, 1922 – November 26, 2005) was a forensic toxicologist born in Vienna, Austria. He emigrated to the U.S. at 16 to escape Nazism. Rieders testified in the O.J. Simpson murder trial in 1995, but his testimony was interrupted as he left the country. He later returned and was described as belligerent and confused. He worked on cases involving Robert Curley (poisoned by his wife with thallium), Michael Swango ("Dr. Death"), and Jack Kevorkian. Rieders testified that Kevorkian may have used excessive thiopental, possibly causing death before potassium chloride. He earned a PhD in Pharmacology-Toxicology from Thomas Jefferson University and served as Chief Toxicologist in Philadelphia for 14 years. He founded NMS Labs in 1970 and established the Forensic Sciences Mentoring Institute. He died at 83.

Vilma Santos-Recto (born November 3, 1953) is a Filipino actress, singer, dancer, TV host, producer, and politician. She served as House Deputy Speaker from 2019 to 2022 and as Representative of Batangas' 6th district from 2016 to 2022. She began her acting career in 1963 with the film *Trudis Liit*, winning her first FAMAS Award for Best Child Performer. She won FAMAS Awards for Best Actress in *Dama de Noche* (1972) and produced *Pagputi ng Uwak, Pag-itim ng Tagak* (1978), which won FAMAS and Gawad Urian awards. She served as mayor of Lipa (1998–2007) and governor of Batangas (2007–2013). She was elected as Batangas' 6th district representative in 2016. She is married to Senator Ralph Recto and has two sons. She received numerous awards, including the FAMAS Lifetime Achievement Award (19

The Atlanta murders of 1979–1981, also known as the Atlanta child murders, involved the killing of at least 28 children, adolescents, and adults in Atlanta, Georgia, between July 1979 and May 1981. Wayne Williams, a 23-year-old Atlanta native, was convicted of two adult murders and sentenced to two consecutive life terms. He was not charged in the child murders but is believed by police to be responsible for many of them. In 2019, Atlanta police reopened the cases for further DNA analysis. Key victims include Edward Hope Smith, Alfred Evans, Milton Harvey, Yusuf Bell, Angel Lenair, and Nathaniel Cater. The investigation involved over 100 agents, curfews, and media attention. FBI agent John E. Douglas linked Williams to the murders, though he acknowledged the possibility of other perpetrators. DNA testing in 2007 did not conclusively prove Williams' guilt. The case has been the subject of media, literature, and documentaries. Williams maintains his innocence.

Michael Swango (born October 21, 1954), an American serial killer and licensed physician, is estimated to have caused 60 fatal poisonings. He admitted to four deaths. Sentenced in 2000 to three consecutive life terms without parole, he is incarcerated at ADX Florence. Swango's early life included a troubled upbringing with an alcoholic father and academic excellence. He graduated from Quincy University summa cum laude and attended Southern Illinois University School of Medicine. During medical school, he displayed troubling behavior, including faking checkups and causing patient deaths. He gained a surgical internship at Ohio State University in 1983, where patients began dying mysteriously. Swango was arrested in 1985 for poisoning coworkers. After multiple jobs and forged documents, he worked at Sanford USD Medical Center, where patients died, leading to his firing. He fled to Zimbabwe, where more deaths occurred. Arrested in 1997, he pleaded guilty to fraud and was sentenced to three-and-a-half years. In 2000, he pleaded guilty to three murders and received three life terms.

input: Which is in the pop genre, Capital Cities or Tweaker?

notes.note_text: Capital Cities is an American pop duo from Los Angeles, formed in 2008 by Ryan Merchant and Sebu Simonian. Their debut EP, released June 7, 2011, included the single "Safe and Sound," which reached #1 on the US Alternative Songs chart and was used in various commercials. The band signed with Capitol Records in 2012 and released their debut album, *In a Tidal Wave of Mystery*, on June 4, 2013. The album featured "Kangaroo Court" and "I Sold My Bed, But Not My Stereo," with guest appearances. The band toured in 2013, including a sold-out show in New York. The "Safe and Sound" music video, directed by Grady Hall, won a 2013 MTV Video Music Award for Best Visual Effects. In 2016, the band hinted at new music, and in 2018, they released their second album, *Solarize*. The band has appeared at festivals like Sundance and SXSW.

Capital Cities/ABC Inc. was formed in 1985 when Capital Cities Communications acquired ABC for $3.5 billion. Founded in 1946 as Hudson Valley Broadcasting Company, it evolved through mergers and acquisitions, including the 1957 merger with Durham Broadcasting Enterprises to form Capital Cities Television Corporation. In 1973, it changed its name to Capital Cities Communications. The merger with ABC in 1985 led to the sale of some stations to comply with FCC rules. The combined company was later acquired by The Walt Disney Company in 1996, rebranded as Disney–ABC Television Group. Key acquisitions included WROW-TV, WTVD, and the Goodwill Stations. The company owned multiple TV and radio stations, newspapers, and publishing entities. Notable stations included WPVI-TV, WKBW-TV, and WABC. The merger with Disney created ABC, Inc., and the structure included ABC Television Network Group, ABC Radio Network, and publishing groups. Financial details include the $3.5 billion purchase of ABC and a $200 million joint venture in 1994.

Thomas Sawyer Murphy (May 31, 1925 – May 25, 2022) was an American broadcasting executive and CEO of Capital Cities / ABC, Inc. until 1996. He co-led the $3.5 billion acquisition of ABC in 1986 with Daniel Burke, who became ABC's president. Murphy was born in Brooklyn, studied at Princeton and Cornell, and earned an MBA from Harvard. He began his career at Kenyon & Eckhardt and Lever Brothers before joining Hudson Valley Broadcasting Company in 1954. He became general manager of WROW stations, leading to profitability. In 1960, he became Capital Cities' first vice president, later president and CEO. He expanded the company into publishing by acquiring Fairchild Publications and newspapers. Capital Cities / ABC was sold to Disney in 1995. Murphy was married to Suzanne Crosby Murphy until her death in 2009; they had four children. He died in Rye, New York, in 2022. Awards include the Television Hall of Fame and the 1996 NATPE Lifetime Achievement Award.

Hwando (Chinese: 丸都; pinyin: Wandu) is a mountain fortress of the ancient Korean kingdom of Goguryeo, built to protect Goguryeo's second capital, Gungnae. Located in present-day Ji'an city, Jilin province, China, it is 2.5 km west of Ji'an, near the North Korean border. Part of the UNESCO World Heritage Site "Capital Cities and Tombs of the Ancient Koguryo Kingdom," it is associated with Gungnae City and Ohnyeosan City. 

In 3 CE, King Yuri moved the capital to Gungnae Fortress and built the Wina Rock fortress, later renamed Hwando by King Sansang. In 244, Wei invaded and sacked Hwando. In 313, Goguryeo conquered the Lelang commandery. In 341, the Xianbei Murong clan attacked and sacked Hwando, capturing thousands of prisoners. The Xianbei also devastated Buyeo in 346, leading to its migration to the Korean peninsula.

Premio Lo Nuestro 2003 marked the 15th anniversary of the awards. Hosted by Marco Antonio Regil and Adal Ramones, the event featured performances by Juanes, Thalía, Marc Anthony, Pilar Montenegro, Sin Bandera, Banda el Recodo, and others. There were 36 award winners and 135 nominations across genres: Pop, Rock, Tropical, Regional Mexican, and Urban. In Pop, awards included Album of the Year, Best Male Artist, Best Female Artist, Best Group or Duo, Best New Artist, and Song of the Year. Juanes won four awards: Best Pop Male Artist, Best Music Video, Best Rock Performance, and Pop Song of the Year. Pilar Montenegro won three awards in Regional Mexican. Celia Cruz won four awards in Tropical, including Best Salsa Performance and Tropical Album of the Year. Special awards included Excellence Award to Luis Miguel and Premio del Pueblo winners: Thalía (Pop), Shakira (Rock), Marc Anthony (Tropical), Vicente Fernández (Regional/Mexican), and El General (Urban).

"Safe and Sound" is a song by American indie pop duo Capital Cities, written and produced by Ryan Merchant and Sebu Simonian. Released as a single on January 6, 2011, it appeared on their debut EP "Capital Cities" (2011) and was the lead single from their debut album "In a Tidal Wave of Mystery" (2013). The song peaked at number eight on the Billboard Hot 100 and achieved commercial success in several territories. It is the theme song for the Washington Capitals. The third music video, directed by Grady Hall and set in the Los Angeles Theatre, was nominated for Best Music Video at the 56th Annual Grammy Awards. The song has been used in various media, including a Coca-Cola commercial, Air New Zealand's safety video, Mazda3 advertisements, and McDonald's promotions. It reached #2 on the Mainstream Top 40 chart and peaked at number 42 on the UK Singles Chart.

Institutional Investor is a periodical published by Euromoney Institutional Investor, founded in 1967 by Gilbert E. Kaplan. An international edition was launched in 1976 for Europe and Asia. Capital Cities Communications acquired the magazine in 1984, and The Walt Disney Company bought Capital Cities in 1996, later selling the magazine back to Euromoney in 1997. The magazine has offices in New York City, London, and Hong Kong. It became digital-only in 2018. Diane Alfano, CEO since 1984, stepped down in June 2021. Euromoney plans to merge Institutional Investor with BCA Research and NDR into an asset management division, with Francis Cashman as CEO of the new unit as of May 2021. The magazine publishes rankings for executive and research teams across regions, including the All-America, All-Europe, All-Asia, All-Japan, Latin America, and other specialized teams.

- The Northwest Territories has had seven capital cities: Fort Garry (1870–1876), Fort Livingstone (1876–1877), Battleford (1877–1883), Regina (1883–1905), Ottawa (1905–1967), Fort Smith (1911–1967), and Yellowknife (1967–present).  
- Fort Garry was the first capital, serving as the seat of government for both the Northwest Territories and Manitoba. It later became Winnipeg.  
- Fort Livingstone was a temporary capital, chosen as a frontier outpost until the railway route was determined.  
- Battleford was the capital until 1883, when the government moved to Regina.  
- Regina was the capital until 1905, when Alberta and Saskatchewan were created, leaving the Northwest Territories with a reduced population.  
- Ottawa became the capital from 1905–1967, with Fort Smith serving as the administrative hub.

Tweaker is an American alternative rock band founded by Chris Vrenna in the late 1990s. Their musical style includes synthpop, progressive rock, modern jazz, and electronica, with a melancholy and somber sound. The Attraction to All Things Uncertain (2001) was Vrenna's "solo" debut, and Clint Walsh became a permanent member with the follow-up album 2 a.m. Wakeup Call (2004). The band composed the theme music for Doom 3 and Xiaolin Showdown, with the Doom 3 theme being a departure into heavy metal. In 2004, Tweaker opened for Skinny Puppy with a live band, performing at QuakeCon 2005 in Dallas, TX. Official members are Chris Vrenna and Clint Walsh. notes.note_text: Fishing rod tapers describe how a rod bends under pressure, with variations categorized as fast, medium, or slow. A fast taper flexes the top 20% of the rod, while medium fast and medium tapers flex 30-60%. Slow tapers allow nearly the entire rod to flex. The action of a taper is determined by how much the tip bends when pressure is applied perpendicularly, with only the tip section bending and the rest remaining rigid. Fast tapers are used for jig lures, offering precise control and aiding in hook setting. Slow tapers are suitable for fighting large fish with light line, as they absorb force and reduce line stress. They are often used with split shot or Lindy rigs for walleye. Rod taper affects the angler's feel of the lure and fish, influencing choice based on fishing scenario and personal preference.

Correct guesses move players forward, with double guesses offering higher rewards. The game was featured in "Games #89" and "Best Games of 1988 in Games #94." An updated version was launched on Kickstarter on May 1, 2023, with updated cultural references and new categories. The original version uses cards with photos or drawings and text descriptions. Players take turns drawing and ranking cards until someone reaches the end of the board.

Jianbing, a traditional Chinese street food similar to crêpes, is a type of bing eaten for breakfast. It is made from a wheat and grain flour batter, eggs, and sauces, often topped with fillings like baocui, ham, mustard pickles, and chili sauce. Originating in northern China, its history dates back 2,000 years to Shandong province during the Three Kingdoms period (AD 220–280). The dish is associated with a legend involving Chancellor Zhuge Liang. Jianbing has regional variations, including Shandong-style (crispy, with coarse grains) and Tianjin-style (softer, with mung bean flour and youtiao stuffing). It has gained international popularity in cities like London, New York, and Sydney, with modifications to suit local tastes. Western vendors and young Chinese entrepreneurs have introduced variations such as vegetarian and gluten-free jianbing, along with Western fillings like bacon and hot dogs. The dish is also known as jianbing guozi in Tianjin.

Tantrix is a hexagonal tile-based game invented by Mike McManaway from New Zealand in 1988, initially called Mind Game. It uses 56 hand-painted tiles with three colored lines (red, yellow, blue, green) and no two tiles are identical. The multiplayer version allows 2-4 players, with the highest-numbered tile starting. The goal is to create the longest line or loop in one's color. Online play exists on platforms like Yahoo! with ratings up to 1000 points. Major tournaments include the World Tantrix Championship (since 1998), World Team, Junior, and Doubles Championships. Offline events like the World Tantrix Table Open have been held in various locations since 2009. The game evolved from cardboard to plastic tiles in 1991, with triple intersections removed in 1993. Tantrix Discovery, Solitaire, Match, and Game Pack are main editions. It was named Toy of the Year in Hungary in 2003.

notes.note_text: The Regional Planning Association of America (RPAA), founded in 1923 by Clarence Stein, aimed to examine and improve urban planning through collaboration. Key members included Benton MacKaye, Lewis Mumford, Charles Harris Whitaker, Alexander Bing, and Henry Wright. The RPAA's first meeting was on April 18, 1923, with eight attendees. MacKaye's Appalachian Trail project, initiated in 1921, influenced the RPAA's focus on environmental preservation. Lewis Mumford, a leading journalist, helped promote the association's ideas. The RPAA developed Sunnyside Gardens in Queens and Radburn, New Jersey, as experimental communities. Alexander Bing, president of the RPAA, funded projects through personal contributions and external support. Henry Wright, an analyst, worked on Sunnyside but later formed the Housing Study Guild, leading to the RPAA's dissolution in the early 1930s. The association's legacy includes advancements in urban planning and community development.

Lewis Mumford House, located on Leedsville Road in Amenia, Dutchess County, New York, is a Federal-style building from the 1830s. Purchased by Lewis Mumford and his wife Sophia in the late 1920s, it became their permanent residence by the mid-1930s, where Mumford lived until his death in 1990. The property, listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 1999, includes a 1.9-acre lot with the house and carriage house, and an adjacent 11.7-acre open field. The house features a three-bay two-story frame structure with a side-gabled roof, clapboard siding, and Federal-style details. Modifications over time included adding electricity, heating, and interior changes. The carriage house, modified into a garage, and landscaping with paths and gardens are contributing resources. Mumford's writings on cities and urban planning were influenced by his rural life here. The house was restored in the 1980s and later sold, eventually becoming an occupied residence again.

Lewis Mumford's *The City in History: Its Origins, Its Transformations, and Its Prospects* is a 1961 National Book Award winner. Published by Harcourt, Brace & World in New York, the book explores the evolution of cities, advocating for an "organic city" where technology and nature coexist. Mumford contrasts this with cities shaped by war, tyranny, and poverty. He emphasizes personal experience and observation in his methodology, focusing on cities he knows firsthand. The book's style is described as "organic," rich in metaphors, similes, and literary references, including works by Charles Dickens such as *Great Expectations* and *Hard Times*. The final chapter, "Retrospect and Prospect," addresses the city's future. Editions include a Hardcover by MJF Books (August 1997, ISBN 978-1-56731-211-9) and a Paperback by Harvest Books (October 1968, ISBN 978-0-15-618035-1).

Megalopolis refers to a group of adjacent metropolitan areas forming a continuous urban area through shared systems. The term originated in 1832, but gained prominence in the 1950s-1960s through Jean Gottmann's analysis of the U.S. Northeast seaboard. A megalopolis typically has a population of 10-25 million. In Brazil, "megarregião" has legal significance, while in China, it is called "城市群" (city cluster). The concept is used in urban planning and policy coordination. The Sprawl trilogy by William Gibson features "the Sprawl," a fictional megalopolis spanning the East Coast of the U.S. The 1927 film *Metropolis* and the 1982 film *Blade Runner* are examples of popular culture depicting megalopolises. The America 2050 program identifies 11 megaregions in the U.S. and Canada.

"Critical Mass: How One Thing Leads to Another" is a 2004 non-fiction book by Philip Ball, an English chemist and physicist. The book explores the concept of a "physics of society," drawing on thinkers like Thomas Hobbes, Lewis Mumford, Emyr Hughes, and Gottfried Achenwall. Ball discusses how social systems may exhibit laws similar to natural physical laws, using statistical mechanics to model people as interacting agents. He addresses challenges such as the theories of being alive and free will. The book covers topics like the business cycle, random walks, phase transitions, traffic flow, Zipf's law, the small-world phenomenon, catastrophe theory, and the Prisoner's dilemma. It won the 2005 Aventis Prize for Science Books and the 2005 Royal Society Winton Prize for Science Books. The concept of a "physics of society" is linked to social physics in the Auguste Comte sense and is based on the idea of modeling human behavior akin to fluid dynamics."

Jack Hillmer (1918–2007) was an American architect based in San Francisco, known for his modernist homes built from redwood. His notable works include the Ludekens house on Belvedere Island, the Munger house in Napa, and the Cagliostro house in Berkeley. Hillmer was born in Texas and visited the 1933 World's Fair in Chicago, where he saw redwood planks that influenced his work. He studied architecture at the University of Texas, served in the air force in San Diego, and explored modernist buildings in southern California. He declined an invitation to join Frank Lloyd Wright's Taliesen Fellowship. Hillmer moved to the San Francisco Bay Area in 1945 and opened an office with Warren Callister. Their first commission was the Haines and Betty Hall house in 1947. After dissolving their partnership, Hillmer's first solo commission was the Ludekens house in 1951. He taught at UC Berkeley and was associated with the Second Bay Tradition. His style emphasized bold lines, minimal details, and integration with the site.

Henry Roth (1906–1995) was an American novelist known for *Call It Sleep* (1934), reissued in 1964 and becoming a classic of Jewish American literature. Born in Tysmenitz, Austro-Hungary (now Ukraine), he moved to the U.S. in 1908, living in New York's Lower East Side, which inspired his novel. After a successful debut, Roth faced a 45-year writer's block, later producing *Mercy of a Rude Stream* (four volumes, 1994–1998) and *An American Type* (2010). His work explores immigrant experience, cultural depravity, and personal conflict. Roth married Muriel Parker in 1939, and their relationship is depicted in *An American Type*. His sister criticized his portrayal of incest in *Mercy*, leading to a contract for $10,000. Roth received honorary doctorates, the Nonino Prize, and the Ribalow Lifetime Achievement Award. *Call It Sleep* sold over 1 million copies and was a bestseller. His final work, *An American Type*, was edited

Lewis Mumford (19 October 1895 – 26 January 1990) was an American historian, sociologist, philosopher of technology, and literary critic. He studied at City College of New York and The New School for Social Research but did not complete his degree. Influenced by Patrick Geddes and associated with Victor Branford, he was a contemporary of Frank Lloyd Wright and others. He worked at The Dial and The New Yorker, writing architectural criticism. His early books, like *The Golden Day* (1926) and *Herman Melville* (1929), influenced American literary criticism. He was a friend of Henry Murray and contributed to the Melville revival. Mumford's work on urban planning and technology emphasized "organic humanism," critiquing "megatechnics" and advocating for "biotechnics." He wrote *The City in History* (1961), which won the National Book Award. He died in Amenia, New York, in 1990. His ideas influenced thinkers like Jacques Ellul, Amory Lovins, and Barry Commoner.

notes.note_text: The Bonus Army, also known as the Bonus Expeditionary Force (B.E.F.), was a group of 43,000 demonstrators, including 17,000 World War I veterans, their families, and affiliated groups, who gathered in Washington, D.C., in mid-1932 to demand early payment of their service bonuses. The World War Adjusted Compensation Act of 1924 issued certificates redeemable in 1945. On July 28, 1932, President Hoover ordered the U.S. Army, led by General Douglas MacArthur, to remove the Bonus Army from their camps, resulting in violence, two deaths, and the destruction of their shelters. A second march in 1933 was defused with offers of jobs in the Civilian Conservation Corps. In 1936, Congress overrode Roosevelt's veto to pay the bonuses early. The Bonus Army camped in Anacostia Flats, with a community structure and internal governance. The event was politically significant, contributing to Hoover's loss in the 1932 election.

The Occupy movement began in 2011, with the Occupy Wall Street protests inspiring global events. On October 15, 2011, the Movimiento 15-M planned protests in 951 cities across 82 countries, with the Occupy movement joining in. Protest camps were established near banking institutions or stock markets. Many protests continued into the following weekends, influenced by the Guy Fawkes mask. American Occupy groups remained active until 2012, with some still active. On September 17, 2012, The Guardian published the "Occupy Directory's" "map of the Occupy world." The movement had locations in Africa, America, Canada, Latin America, the United States, Asia, Europe, and Oceania. The protests were non-violent, targeting the wealthy and banking institutions.

- **Event**: Manjolai Labourers massacre (also known as Thamirabarani massacre) occurred on 23 July 1999 in Tirunelveli, Tamil Nadu.  
- **Victims**: 17 Dalit labourers, including two women and a two-year-old child, were killed.  
- **Cause**: The massacre resulted from a police lathi-charge during a protest by tea plantation workers demanding better wages and working conditions.  
- **Background**: Workers were paid ₹70 per day and demanded an increase to ₹100, along with maternity leave, rest breaks, and improved living conditions.  
- **Outcome**: Justice Mohan Commission found 11 died from drowning, and the rest from injuries.  
- **Documentary**: "Death of a river" (Oru Nathiyin Maranam), a 59-minute Tamil film by Kanchanai Film Society, directed by R R Srinivasan, was released in 1999.  
- **Human Rights Watch**: Condemned the police attack and killings.  
- **Current Status**: Workers are now paid ₹138 per day, but many demands remain unmet.

Pelham Road, also known as Shore Road in the Bronx, is a 4.1-mile east-west arterial road along the Long Island Sound shoreline, running from Pelham Bay Park in the Bronx through New Rochelle and Pelham Manor in Westchester County, NY. It originated as a Native American trail linking Davenport Neck and Pelham Neck. The segment in Westchester is County Route 65 but not signed. The road was historically called "way to Mr. Pell's" and "Road to Pell's Manor." By 1710, more houses existed along the New Rochelle shore than on Boston Road. Ferries were established in 1754 and 1785. Steamboats arrived in 1829, and the Neptune House hotel was built in 1837. The New York and New Haven Railroad (1849) reduced its significance. The Village of New Rochelle was incorporated in 1857. The road was widened in 1928. Today, it connects residential areas with the Downtown business district and includes parks like Glen Island Park, Neptune Park, and Hudson Park. The College of New Rochelle and Residence Park neighborhood are located in the area.

Westchester Avenue is a major east-west street in the South and East portions of the Bronx, New York City. It runs from Third Avenue and East 150th Street in the Hub to Pelham Bay Park in the Pelham Bay section. The avenue crosses neighborhoods including Melrose, Longwood, Soundview, Parkchester, and Pelham Bay. It parallels the Bruckner Expressway until their junction at Pelham Bay Park. Except for 0.5 miles (0.80 km), Westchester Avenue is underneath elevated subway tracks. The IRT White Plains Road Line (2 and 5 trains) runs over it from Brook Avenue to Southern Boulevard. The IRT Pelham Line (6 and <6> trains) runs over it from Whitlock Avenue to Pelham Bay Park. Bx4/Bx4A buses use Westchester Avenue between Bergen Avenue and Parkchester (Bx4A) or Westchester Square (Bx4). The Bx24 uses it north of Westchester Square. The Bx8 and Bx27 use the road for short segments.

Nichidatsu Fujii organized a global disarmament march in 1981. His followers marched and chanted worldwide to support the U.N. 2nd special session for disarmament. In the U.S., marches began in New Orleans, Los Angeles, and San Francisco. The San Francisco march started on Oct. 21, 1981, with a ceremony on Alcatraz. Initially, 13 marchers, including Buddhist followers of Nipponzan-Myōhōji, Native Americans, U.S., and German citizens, participated. They marched about 20 miles per day and were hosted by community groups. By the time they reached Chicago, the group had grown to about 30. In May 1982, 40 marchers from Toronto joined them in Buffalo, N.Y., doubling the group. The march continued through New York, with 10–20 new participants daily. Pelham, New York, a suburban town in Westchester County, is 10 miles northeast of Midtown Manhattan with a 2020 population of 13,078. It includes two villages: Pelham and Pelham Manor. The town borders Eastchester, New Rochelle, and Mount Vernon. Established in 1788, it incorporated in 1889 and merged villages in 1975. The population was 12,107 in 2000, with 87.33% White and 6.02% Hispanic or Latino. Median household income was $91,810, and 2.2% of families were below the poverty line. Major employers include Pico Electronics and Pelham Public Schools. The town has four elementary schools, one middle school, and one high school. St. Catharine's Catholic Church, established in 1896, closed its school in 1983. Pelham is served by Metro-North Railroad and is 28 minutes from Grand Central Terminal. Notable residents include Nancy Allen, Nick Bollettieri, and C. P. H. Gilbert.

Pelham D. Glassford (August 8, 1883 – August 9, 1959) was a U.S. Army officer who attained brigadier general rank during World War I. Born in Las Vegas, New Mexico, he graduated from West Point in 1904 and served in the Field Artillery. He commanded units in the Pancho Villa Expedition and during World War I, including the 103rd and 51st Field Artillery Regiments. He was the Army's youngest general at the time of his 1918 promotion. Post-war, he served in staff roles and retired in 1931. As D.C. Police Superintendent, he was blamed for the 1932 Bonus Army violence, leading to his resignation. He later served as Phoenix Police Chief and a labor mediator. Glassford returned to active duty in WWII and retired in 1943. He was an artist, known for watercolor landscapes. He died in Laguna Beach, California, and was buried at Fort Rosecrans National Cemetery. Married twice, with four children. His wife Cora authored a biography of him.

The story follows Mariana Cisneros, an orphaned girl shut in by an aunt who despises her. After receiving an education, she becomes a governess to Adela, the silent daughter of Eduardo. Mariana wins Adela's affection and develops feelings for Eduardo. Their love is tested by a secret revealed on their wedding day, leading Mariana to flee but eventually return for love. The telenovela features Daniela Romo as Mariana, Joaquín Cordero as Eduardo, Patricia Tanus as Adela, and Erika Carrasco as child Mariana. Other cast members include Lorena Velázquez, Virginia Manzano, Dolores Tinoco, Ada Carrasco, and Eduardo Liñán.

"The Dice Man" is a 1971 novel by George Cockcroft, written under the pen name Luke Rhinehart. The story follows a psychiatrist who makes life decisions by rolling a die. The book was initially controversial, featuring themes of anti-psychiatry and content involving rape and murder, leading to bans in several countries. It was unclear at first whether it was fiction or autobiography, as the protagonist and author shared similar traits. The book became a cult classic, selling over 2 million copies in multiple languages and remaining in print for over 45 years. It was republished several times with different ISBNs, including 0-900735-00-7 (1971), 0-586-03765-9 (1989), and 0-00-716121-2 (2003). Cockcroft wrote two sequels: "Adventures of Wim" (1986) and "The Search for the Dice Man" (1993), and a companion title, "The Book of the Die" (2000). Colin Falconer is a pen name of Colin Bowles, an English-born Australian writer, born in 1953. Bowles also uses the pen name Mark D'Abranville. He moved to Australia in his twenties, worked as a taxi driver and guitarist, then joined an advertising agency. In 1984, he moved to Sydney to pursue writing. He worked as a freelance journalist and wrote scripts for radio and television before becoming a full-time novelist in 1990. His works include thrillers, children's books, satirical fiction, non-fiction, and scripts. His novels have been translated into 17 languages. Notable works under Colin Falconer include *Harem* (1993), *Aztec* (1999), *The Sultan's Harem* (2004), and *Lord of the Atlas* (2022). Under his original name, he wrote *Wit's Dictionary* and *G'day, Teach Yourself Australian*. He lived in Western Australia and worked in the volunteer ambulance service. He is married and lives in Australia.

The Cuckoo Clock is a 1877 British children's fantasy novel by Mary Louisa Molesworth, published by Macmillan. Initially released under the pen name Ennis Graham, it was reissued in 1882 as by Mrs. Molesworth. Both editions and many later ones were illustrated by Walter Crane. An 1893 uniform edition is available online at the University of Pennsylvania. A 1914 edition illustrated by Maria L. Kirk is available at HathiTrust. The story follows a child and a cuckoo clock who become friends, with the clock transporting her to magical places. Themes include love, friendship, and the moral didactic tale. The novel was adapted into an animated short film by Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer in 1950, directed by Tex Avery. A review from the Pall Mall Gazette praises the book as a "beautiful little story" accessible to children.

**Notes:**

Jane Eyre is a novel by Charlotte Brontë, published on 19 October 1847 under the pseudonym "Currer Bell." It follows the life of Jane Eyre, an orphaned girl who endures abuse at Gateshead Hall, attends Lowood Institution, becomes a governess at Thornfield Hall, and eventually marries Edward Rochester. The novel is divided into 38 chapters and was originally published in three volumes. It is a Bildungsroman focusing on Jane's moral and spiritual growth. Key characters include Jane Eyre, Edward Rochester, Bertha Mason (Rochester's first wife), St. John Rivers, and the Reed family. The novel explores themes of class, feminism, religion, and race, with Bertha Mason representing the racialized "other." Jane's uncle, John Eyre, leaves her a fortune. The novel was adapted into various forms and influenced writers like Jean Rhys, who wrote *Wide Sargasso Sea*. It was initially criticized for its anti-Christian tone and perceived immorality but is now considered a classic of English literature.

"Aunt Jane's Nieces" is a 1906 juvenile novel by L. Frank Baum, published under the pseudonym "Edith Van Dyne." It initiated a ten-book series published between 1906 and 1918. The story follows Jane Merrick, an elderly invalid who invites her three nieces—Louise, Beth, and Patsy—to decide the estate's heir. The series includes titles like "Aunt Jane's Nieces Abroad" (1907) and "Aunt Jane's Nieces in the Red Cross" (1915/1918). The books were illustrated by Emile A. Nelson, James McCracken, and Norman P. Hall. Initially successful, they were reprinted between 2005 and 2007. The series features themes of inheritance, character development, and social issues, with the final book addressing World War I. The books were popular as graduation gifts and outsold Oz books toward the end of Baum's life.

The bazaar connects Naqsh-e Jahan Square to Kohneh Square and the Seljukid part of Isfahan. It includes sections such as Orian bazaar, Harounie, Nimavard-e Golshan, Makhlas, Samavarsazha, and Maqsudbeyk. Notable historical buildings within the bazaar include the Nimavar school, Sadr school, Khayyatha mosque, Zolfaghar mosque, Shishe mosque, and Jarchi mosque. The main entrance is called the Qeysarieh gate. The bazaar is a vaulted two-kilometre street linking the old city with the new. It is situated near the Jameh Mosque, one of the oldest mosques in Isfahan and Iran. The square is one of the largest in the world

Ramaipur is a village in Bhadohi district, Uttar Pradesh, India. It lies on the link road connecting Chauri Bazar (Varanasi-Bhadohi road) to Maharazganj Bazar (Varanasi-Allahabad road). The nearest railway station is Parasipur, 7 km away. The village market includes at least 10 grocery shops, three primary schools, four barber shops, half a dozen sweet shops, and a dozen chai and pan shops. The weekly sabzi bazar occurs on Thursday. The market serves nearby villages. Over twenty self-appointed medical practitioners, none academically qualified, provide primary health services. The main economic activities are agriculture (subsistence-based) and carpet weaving, with bhadohi woolen carpets woven by landless people, excluding Brahmins. Migration to Kolkata and Mumbai contributes to income via remittances. The village has rabi wheat and kharif rice crops, relying on groundwater irrigation from government and private bore wells. Much of the land is alkaline, challenging agriculture.

It has the second-largest fish market in Hyderabad, after Musheerabad. Adjacent Moazzam Jahi Market is the largest fruit and vegetable market, though it is being replaced by Kothapet's market. input: Which case was brought to court first Miller v. California or Gates v. Collier ?

notes.note_text: The Trusty System was a prison disciplinary and security method used in the U.S. until the 1980s, enforced in states like Mississippi, Arkansas, Alabama, Louisiana, New York, and Texas. It was made compulsory under Mississippi state law and replaced convict leasing in 1901 at Mississippi State Penitentiary at Parchman. The system allowed inmates, particularly those in the hierarchy known as "trusty shooters" (armed inmates) and unarmed trusties, to control other inmates, perform administrative tasks, and enforce discipline. Parchman had about 16,000 acres of farmland, with inmates doing labor. The system was abolished by the 1970–1971 Gates v. Collier ruling, which ended racial segregation and replaced trusty shooters with civilian guards. Some states, like Texas, continued using similar systems until the 1980s, when Ruiz v. Estelle mandated replacement with the SSI system. Inmate trusties could recommend punishments and were involved in physical abuse, including whipping for failing to meet work quotas.

Brockmeyer v. Dun & Bradstreet, 113 Wis. 2d 561, 335 N.W.2d 834 (Wis. 1983). The Wisconsin Supreme Court recognized judicial exceptions to the employment at will doctrine. Charles J. Brockmeyer, a district manager of credit services at Dun & Bradstreet, was fired after the employer settled a sex discrimination suit involving Brockmeyer's former secretary. The court determined that the termination did not violate a well-defined public policy, as the employer's actions did not contravene any statute or constitutional provision. The court affirmed the lower court's decision in favor of the employer. The case is cited in Bammert v. Don's Super Valu, Inc.

Miller v. California, 413 U.S. 15 (1973), established the Miller test for obscenity. Marvin Miller, a California mail-order business owner, was arrested for distributing graphic sexual content in brochures. The California Penal Code 311.2(a) charged him with obscenity, based on Memoirs v. Massachusetts and Roth v. United States. The Supreme Court rejected Miller's argument for a national standard, adopting a three-prong test: (1) appeals to prurient interest under community standards, (2) depicts offensive sexual conduct, and (3) lacks serious value. The decision overturned Memoirs' "utterly without redeeming social value" standard. The case was remanded to the California Superior Court. The Miller test allowed states to regulate obscenity under local community standards, leading to controversies over forum shopping. The decision influenced later cases like Paris Adult Theatre I v. Slaton and Reno v. ACLU, and shaped obscenity law in the digital age.

Gasser v MISAT (C–116/02) is a 2002 European Court of Justice (CJEU) case concerning the interpretation of the Brussels Convention of 1968. Austrian supplier Gasser and Italian distributor MISAT had a choice-of-court agreement favoring an Austrian court. When a dispute arose, MISAT initiated proceedings in an Italian court, citing Article 21 of the Brussels Convention, which includes a lis alibi pendens rule requiring the second-seized court to stay proceedings until the first court determines its jurisdiction. The CJEU ruled that the lis pendens rule takes precedence over party autonomy, upholding the "first come, first served" principle. The decision affected the 2001 Brussels Regulation and Lugano Conventions. The Recast Brussels I Regulation (2012) later reversed this priority, giving chosen courts precedence. The case highlighted risks of tactical litigation and "torpedo claims," where delays in one jurisdiction deter parties from pursuing agreements.

Adams v. Burke, 84 U.S. (17 Wall.) 453 (1873), is a U.S. Supreme Court case that established the exhaustion doctrine. The case involved a patented coffin lid, U.S. Patent No. 38,713, issued in 1863 to Merrill and Horner. The patent was assigned to Lockhart & Seelye for a ten-mile radius around Boston. Adams, the plaintiff, held the patent in an area outside this radius, including Natick, Massachusetts. Burke, an undertaker in Natick, purchased patented coffin lids from Lockhart & Seelye and used them in his business, leading to a lawsuit by Adams. The Massachusetts circuit court dismissed the case, and the Supreme Court affirmed the decision. The Court held that once a patented product is lawfully sold, it is no longer under the patentee's monopoly, and the purchaser may use or resell it freely. Subsequent cases applying this doctrine include Motion Picture Patents Co. v. Universal Film Mfg. Co., 243 U.S. 502 (1917), and Quanta Computer, Inc. v. LG Electronics, Inc.,

Jones v. Cunningham, 371 U.S. 236 (1963), was a Supreme Court case that established the right of state inmates to file a writ of habeas corpus to challenge both the legality and conditions of their imprisonment. Prior to this case, the Court maintained a "hands off" policy, as seen in Pervear v. Massachusetts, 72 U.S. 475 (1866), where it refused federal interference with state incarceration practices, asserting that the Bill of Rights did not apply to the states. This changed with Jones v. Cunningham, allowing federal review of state prison conditions. In Cooper v. Pate (1964), an inmate successfully used a habeas corpus writ to challenge the denial of his right to practice his religion, building on the precedent set by Jones v. Cunningham.

Cheff v. Mathes, 199 A.2d 548 (Del. 1964), addressed director conflict of interest in a corporate change of control. Holland Furnace Company, controlled by the Cheff-Landwehr family (18.5% stock), used door-to-door sales, which declined by 25% from 1948-1956. Arnold Maremont, a businessman, purchased 6% of Holland stock in 1957, later increasing to 11%. He criticized Holland's sales tactics and suggested a shift to wholesaler marketing. The board, fearing Maremont's threat, authorized repurchasing his shares at a premium, effectively paying greenmail. The Delaware Supreme Court applied the business judgment rule, finding the board's actions were protected by a good faith belief in Maremont's threat. The court noted the FTC had investigated Holland's unfair trade practices, and the company later faced contempt for violating a cease and desist order. Maremont, who died in 1978, was also involved in arts and social justice. Holland's sales dropped sharply after 1958, and the company disappeared from Moody's Manual in 19

Gates v. Collier (501 F.2d 1291, 5th Cir. 1974) ended the trusty system and inmate abuse at Mississippi State Penitentiary (Parchman Farm), established in 1904 in Sunflower County, Mississippi. Parchman, styled after plantations, housed mostly Black men and used convict leasing. The prison had harsh conditions, including filthy barracks, open ditches, and severe punishments like handcuffing and forced awkward positions. Roy Haber, a civil rights lawyer, documented abuse between 1969-1971. A class action lawsuit in 1971, led by Nazareth Gates, challenged conditions under the 14th and 8th Amendments. Judge William Keady ruled against Parchman in 1972, calling it "unfit for human habitation." The Fifth Circuit upheld this, abolishing racial segregation and the trusty system, influencing other states.

WN Hillas & Co Ltd v Arcos Ltd [1932] UKHL 2 is a House of Lords case concerning English contract law. The case involved Hillas & Company, merchants purchasing timber from Arcos. An agreement was made for the purchase of 22,000 standards of timber, with an option to buy 100,000 standards the following year at a 5% price reduction. Arcos refused to sell the 100,000 standards, leading Hillas to win at trial but lose on appeal to the Court of Appeal. The House of Lords ruled that judges may imply terms into a contract based on past dealings, moving away from strict literal interpretation. Lord Wright suggested that good consideration could bind parties to negotiate in good faith, but this view was later rejected in Walford v Miles (1992). The case is notable for its influence on contract interpretation principles.

Fletcher v. Peck, 10 U.S. (6 Cranch) 87 (1810), was a landmark Supreme Court case where the Court first ruled a state law unconstitutional. The case involved the Yazoo Land Act of 1795, under which Georgia sold 54,000 sq mi of land to four companies for $500,000. The sale was part of the Yazoo Land Scandal, involving bribes. The law was later repealed, but the Supreme Court ruled it unconstitutional, upholding the validity of the land sale. Robert Fletcher and John Peck were speculators; Fletcher sued Peck in 1803, claiming Peck lacked clear title. The Court, led by Chief Justice John Marshall, held that the sale was a binding contract under the Contract Clause (Article I, Section 10, Clause I), and the legislature could not invalidate it. The decision reinforced the sanctity of contracts and hinted at Native American land rights limitations.

Rabbi Anani ben Sason (Hebrew: רבי ענני בר ששון), also called 'Anani, 'Inani, and 'Inyani, was a Jewish Talmudist from the third century CE in the Land of Israel, part of the third generation of amoraim. He was a contemporary of Rabbi Ammi. Anani rarely discussed Halakhot and was not original in his halakhic discussions. In aggadah, he was often original, offering explanations such as the priestly vestments providing atonement like sacrifices. He cited R. Chanina regarding the miter atoning for haughtiness. He also interpreted God's appearance in the burning bush, referencing Scripture. His name may have been Ananiel, with "Anani" being an apocopated form to avoid mentioning "El." There is a possible connection to R. Chanina b. Issi (Sissi), though chronological issues complicate this. Isaac Reichlin proposed the name Ananiel.

Lev Kuleshov (1899–1970) was a Russian and Soviet filmmaker and film theorist, a founder of the Moscow Film School, and a key figure in Soviet montage theory. He developed the Kuleshov effect, demonstrating how editing influences audience emotions. He also created the theory of creative geography. Born into an intellectual family, he moved to Moscow after his father's death in 1916 and worked in film production. He co-directed his first film, "Twilight," in 1917. Kuleshov taught at the National Film School and influenced notable students like Vsevolod Pudovkin and Sergei Eisenstein. His notable films include "The Extraordinary Adventures of Mr. West in the Land of the Bolsheviks" (1924) and "By the Law" (1926). He received the Order of Lenin (1967) and the title People's Artist of the RSFSR (1969). He died in Moscow in 1970 and was buried at the Novodevichy Cemetery. His wife was Aleksandra Khokhlova, an actress and educator.
