notes.note_text: The Cass Corridor is a neighborhood in west Midtown Detroit, encompassing Cass Park Historic District, Cass-Davenport Historic District, and Old Chinatown. Cass Avenue runs parallel to Woodward Avenue (M-1). The corridor is generally defined between I-75 and I-94, stretching from Woodward to John C. Lodge (M-10) and Grand River Avenue. Notable landmarks include the Detroit Masonic Temple, Cass Technical High School, and Little Caesars Arena (opened September 5, 2017). The area became culturally significant in the 1960s-70s with artists like Tyree Guyton and the White Stripes. It was also known for social issues in the 1970s. Joel Landy renovated buildings since the 2000s, and Third Man Records opened in 2015. Dr. Alesia Montgomery conducted a 5-year study on reinventing Detroit as a green city, focusing on the Cass Corridor, from 2009. The Dally in the Alley arts festival is held there. Avalon International Breads has been located in the area since 1997.

Possessed is an Inverted Impulse roller coaster located at Dorney Park & Wildwater Kingdom in Allentown, Pennsylvania. Manufactured by Intamin and designed by Werner Stengel, it originally debuted as Superman: Ultimate Escape at Six Flags Ohio on May 5, 2000. After Cedar Fair acquired the park in 2004, the coaster was renamed Steel Venom. It closed in 2006 and was moved to Dorney Park, reopening in 2008 as Voodoo before being renamed Possessed in 2009. The ride closed for the 2020 season due to the COVID-19 pandemic and reopened in 2021. The coaster features a "U" layout with two vertical spikes, one twisted and one straight, connected by a launch tract. It originally used linear induction motors and had a holding brake at the top of the rear spike, which is no longer operational. The maximum G-force is 3.7 Gs. A larger version, Wicked Twister, operated at Cedar Point until its closure in September 2021.

- **Georgia Depression**: A depression in the Pacific Northwest region of western North America, encompassing lowland areas of southwestern British Columbia and northwestern Washington along the Salish Sea.  
- **Formation**: Formed 150 million years ago due to continental plate collision. It manifested as a broad valley with rivers flowing into the Pacific Ocean near the Strait of Juan de Fuca.  
- **Geology**: Landscape features glacially striated tablelands and rolling hills underlain by sedimentary rocks. Soils are formed from glacial till, outwash, and lacustrine deposits.  
- **Geography**: Bounded by Pacific Ranges (north), Vancouver Island Ranges and Olympic Mountains (west), and North Cascades (east). Includes Fraser Lowland, Nanaimo and Nahwitti lowlands, Puget Sound basin, and Salish Sea islands and waterways.  
- **Ecology**: Dry, flat, low-elevation area with diverse flora and fauna. Human activity has altered the natural environment through industrialization, agriculture, forestry, urbanization, and suburban sprawl.  
- **Erosion**: Shaped by the Cordilleran Ice Sheet during the Vashon Glaciation (19,000

Steel Venom is an inverted launched roller coaster located at Valleyfair amusement park in Shakopee, Minnesota, United States. It is an Impulse Coaster model manufactured by Intamin, opening in 2003. The ride was unveiled in September 2002 for the 2003 season and officially opened to the public on May 17, 2003. Steel Venom is Valleyfair’s and Minnesota’s first and only launch coaster. The coaster features a single seven-car train with 28 passengers, running along a 200-meter U-shaped track. It includes two 185-foot vertical spikes, with a forward spike featuring a twisted spiral and a rearward spike providing a straight freefall. The train is propelled by linear induction motors (LIMs) and reaches a maximum speed of 68 mph (109 km/h) in under four seconds. A holding brake on the rear straight tower can suspend the train momentarily, typically during the final ascent.

Alouette Lake, originally Lillooet Lake, is a lake and reservoir in Maple Ridge, British Columbia, Canada. Located at the southeast foot of the Golden Ears mountain group, it is approximately 16 km long on a northeast–southwest axis. Renamed in 1914 to avoid confusion with a larger lake and river farther north, it was given the French name "Alouette," meaning "lark." Most of the lake's basin is unlogged, with its north flank protected as part of Golden Ears Provincial Park. A small portion near the narrows is part of the District of Mission. The Alouette Dam, constructed in 1928, is 11.5 km along the South Alouette River and connects to Stave Lake via a 1,067 m tunnel. The Alouette Powerhouse, an 8 MW facility operated by BC Hydro, is located midway along the west shore of Stave Lake. The lake's western shore features a public beach, picnic site, and campground.

Excalibur is a steel roller coaster with a wooden structure located at Valleyfair in Shakopee, Minnesota. Built in 1989 by Arrow Dynamics at a cost of $3,000,000, it stands 105 feet (32 m) tall, reaches a top speed of 54.5 mph (87.7 km/h), and has a minimum height requirement of 48 inches. The ride follows a customized figure-eight track layout and has a ride duration of two minutes and thirteen seconds. Trim brakes were added at the top of the first hill a few years after construction. The bottom and first half of the turn were re-profiled to reduce roughness. The photo spot and "Excalibur Photos" booth were removed and replaced with a Refreshment stand, which was later removed. Valleyfair has applied for a permit to remove Excalibur and replace it with a road and parking lot. The permit involves discharging dredged and fill material into 4.52 acres of wetland.

Bobo people are a Mande ethnic group primarily in Burkina Faso, with some in Mali. They are also the name of the second-largest city, Bobo-Dioulasso. The Bobo-Fing, or "black Bobo," are a Mande people, distinct from the Bwa (Bobo-Oule/Wule), a Gur-speaking group. The Bobo population is about 110,000, with the majority in Burkina Faso. Key towns include Bobo-Dioulasso, Fô, Kouka, and Boura. The Bobo are a decentralized society organized around patrilineages, with each lineage led by a wakoma, or "father of the lineage." Farming is central to their economy, with crops like sorghum, millet, yams, and maize. Cotton is also cultivated and sold to mills in Koudougou. The Bobo believe in a creator god, Wuro, who created the world and established opposing forces. They recognize two epochs: the time of Wuro and the historical time when Dwo, Wuro's son, was given to humanity. Sources include Christopher Roy and Guy Le Moal.

Eureka is a research base on Ellesmere Island, Nunavut, Canada. It is the third-northernmost permanent research community, after Alert (Ellesmere Island) and Nord (Greenland). Eureka has the lowest average annual temperature and precipitation in Canada. Its postal code is X0A 0G0, and area code is 867. The base includes the Eureka Aerodrome, Environment and Climate Change Canada Weather Station, and the Polar Environment Atmospheric Research Laboratory (PEARL), which ceased full-time operation in 2012 but resumed in 2013. Founded on April 7, 1947, it began regular weather observations in 1948. The station has a rotational staff of at least 8. It is supplied every six weeks by air and annually by a supply ship. Eureka experiences a polar climate (ET), with the midnight sun from April 10 to August 29. The annual mean temperature is −18.8 °C, and the highest recorded temperature is 20.9 °C (July 14, 2009). Flora and fauna include muskox, Arctic wolves, and various birds.

The Battle of White Plains occurred on October 28, 1776, during the American Revolutionary War. It was part of the New York and New Jersey campaign. British General William Howe aimed to cut off George Washington's retreat, leading to the battle near White Plains, New York. Washington established a defensive position but failed to control high ground. The battle involved British and Hessian forces, including regiments like the 42nd (Black Watch) and the Grenadier Regiment von Rahl. American forces included units like Spencer's Division and Parson's Brigade. The battle resulted in significant casualties, with estimates of 267 British and Hessians killed, wounded, or missing. American losses are uncertain but range from 150–500. After the battle, Washington retreated north, leading to the December 26 Battle of Trenton. The White Plains Historical Society commemorates the event annually.

Wicked Twister was an inverted roller coaster at Cedar Point, Sandusky, Ohio, USA. Designed by Werner Stengel, it was a double-twisting Impulse model by Intamin. Opened May 5, 2002, as the tallest and fastest inverted coaster, it held the record until 2021. Closed September 7, 2021, after 20 seasons and 16 million rides. Announced for retirement in May 2021, confirmed August 6, 2021. Demolished November 3, 2021, completed February 8, 2022. The ride featured two 215-foot spikes with 450-degree vertical twists. It had one train with eight cars, seating 32 riders. The theme song was "The Winner" by the Crystal Method. The ride used linear induction motors for launches, reaching a maximum speed of 72 mph and height of 206 feet. Similar coasters include The Flash, Possessed, and Steel Venom.

notes.note_text: 2016 Honda Indy Grand Prix of Alabama: 4th round of 2016 IndyCar Series, held at Barber Motorsports Park, Birmingham, Alabama, over 90 laps. Simon Pagenaud won, his second consecutive victory, leading most of the race. He finished 13.7 seconds ahead of Graham Rahal, who finished second despite contact with Jack Hawksworth. Josef Newgarden was third. Juan Pablo Montoya, who qualified 21st, finished fifth. Alexander Rossi, the highest-finishing rookie, placed 15th. Sébastien Bourdais set a new track record in qualifying but started fifth. Qualifying pole was taken by Pagenaud, beating Will Power. The race had one caution flag due to an incident involving Carlos Muñoz and Mikhail Aleshin. No DNFs occurred. Championship points included 1 point for leading at least 1 lap, 2 points for leading most laps, and 1 point for pole position. Championship standings after the race are noted, with top five positions included.

Scott Dixon entered as reigning Drivers' Champion; Chevrolet as Manufacturer's Champion. Simon Pagenaud won Drivers' Championship, Chevrolet retained Manufacturer's title. Pagenaud was first European driver to win title since Dario Franchitti (2011).

Simon Pagenaud (born 18 May 1984) is a French IndyCar driver contracted to Meyer Shank Racing in the No. 60 Honda. He won the 2016 IndyCar championship, the 2019 Indianapolis 500 (first French winner since 1920), and both 2022 and 2023 24 Hours of Daytona. He began racing in French Formula Renault, moved to the U.S. in 2006, and won the 2007 Champ Car Atlantic. He competed in the American Le Mans Series (ALMS), winning LMP1 class in 2009 and 2010. Pagenaud joined Team Penske in 2015, nearly winning the 2015 Indy 500, and won the 2016 IndyCar title. He moved to Meyer Shank Racing in 2022. Pagenaud competed in the 24 Hours of Le Mans in 2009, 2010, and 2023. He has also participated in the iRacing virtual Indy 500 and the

2017 Honda Indy Toronto was an IndyCar Series event held on July 16, 2017, in Toronto, Ontario, Canada, as the 12th round of the 2017 season. Simon Pagenaud qualified on pole position, setting a new track record of 58.9124 seconds at 109.14 mph. Josef Newgarden won the race, his second victory of the season. Pre-race, Schmidt Peterson Motorsports replaced Mikhail Aleshin with Sebastián Saavedra. Qualifying saw Esteban Gutiérrez crash in turn 11 and J. R. Hildebrand hit the wall in turn 8. During the race, Hélio Castroneves took the lead early, but Will Power crashed in turn 3, retiring. Newgarden overtook Pagenaud on lap 57 to win by 1.87 seconds over Alexander Rossi. Scott Dixon led the championship but fell behind by three points over Hélio Castroneves. Simon Pagenaud remained in third, and Newgarden moved past Will Power in the standings.

The 2011 Indy Grand Prix of Sonoma was the seventh running of the event and the fourteenth round of the 2011 IndyCar Series season. Held on August 28, 2011, at the 2.303-mile Infineon Raceway in Sonoma, California, the race consisted of 75 laps. Will Power led 71 laps and finished first, with Team Penske securing 1st–2nd–3rd positions on the podium. This marked the first 1–2–3 finish for Penske in an IndyCar race since Nazareth in 1994. Power closed the gap to championship leader Dario Franchitti, narrowing the points difference to 26 and the Mario Andretti Road Course Trophy gap to 7 points. Simon Pagenaud replaced Simona de Silvestro due to visa complications, as U.S. Customs denied her entry. One driver received a penalty for blocking, resulting in a position drop to the end of the lead lap. Championship standings after the race are noted, with only the top five positions included.

The 2009 Monterey Sports Car Championships, presented by Patrón, was the tenth and final round of the 2009 American Le Mans Series season. The event took place on October 11, 2009, at Mazda Raceway Laguna Seca in Monterey, California. The overall race was won by the Acura of de Ferran Motorsports, driven by Simon Pagenaud and Gil de Ferran, featuring a tribute livery based on Jim Hall's Chaparrals. Adrian Fernández and Luis Díaz secured the LMP2 category victory, finishing just six tenths of a second behind the overall winner. The GT2 class was won by the #45 Flying Lizard Motorsports Porsche after contact with the #3 Corvette Racing car on the final lap. Guy Cosmo and John Baker of Orbit Racing won the ALMS Challenge category after the Velox Motorsport entry was disqualified. Qualifying results and race results include class winners and cars not classified (NC) for failing to complete 70% of the winner's distance.

Simona de Silvestro (born 1 September 1988) is a Swiss-Italian racing driver currently employed by Porsche. She competed in the 2015/16 FIA Formula E Championship with Amlin Andretti and previously in the IndyCar Series. Nicknamed "Iron Maiden" and "Swiss Miss," she won the 2008 Atlantic Championship Grand Prix of Long Beach, becoming the second woman to win in that series. She competed full-time in IndyCar from 2010–2012, achieving a podium finish in 2013. De Silvestro joined Sauber's Formula One program in 2014 but was suspended due to contractual issues. She scored points in Formula E in 2016 and competed in V8 Supercars and GT3 racing. De Silvestro participated in the 2021 Indianapolis 500 with Paretta Autosport. Her career includes notable crashes, injuries, and challenges with car performance and team support.

The 2003 Formula Renault 2000 Masters season was the thirteenth Eurocup Formula Renault 2.0 season. It ran from 24 May to 26 October, consisting of eight races. Cram Competition's Esteban Guerrieri, also Argentine Formula Renault champion, won three races and secured the championship by a 36-point margin over Danish driver Robert Schlünssen. Schlünssen won an abandoned race at Assen. ASM's Simon Pagenaud finished two points behind Schlünssen and also won a race at TT Circuit Assen. Other race winners included Paul Meijer, Ryan Sharp, and Reinhard Kofler. The first race at Assen was abandoned after three laps due to a massive crash, resulting in no points being awarded. The championship standings include Guerrieri, Schlünssen, and Pagenaud as top drivers.

The 2006 Champ Car Atlantic season was the 33rd season of the Champ Car Atlantic Championship. It ran from April 9 to September 24, with races held at various tracks including Long Beach and Road America. Simon Pagenaud won the Drivers' Championship, driving for Team Australia. The series was sponsored by Yokohama and powered by Mazda. The season included oval and speedway tracks, as indicated by the "(O)" notation in the schedule. Final driver standings and race results were documented. Related information includes the 2006 Champ Car season, the 2006 Indianapolis 500, and the 2006 IndyCar Series season. External links to ChampCarStats.com are provided for further reference.

The 2014 Shell and Pennzoil Grand Prix of Houston was the second doubleheader of the 2014 season, featuring Rounds 9 and 10 of the 2014 IndyCar Series. Carlos Huertas won Race 1, and Simon Pagenaud won Race 2. The event took place in Houston. The race results are classified as follows: Huertas first in Race 1, Pagenaud first in Race 2. input: The 53rd National Hockey League All-Star Game took place at the indoor arena that was completed in what year?

notes.note_text: The 6th National Hockey League All-Star Game was held on October 5, 1952, at the Detroit Olympia, home of the Detroit Red Wings. The game followed a format where the first and second All-Star teams, each with additional players, competed against each other. It ended in a tie for the second consecutive year. As a result, the NHL decided to revert to the previous format, where the Stanley Cup winner plays an all-star team. The game was officiated by referee Bill Chadwick and linesmen George Young and Doug Young. The event is notable for its continuation of the All-Star format despite the tie, leading to a change in the NHL's approach for future games.

The 2018 NHL All-Star Game took place on January 28, 2018, at Amalie Arena in Tampa, home of the Tampa Bay Lightning. It was the first time Tampa hosted since 1999. The game used a 3-on-3, single-elimination format with teams from each of the four NHL divisions. The Pacific Division won, with Brock Boeser of the Vancouver Canucks named MVP. The Skills Competition occurred on January 27, with winners including Connor McDavid (Fastest Skater) and Alexander Ovechkin (Hardest Shot). Uniforms featured Adidas three stripes and color schemes mirroring the Lightning's home colors. Coaches were selected based on team performance, with Jon Cooper of the Lightning as Atlantic captain. Brock Boeser was the sole rookie selected. Jonathan Quick withdrew, replaced by Mike Smith, and Taylor Hall was injured, replaced by Brian Boyle. The event included festivities like the Gasparilla Pirate Festival and performances by Kid Rock and Lindsay Ell. The game was broadcast by NBC in the U.S. and CBC/Sportsnet in Canada.

The 53rd NHL All-Star Game took place on February 2, 2003, at the Office Depot Center in Sunrise, Florida. It was the first All-Star Game since 1997 using the Eastern Conference–Western Conference format. The YoungStars Game, held on February 1, featured rookies coached by assistant coaches based on team performance. The Western Conference won the Skills Competition. The All-Star Game saw Dany Heatley score four goals, tying a record, and the game ended in a shootout where the West won 6–5. Heatley was named MVP. The Eastern Conference had five injury replacements. Uniforms featured black trim with silver and white accents, and national flags were worn on the left shoulder. Referees were Dennis LaRue and Dan O'Halloran. Canadian anthem by Paul Brandt, American by Jorge Moreno.

The 1997 NHL All-Star Game was held on January 18, 1997, at the San Jose Arena in San Jose, home of the San Jose Sharks. The Eastern Conference defeated the Western Conference 11–7. The game, originally scheduled for the 1994–95 season, was canceled due to the NHL lockout. The Eastern Conference won the skills competition for the first time since 1992. Al MacInnis (St. Louis Blues) won the Hardest Shot at 98.9 mph. Ray Bourque (Boston Bruins) won Shooting Accuracy with 4 hits in 7 shots. John Vanbiesbrouck (Florida Panthers) won the Goaltenders Competition. Mark Recchi (Montreal Canadiens) led the Eastern Conference with a hat-trick and was named MVP. Owen Nolan (San Jose Sharks) scored two goals in eight seconds in the second period. The game was officiated by Rob Shick, with linesmen Ron Asselstine, Bob Hodges, and Leon Stickle. It was televised by FOX, CBC, and SRC.

The 52nd NHL All-Star Game took place on February 2, 2002, at the Staples Center in Los Angeles. The World team defeated North America 8-5, marking the last All-Star Game using the North America vs. World format. The YoungStars Game featured Team Melrose and Team Fox, with Melrose winning 13-7. notes.note_text: Austrobaileyales is an order of flowering plants with about 100 species, including trees, shrubs, and lianas. It is part of the basal angiosperms, specifically the ANA grade, which diverged early from other flowering plants. The order includes three families: Austrobaileyaceae (monotypic, containing Austrobaileya scandens), Schisandraceae (trees, shrubs, lianas with essential oils), and Trimeniaceae (essential oil-bearing trees and lianas). The APG II system (2003) recognizes Austrobaileyales, placing it among basal angiosperms. The Cronquist system (1981) grouped these plants into the order Illiciales, with families Illiciaceae and Schisandraceae. Illicium verum, or star anise, is the best-known species. The Schisandraceae family includes several dozen species in East and Southeast Asia and the Caribbean. The Trimeniaceae family has about six species in Southeast Asia, eastern Australia, and the Pacific Islands. The APG system (1998) did not recognize the order.

Tibouchina is a neotropical flowering plant genus in the Melastomataceae family, native to Mexico, the Caribbean, and South America (as far south as northern Argentina). It includes subshrubs, shrubs, and small trees with purple flowers. The genus was established by Aublet in 1775, with T. aspera as the type species. A 2013 phylogenetic study found Tibouchina paraphyletic, leading to a 2019 split into four genera: Tibouchina, Pleroma, Chaetogastra, and Andesanthus. As of May 2022, Plants of the World Online recognizes several species within Tibouchina. All species are native to the Americas and are considered noxious weeds in Hawaii. Some species, like T. araguaiensis and T. mathaei, have narrow distributions, while others, such as T. aspera and T. barbigera, are more widespread. The genus is monophyletic in its re-circumscribed form, with diagnostic features including scale-like trichomes and a long pedoconnective on anthers.

Cyrtandra is a genus of flowering plants in the family Gesneriaceae, containing about 600 species, with more being discovered. It is the largest genus in the family. Native to Southeast Asia, Australia, and the Pacific Islands, with the center of diversity in Southeast Asia and the Malesian region. The genus includes small herbs, vines, shrubs, epiphytes, and trees. It is characterized by two stamens and mostly white flowers, though some species have red, orange, yellow, or pink flowers. Almost all species live in rainforest habitats. The genus is considered a supertramp genus. Hawaiian Cyrtandra are known as ha‘iwale. Selected species include Cyrtandra aurantiicarpa, Cyrtandra biserrata (Molokai cyrtandra), Cyrtandra hawaiensis (Hawaii cyrtandra), and Cyrtandra kauaiensis (ulunahele). Many species are rare, localized, and endangered. The plants are highly polymorphic and readily hybridize.

Pothos is a genus of flowering plants in the family Araceae, native to regions including China, the Indian Subcontinent, Australia, New Guinea, Southeast Asia, and various Pacific and Indian Ocean islands. The common houseplant Epipremnum aureum, also known as "pothos," was previously classified under this genus. Neo P1 is a genetically engineered variant of pothos designed to remove volatile organic compounds from air. The genus includes numerous species, such as Pothos chinensis found in China, Taiwan, Japan, and Indochina, and Pothos scandens native to the Indian subcontinent and Indo-China. Other species are listed with their respective geographic locations, including Borneo, Sumatra, Philippines, and New Guinea.

Chiranthodendron is a flowering plant genus in the Malvaceae family, containing one species: Chiranthodendron pentadactylon. Common names include devil's hand tree, monkey's hand tree, Mexican hand tree, hand-flower, árbol de las manitas, and mācpalxōchitl. The scientific name translates to "five-fingered hand-flower tree." Native to Guatemala and southern Mexico, the tree grows on wet slopes, reaching 10.5–27.5 m in height. It has large, shallowly lobed leaves with brown indumentum on the underside. Flowers appear in late spring/early summer, with five bright red, upward-curving stamens resembling a clawed hand. The fruit is a 7.5–10 cm long, five-lobed capsule with black seeds. Originally described from a cultivated specimen in Toluca, outside its native range. The Aztecs revered the tree. It is closely related to Fremontodendron, producing the intergeneric hybrid ×Chiranthofremontia lenzii with yellow flowers. The Aztecs used its flowers for remedies for abdominal pain, heart issues,

Zeltnera is a genus of flowering plants in the gentian family, established in 2004 when the genus Centaurium was split due to genetic analysis revealing it was polyphyletic. The new genus Zeltnera contains most North American centauries, with about 25 species. It includes annual, biennial, or short-lived perennial herbs with taproot or fibrous root systems. The flowers have a tubular throat opening into a flat corolla with four or five lobes, varying in color. Zeltnera is divided into three groups: "Californian," "Texan," and "Mexican," based on geography. The genus is named after Swiss botanists Louis and Nicole Zeltner. Species include Zeltnera abramsii, Zeltnera arizonica, Zeltnera beyrichii, and others, with common names such as Arizona centaury and Lady Bird's centaury.

Psychotria is a genus of flowering plants in the family Rubiaceae, containing 1,582 species, making it one of the largest genera of flowering plants. It has a pantropical distribution and consists of small understorey trees in tropical forests. Some species, particularly in central Africa and the Pacific, are endangered due to deforestation. Certain species, including Psychotria viridis, produce dimethyltryptamine (DMT), a psychedelic chemical. The passage also notes that some species were formerly classified under other genera, such as Psychotria elata, now classified as Palicourea elata, and Psychotria poeppigiana, now Palicourea tomentosa. Pleroma heteromallum, also known as Tibouchina heteromalla, Tibouchina grandifolia, and silverleafed princess flower, is an evergreen flowering plant in the Melastomataceae family. Native to French Guiana, Bolivia, and Brazil. It grows to an average height of 4–6 feet (1.2–1.8 m), with a maximum of 8–10 feet (2.4–3.0 m). The plant has woody stems, large silvery green, simple, ovate, velvety, oppositely arranged leaves. Leaves are 4–6 inches (10–15 cm) long with prominent puffed-up veins. Old leaves turn orange before dropping. Inflorescence is a panicle of purple flowers with five petals. Cultivated as an ornamental for foliage and flowers. Sensitive to cold but tolerates light frost.

Aureusvirus is a genus of viruses in the family Tombusviridae. It includes six species: Cucumber leaf spot virus, Elderberry aureusvirus 1, Johnsongrass chlorotic stripe mosaic virus, Maize white line mosaic virus, Pothos latent virus, and Yam spherical virus. These viruses are non-enveloped, with icosahedral and spherical geometries, T=3 symmetry, and a diameter of approximately 30 nm. Their genomes are linear and about 4.4 kb in length. Viral replication is cytoplasmic and lysogenic. Entry occurs via penetration, and replication follows the positive-stranded RNA virus model. Transcription uses premature termination for subgenomic RNA, while translation involves leaky scanning and termination suppression. The virus exits via tubule-guided movement. Plants are the natural hosts, and transmission occurs mechanically, seed-borne, or through contact.

The tribe Anthurieae contains the genus Anthurium Schott. The tribe Pothoeae includes the genus Pothos L., Pedicellarum M.Hotta (a monotypic genus), and Pothoidium Schott (also monotypic). Eric M. Plakun is an American psychiatrist, psychoanalyst, researcher, and forensic psychiatrist serving as the medical director/CEO at the Austen Riggs Center in Stockbridge, Massachusetts. He graduated from Columbia University College of Physicians and Surgeons in 1972 and completed his psychiatric residency and fellowship at Dartmouth-Hitchcock Medical Center. Plakun is a Distinguished Life Fellow of the American Psychiatric Association (APA) and a founding leader of the APA Psychotherapy Caucus, established in 2014. He has authored nearly 100 articles and book chapters, focusing on borderline personality disorder, treatment-resistant disorders, and psychosocial treatments. Steve Robinson (born September 7, 1946) is an American radio manager, producer, and executive producer. New Jersey Network (NJN) was a public TV and radio network serving New Jersey, operating from 1968 to 2011. NJN's TV network covered all of New Jersey and parts of PA, NY, CT, and DE. Radio stations began in 1991, with WNJT-FM in Trenton. NJN's TV stations were transferred to WNET under Public Media NJ, while radio stations were sold to New York Public Radio and WHYY-FM. NJN produced programs like "Due Process" and "Shepherd's Pie." The stations primarily serve underserved populations, including greater Minnesota, diverse communities, and students, reaching a combined audience of about 300,000 listeners. The B-side, an instrumental version of "Every Beat of My Heart," reached No. 99 on the Billboard Hot 100. The song was also recorded by Wanda Jackson (2011 album *The Party Ain't Over*) and Glenn Danzig (2020 album *Danzig Sings Elvis*). Personnel for Elvis's version include Elvis Presley (lead vocals, acoustic guitar), Scotty Moore (electric guitar), D. J. Fontana (drums), Hank Garland (bass), Bob Moore (double bass), Floyd Cramer (piano), Boots Randolph (saxophone), Buddy Harman (drums), and The Jordanaires (backing vocals). "Santa Bring My Baby Back (To Me)" is a 1957 Christmas song written by Aaron Schroeder and Claude Demetrius, recorded by Elvis Presley. It was released on RCA Victor's Elvis' Christmas Album in 1957. The song was recorded on September 7, 1957, and features the Jordanaires. It appeared on an RCA Victor 45 EP, EPA-4108, with "Santa Claus is Back in Town", "Blue Christmas", and "I'll Be Home for Christmas", which reached #1 on the Billboard EP chart. The single reached #7 on the UK Singles Chart in November 1957. The song has appeared on multiple reissues of the Elvis' Christmas Album, including 1958, 1970, 1975, and 1985 versions. Cover versions include "Baby Come Back" by Johnny Rivers (1958), and recordings by The Smithereens, The Refreshments, Jeff Healey, and others. John Candy performed the song in a Christmas-themed SCTV episode. Train covered it on their 2015 album *Christmas in Tahoe*.

Britney Spears, an American pop singer, made her chart debut in November 1998 with "...Baby One More Time," which became globally successful. Her debut album, ...Baby One More Time (1999), reached number one in Canada and the US and was certified fourteen-times platinum by the RIAA. Her second album, Oops!... I Did It Again (2000), was the fastest-selling female album in the US. The third album, Britney (2001), included "I'm a Slave 4 U" and "Toxic," the latter earning her a Grammy. Her fourth album, In the Zone (2003), featured "Me Against the Music" with Madonna. Blackout (2007) and Circus (2008) were her fifth and sixth albums, with the latter achieving four album debuts over 500,000 units. Femme Fatale (2011) and Britney Jean (2013) followed, with "Work Bitch" certified platinum. Glory (2016) received critical praise. Heaven Only Knows is the seventh album by R&B artist Teddy Pendergrass. Released in 1984, it was his final studio album for Philadelphia International Records, following his departure from the label to join Asylum Records. The album produced one single, "I Want My Baby Back," which reached #61 on the Billboard charts. The critical reception noted that, aside from "Crazy About Your Love," the Gamble- and Huff-produced tracks were described as mawkish and overblown. The track listing includes songs such as "Crazy About Your Love" (Bobby Womack, Kenny Gamble, Leon Huff), "I Want My Baby Back" (Womack, Gamble), and "Heaven Only Knows" (LeRoy Bell, Casey James). Other tracks include "Judge for Yourself," "Life Is for Living," "You and Me for Right Now," "Just Because You're Mine," and "Don't Ever Stop (Giving Your Love to Me)."

Mark Chesnutt is the tenth studio album by American country music artist Mark Chesnutt. It was released under Columbia Records Nashville and features three singles: "She Was", "I Want My Baby Back", and "I'm in Love with a Married Woman". These singles peaked at #11, #47, and #48 on the Billboard Hot Country Songs charts, respectively. The album marks Chesnutt's only release with Columbia Records Nashville. The track "I'm in Love with a Married Woman" was later recorded by Blaine Larsen on his 2006 album "Rockin' You Tonight". - The song is an up-tempo R&B track about Carey pleading with Santa to bring back her partner for Christmas. It reached number one on the Billboard Adult Contemporary chart, becoming Carey's seventh number-one hit on the chart.  
- The music video, directed by Ethan Lader, was shot in Los Angeles in October 2010 and features Carey in a "sexy Santa" outfit, inspired by 1960s variety shows.

- The song charted in several international markets, including South Korea, Japan, and Canada.  
- It was later adapted for the 2015 Hallmark movie *A Christmas Melody*.

Kool Keith's fourth solo studio album, *Black Elvis/Lost in Space*, was released on August 10, 1999, under the alias 'Black Elvis' through Relativity Entertainment Distribution. It was delayed from its original release date and did not use the customary Sony Music Distribution prefix (CK) but instead used WK. A sequel, *Black Elvis 2*, was released in 2023. The album features complex rhymes on topics like Black Elvis' viewpoint and space travel. Kool Keith handled all production, with drum programming by Kutmasta Kurt and Marc Live. Guest appearances include Sadat X, Black Silver, Roger Troutman, Motion Man, Kid Capri, and Pimpin' Rex. A promotional video for "Livin' Astro" aired on MTV's *Amp* in early 2000. The album peaked at #180 on the US Billboard 200, #74 on Top R&B/Hip-Hop Albums, and #10 on Heatseekers Albums. Track samples include works by Teddy Pendergrass, Madness, Charles Earland, and Faith Evans.

During his tenure, he compiled a coaching record of 224 wins and 51 losses. Fincham played football at Ohio University from 1983 to 1986. On September 25, 2010, he won his 130th game, surpassing Dave Maurer to become the all-time winningest coach in Wittenberg Tigers football history. James C. Donnelly (December 9, 1881 – March 24, 1952) was an American college football player and coach. Born in Clinton, Massachusetts, he was the oldest of seven children. He attended Classical High School in Worcester, where he played football, then Dartmouth College, graduating in 1905 with an A.B. He played end on the first Dartmouth team to beat Harvard. After law school at Harvard, he practiced law in Worcester and served as a Superior Court judge in 1931. He coached football at Worcester Polytechnic Institute (1909, 1911, 1915), Howard College (1910), and Miami University (1912–1914), compiling a 22–32–4 record. He married Mary O'Reilly in 1920 and had three children. He died in a traffic accident in Ashland, Virginia, on March 24, 1952, along with his wife and daughter Rosemary. His brothers, Charley and Ralph E. Donnelly, were also involved in football.

Joseph F. Simmons (June 5, 1895 – March 4, 1973) was an American football, basketball, and baseball coach. He served as the head football coach at Central Michigan University for one season in 1920, with a record of 4–3–1. During the same academic year, he was also the head basketball and head baseball coach at Central Michigan. Simmons graduated from Carthage College, where he played football, basketball, baseball, and ran track. He coached high school football at South Milwaukee High School in the late 1920s and at Milwaukee Country Day School from 1928 to 1936. He was an assistant football coach at Yale University from 1937 to 1939.

Joe Odom, full name Joseph Edward Odom, was born on December 14, 1979. He is a former NFL linebacker who was selected in the sixth round of the 2003 NFL Draft (191st overall) by the Chicago Bears. Odom was claimed off waivers by the Buffalo Bills on August 23, 2006. He suffered a career-ending knee injury and medically retired after the 2006 season. Currently, he works for the Stephen Gould Corporation in Tampa, FL. He is married to Aline Odom from Brazil and has three daughters: Stella, Luna, and Beatriz Odom. The family resides on a small farm in Myakka City, FL.

Sammy Joe Odom (November 13, 1941 – January 18, 2001) was a professional football player. Born in Shreveport, Louisiana, he attended Minden High School and played for Northwestern State University's Demons football team as a linebacker/defensive tackle in the Gulf States Conference. Drafted in the seventh round (pick 95) of the 1964 NFL Draft by the Cleveland Browns and the tenth round (pick 78) of the 1964 AFL Draft by the Houston Oilers, Odom chose to play for the Oilers. He played 14 games in 1964 as a defensive tackle, recording two interceptions for 22 yards. The following year, he joined the Richmond Rebels in the Continental Football League but did not play and was delisted. Odom died on January 18, 2001, in Mansfield, Louisiana.

Purdue University, established in 1869 in West Lafayette, Indiana, is a public land-grant research university and a member of the Association of American Universities. Founded by John Purdue's donation, it began classes in 1874 with six instructors and 39 students. It offers over 200 undergraduate majors, 70+ graduate programs, and has 18 intercollegiate sports teams. Purdue is known for its engineering program and has 400,000 living alumni. It has 13 Nobel laureates, 1 Turing Award winner, and notable alumni like Neil Armstrong and John Wooden. The university's main campus includes the Purdue Mall, Memorial Mall, and South Campus. Purdue's research expenditures in 2017 were $622.8 million, and it ranks among the top research universities. The university has a strong focus on sustainability and offers over 200 online programs through Purdue Online. Purdue's football team, the Boilermakers, plays at Ross-Ade Stadium and is part of the Big Ten Conference.

Joe West (born October 31, 1952) was an MLB umpire from 1976 to 2021, officiating 5,376 games and setting a record. He worked in the NL, became a crew chief for the 2005 World Series, and was president of the MLB Umpires Association from 2008-2018. He umpired six World Series, three All-Star Games, ten LCS, eight LDS, and four Wild Card Games. West was known for working no-hitters, including Félix Hernández's 2012 perfect game. He was involved in controversies, such as a 1983 incident with Joe Torre, a 2010 comment on the Yankees-Red Sox series, and a 2014 suspension for contact with Jonathan Papelbon. He also faced a defamation lawsuit in 2019. West was nicknamed "Cowboy Joe" and was a singer-songwriter, releasing albums like "Blue Cowboy" and "Diamond Dreams." The Dáil lasted 808 days and had no by-elections. Fianna Fáil formed the 20th Government of Ireland. Seán Treacy (Ind) was elected as Ceann Comhairle on 10 March 1987, proposed by Charles Haughey and seconded by Brian Lenihan. The Dáil consisted of 166 TDs, listed alphabetically by constituency. Fianna Fáil formed the 15th Government under Jack Lynch, who was succeeded by Charles Haughey as Taoiseach in December 1979, forming the 16th Government. Joseph Brennan (FF) was elected Ceann Comhairle on 5 July 1977 with 84 votes, but died on 13 July 1980. P. J. Mara (Patrick James Mara), born 1 February 1942, died 15 January 2016, was an Irish public affairs consultant and politician. He served as Senator from July 1981 to October 1981 and May 1982 to December 1982. Mara was a political adviser to Charles Haughey and served as Fianna Fáil Press Secretary from 1983 to 1987 and Government Press Secretary from 1987 to 1992. He was Director of Elections for Fianna Fáil in 1997, 2002, and 2007. Mara was involved in the Flood Tribunal, where he faced criticism for not cooperating fully. He was married to Breda Brogan, with whom he had a son, John. He also had a daughter, Elena, with partner Sheila. Mara died at Beacon Hospital, leaving an estate of €1,593,213. He was buried in Kinvara, County Galway.

- **Background**: Occurred during the Fianna Fáil government of Jack Lynch, amid the 1969 Northern Ireland riots. A £100,000 government fund was set up for relief, with Haughey in charge.  
- **Key figures**: Haughey (Minister for Finance), Blaney (Minister for Agriculture and Fisheries), Captain James Kelly (Irish Army intelligence officer), John Kelly (Belfast republican leader), Albert Luykx (Belgian businessman), and Mícheál Ó Móráin (Minister for Justice).  
- **Events**: In October 1969, Kelly promised £50,000 to the IRA for weapons. Haughey provided funds and attempted customs clearance. The plot was uncovered by Garda Síochána Special Branch in late 1970.

input: The song that came out ahead of The Wanted's "Lightning" on the UK Singles Chart was featured on which album?

notes.note_text: "Honey to the Bee" is a song by Billie from her 1998 debut album *Honey to the B*. Released on 22 March 1999, it peaked at number three on the UK Singles Chart. It charted at number six in Australia and number five in New Zealand, becoming one of Billie's highest-charting songs in those regions. In Australia, it was the 48th-best-selling song of 1999. In January 2007, it reached number 17 on the UK Singles Chart due to a test by Radio 1 DJ Chris Moyles. The music video, directed by Katie Bell, uses the shorter radio edit. The song was recorded at Ridge Farm and Marcus Studios in London, mixed at Metropolis Studios. In 2003, Swedish group Play covered the song on their album *Replay*, featuring a trip hop beat and soprano vocals.

Clean Bandit is an English electronic music group. They have released two studio albums, two extended plays, 22 singles (including four as a featured artist), 22 music videos, and 13 remixes. Their debut single "A+E" was released in December 2012 and peaked at number 100 on the UK Singles Chart. The debut album *New Eyes* was released in May 2014. The album's second single, "Mozart's House," reached number 17 on the UK chart. The third single, "Dust Clears," peaked at number 43. The fourth single, "Rather Be" (featuring Jess Glynne), topped the UK chart. In 2016, "Rockabye" (featuring Sean Paul and Anne-Marie) became their second UK number one and Christmas number one. "Symphony" (featuring Zara Larsson) was their third UK number one. Their second album, *What Is Love?*, was released on 30 November 2018.

"We Found Love" is a 2011 song by Rihanna from her album *Talk That Talk*, produced by Calvin Harris. It premiered on September 22, 2011, on Capital FM and became a global success, topping the US Billboard Hot 100 for ten non-consecutive weeks. It was Rihanna's eleventh number-one single and the longest-running of 2011. The song charted in 25 countries and sold 10.5 million copies worldwide by 2015. The music video, directed by Melina Matsoukas, won a Grammy for Best Music Video. It features themes of love and loss, with Rihanna's vocals spanning an octave. The song received mixed critical reviews but was praised for its chart success and influence. It was certified nine times platinum in the US and three-times platinum in New Zealand. The video sparked controversy due to its depiction of domestic violence and drug use. The song was performed at major events, including the 2012 Summer Paralympics and Super Bowl LVII.

"Lightning" is the third single from the Wanted's second studio album, *Battleground*, released on 16 October 2011. Written by Steve Mac, Wayne Hector, and Ed Drewett, the song debuted at number two on the UK Singles Chart. Originally intended for the U.S., its release was cancelled. Premiered during the Spring 2011 tour and on mainstream radio on 17 September 2011. The music video, directed by Matt Stawski, was filmed in LA and premiered on 22 September 2011. The band performed the song live on the X Factor and in the Strictly Come Dancing Halloween Special. The track listing includes various remixes and edits. The song received positive reviews from CBBc Newsround and Digital Spy. Band members described it as a new sound and a filler track.

The Wanted, a British-Irish vocal pop group, released three studio albums, one compilation, two extended plays, and fifteen singles. Their debut album, *The Wanted*, was released by Geffen Records in October 2010, reaching number four in the UK and number eleven in Ireland. The album's first single, "All Time Low," peaked at number one in the UK and thirteen in Ireland. "Heart Vacancy" reached number two in the UK and eighteen in Ireland. "Lose My Mind" was less successful, peaking at 19 in the UK and 30 in Ireland. In 2011, they released the charity single "Gold Forever," which peaked at three in the UK and thirteen in Ireland. "Glad You Came" became their second UK number one and first in Ireland. Their second album, *Battleground*, reached number five. In 2013, their third album *Word of Mouth* reached number nine in the UK and seventeen in the US. The band announced an indefinite hiatus but reunited in 2021, releasing a greatest hits album in November 2021 with two new songs.

Gabrielle Aplin's discography includes four studio albums, 17 extended plays, three live albums, and 18 singles. Her first EP, "Acoustic," was released on 13 September 2010. The second EP, "Never Fade," came out on 9 May 2011, featuring a folk rock sound. In April 2011, she performed at BBC Introducing. She signed with Parlophone on 29 February 2012. Aplin provided the soundtrack for the John Lewis 2012 Christmas ad, covering "The Power of Love." Her debut album, "English Rain," was announced on 12 December 2012, with a release date of 13 May 2013. The album reached number 2 on the UK Albums Chart. In 2014, the "English Rain" EP was released in the U.S. on 6 May. Her second studio album, "Light Up the Dark," was released in 2015 and debuted at number 14 on the UK Albums Chart.

"Gold Dust" is a song by DJ Fresh, released as the third single from his second album *Kryptonite*. Initially released in 2008 as a 12", it was re-released in 2010 with vocals from Ce'cile and later included on *Nextlevelism* with Ms. Dynamite. The 2010 version peaked at #24 on the UK Singles Chart. A 2012 re-edit by Shy FX reached #22 in the UK and #39 in Ireland. Combined sales exceeded 600,000 copies, earning a Platinum certification. The music video, directed by Ben Newman and edited by Jacek Zajkowski, was filmed at the Brownsville Project in Brooklyn and features American Double Dutch champions Jumpers in Command performing skipping, skateboarding, and free running. Fraser McAlpine of BBC Chart Blog praised the song and video, calling it "life-affirming" and "astonishingly chipper."

"Grace Kelly" is the second single by British singer Mika, released in 2007 as the opening track of his debut album *Life in Cartoon Motion*. The song reached number one on the UK Singles Chart, becoming the second single to top the chart without physical sales. It was also number one in Ireland, Italy, Norway, and Turkey. The track was inspired by Mika's frustration with record executives wanting him to sound like Craig David, and it features a melody based on Rossini's *Largo al factotum*. The song includes dialogue from *The Country Girl* and references Freddie Mercury. It received positive reviews and was performed at major awards shows. The music video, directed by Sophie Muller, features Mika and Mae Muller. The song has over 5 million sales globally and was part of various media appearances and parodies. It was also performed at Eurovision 2022.

Royal Blood is an English rock duo formed in Brighton in March 2011, consisting of Mike Kerr (bass, vocals) and Ben Thatcher (drums). They signed with Warner Bros. Records and released their debut single "Out of the Black" in October 2013. Their self-titled debut album, released in August 2014, topped the UK, Irish, and Scottish Albums Charts. The album was certified gold by the BPI by September 2014 and platinum for over 300,000 sales. Their second album, *How Did We Get So Dark?*, was released in June 2017. Their third album, *Typhoons*, was announced in January 2021, with a release date of April 30, 2021. The first single from their fourth album, *Back to the Water Below*, was "Mountains at Midnight," released on May 26, 2023, with the album set for September 8, 2023.

notes.note_text: Mirtemir Tursunov (Uzbek: Миртемир Турсунов), known as Mirtemir, was an Uzbek poet and literary translator born on May 30, 1910, in Ikan, Turkistan. He graduated from the Pedagogical University of Samarkand in 1932 with a literature degree. Mirtemir's first poetry collection, *Shuʼlalar qoʻynida* (Under the Lights), was published in 1928. He translated works by Abai Qunanbaiuli, Aleksandr Pushkin, Heinrich Heine, Magtymguly Pyragy, Maxim Gorky, Mikhail Lermontov, Nâzım Hikmet, Nikolay Nekrasov, Pablo Neruda, Samad Vurgun, Shota Rustaveli, and the Kyrgyz epic *Manas*. He was awarded the title of National Poet of the Uzbek SSR in 1971 and received the State Berdaq Prize (1977) and the State Hamza Prize (1979). Posthumously, he was awarded the National Order of Merit in 2002. Mir

Lavinia exilicauda, the hitch, is a cyprinid fish endemic to central California, the only species in the monospecific genus Lavinia. First described in 1854 by Baird and Girard, with the type locality in the Sacramento River. Closely related to the California roach (Hesperoleucus symmetricus), which can hybridize with it. Genomic data support separate lineages. Three DPS/subspecies: Clear Lake hitch (L. e. chi), Monterey hitch (L. e. harengus), and Sacramento hitch (L. e. exilicauda). The hitch is deep-bodied, laterally compressed, with a terminal mouth, silver coloration, and a long anal fin. They grow up to 36 cm, are omnivorous, and tolerate high salinity. Found in lakes, sloughs, and slow-moving rivers. Declining populations due to loss of spawning flows. Listed as threatened under California ESA in 2014.

The University of East Anglia (UEA) Creative Writing Course was established in 1970 by Sir Malcolm Bradbury and Sir Angus Wilson. It offers an M.A. qualification across four strands: Prose, Creative Non-Fiction, Poetry, and Scriptwriting (Skillset accredited). Current course directors include Andrew Cowan, Kathryn Hughes, Lavinia Greenlaw, and Val Taylor. Notable tutors are Margaret Atwood, Amit Chaudhuri, and Trezza Azzopardi. Alumni include Nobel Prize winner Kazuo Ishiguro (1980), Booker Prize winners Anne Enright (1987), Ian McEwan (1971), and Kazuo Ishiguro (1980). Other notable alumni include Costa Book Award winners such as Emma Healey and Andrew Miller, and Women's Prize for Fiction winner Naomi Alderman. The course has also produced Betty Trask Award winners like Rowan Hisayo Buchanan and Imogen Hermes Gowar.

The International Nazim Hikmet Poetry Award honors world poets and writers every two years, established by the Nazim Hikmet Culture and Arts Foundation in 1991. Nazim Hikmet Ran, a Turkish poet, playwright, and political figure, was born on 15 January 1902 in Salonica. He studied in Moscow, faced political arrests, and won the Nobel Peace Prize in 1950. He died in Moscow in 1963. The award's first recipient was Syrian poet Adonis in 1995, followed by Aime Cesaire (1997), Mahmoud Darwish (2003), Erik Stinus (2009), and Zalimkhan Yagub (2014), the first Azerbaijani recipient. The foundation aims to preserve Hikmet's legacy and promote contemporary poetry. The award has faced challenges, including financial issues and international voter recruitment.

Lavinia Elaine Greenlaw (born 30 July 1962) is an English poet, novelist, and non-fiction writer. She won the Prix du Premier Roman for her first novel, *Mary George of Allnorthover* (2001). Greenlaw has been shortlisted for awards including the T. S. Eliot Prize, Forward Prize, and Whitbread Poetry Prize. She was shortlisted for the 2014 Costa Poetry Award for *A Double Sorrow: A Version of Troilus and Criseyde*. Greenlaw is currently Professor of Creative Writing (Poetry) at Royal Holloway, University of London. She studied at Kingston Polytechnic, the London College of Printing, and the Courtauld Institute. Greenlaw has worked as an editor and arts administrator and has held residencies at the Science Museum and Royal Society of Medicine. She has written libretti, radio documentaries, and memoirs, including *The Importance of Music to Girls* (2007) and *Some Answers Without Questions* (2021). Her work often explores themes of displacement, loss, and belonging.

Nâzım Hikmet (15 January 1902 – 3 June 1963), a Turkish poet, playwright, and communist, was born in Selânik. He had mixed heritage, including Turkish, German, Polish, and Georgian. He studied in Istanbul and joined the Turkish War of Independence. Influenced by Soviet poets, he adopted free verse. His poem "Kız Çocuğu" ("The Girl Child") became an anti-war anthem. Banned in Turkey from 1938–1965, he was imprisoned in the 1940s and later exiled to Romania and the Soviet Union. He died in Moscow in 1963. His works were translated into over 50 languages. His family sought repatriation of his remains. His poetry includes "Human Landscapes from My Country" and "The Epic of the War of Independence." His works were published in communist Bulgaria. He was a key figure in Turkish avant-garde and influenced many artists.

Mehmed Ali Pasha (November 18, 1827 – September 7, 1878) was a Prussian-born Ottoman officer and marshal. Warren Weir (born October 1989) is a retired Jamaican sprinter specializing in the 200 metres. He won bronze at the 2012 London Olympics, helping Jamaica sweep the medals. At the 2013 Moscow World Championships, he earned silver, equaling his personal best of 19.79 seconds set in Kingston, Jamaica. Weir trained with the Glen Mills-coached Racers Track Club, alongside Usain Bolt and Yohan Blake. He competed in the 100m and 200m for Calabar High School, setting personal bests of 10.69s (100m) and 13.65s (hurdles) in 2007. Weir's 200m personal best of 19.79s was achieved in 2013. He competed in the 2014 Commonwealth Games, winning silver in the 200m. Weir retired in 2017 after not advancing from heats at the World Championships. He later played rugby sevens for Jamaica, finishing third at the 2018 Central American and Caribbean Games.

The Four-man bobsleigh event included a medal table, though specific results are not detailed in this passage. Steven Daniel Langton (born April 15, 1983) is an American bobsledder. He won silver medals in the two-man and four-man events at the 2014 Winter Olympics and gold in both events at the 2012 FIBT World Championships. Langton attended Northeastern University, graduating cum laude in 2006 with a degree in Business Management and Entrepreneurship. He was a two-year team captain on the track and field team with personal bests in sprint and long jump. Inspired by the 2006 Winter Olympics, he transitioned to bobsledding. At the 2010 Olympics, he competed with John Napier, finishing tenth in the two-man event. At the 2014 Olympics, he competed with Steven Holcomb, winning silver in both two-man and four-man events. Langton has four world championship medals (bronze in 2011 and 2013, gold in 2012) and 21 World Cup medals (11 gold, 7 silver, 3 bronze). Urs Aeberhand (also spelled Aeberhard) is a Swiss bobsledder who competed from the late 1990s to the early 2000s. He won three bronze medals at the FIBT World Championships: two-man event in 2000 and four-man event in 2000, and another four-man event in 2001. Aeberhand also competed in the four-man event at the 2002 Winter Olympics in Salt Lake City, where he and his team finished sixth. Cortina previously hosted in 1937 (Two-man), 1939 (Four-man), 1950, 1954, 1960, and 1966. After Toni Pensperger's death in 1966, safety improvements were made, allowing the 1981 championships. However, James Morgan, an American bobsled driver, died during the third run of the four-man event. A stuntman was killed a week later during filming of *For Your Eyes Only*, leading to track shortening. Cortina did not host another championship until 1989. The event took place on February 8, 1981, with categories for two-man and four-man bobsleigh. A medal table is listed, though its contents are not detailed in this passage.

The Eugenio Monti Olympic Track is a bobsleigh and skeleton track in Cortina d'Ampezzo, Italy, named after Eugenio Monti (1928–2003), who won six bobsleigh medals between 1956 and 1968. The track was first used in 1905-6 and underwent several renovations, including a 1923 construction of a 1200-meter track. It hosted its first FIBT World Championships in 1937 and was used for the 1956 Winter Olympics. The track was shortened after the 1981 FIBT World Championships to 1350 meters and closed in January 2008. It was featured in the 1981 James Bond film *For Your Eyes Only*, and a stuntman was killed during filming. The track was renamed after Monti in 2004 and was set to host the 2011 World Championships but withdrew its bid. It is now artificially refrigerated and could be used for the 2026 Winter Olympics. The track has hosted multiple championships, including Winter Olympics in 195

Katie Uhlaender (born July 17, 1984) is an American skeleton racer who competed since 2003. She won six medals at the FIBT World Championships: two gold (2012, mixed bobsleigh-skeleton team event; 2012 women's skeleton), one silver (2008 women's skeleton), and three bronze (2007 women's skeleton; 2008, 2009 mixed bobsleigh-skeleton team event). She won the women's Skeleton World Cup title twice (2006-7, 2007-8) and placed sixth at the 2006 Winter Olympics. After a snowmobile accident in April 2009, she earned a medical waiver to compete in the 2009-10 season, later undergoing multiple surgeries. She qualified for the 2010 and 2014 Winter Olympics, placing 11th and fourth, respectively. In 2018, she competed in the Pyeongchang Winter Olympics. She testified before the U.S. Helsinki Commission in July 2018 on doping in sports.

The FIBT World Championships 1951 were held in Alpe d'Huez, France. This event marked Germany's return to the FIBT World Championships for the first time since World War II, with the country represented by East Germany and West Germany as separate entities. The championships featured two man bobsleigh and four man bobsleigh events. A medal table was also included. No specific medalists or results are mentioned in this passage. The event took place in 1951 and is associated with the location Alpe d'Huez. The passage highlights the historical significance of Germany's participation under divided national teams.

Andreas Barucha is a German bobsledder born on 2 April 1979 in Potsdam. He has competed since 1999. Barucha won a gold medal in the mixed team event at the 2009 FIBT World Championships in Lake Placid, New York. His best finish at the FIBT World Championships was seventh in the four-man event at Calgary in 2005. His best World Cup finish was second, achieved three times in the four-man event (2005, 2006, 2009). He finished fourth in the four-man event at the 2010 Winter Olympics in Vancouver.

Cortina d'Ampezzo is a town in the Veneto region of Northern Italy, located in the Dolomitic Alps. It was under the Patriarchate of Aquileia and Holy Roman Empire in the Middle Ages, then conquered by Venice in 1420 and Habsburgs in 1508. It hosted the 1956 Winter Olympics and will co-host the 2026 Winter Olympics with Milan. The town's population increases to 40,000 in winter. It has a humid continental climate. The economy relies on tourism, with notable landmarks including the Basilica Minore dei Santi Filippo e Giacomo and museums like the Rinaldo Zardini Palaeontology Museum. Cortina has a Ladin language variant and has a history of hosting cultural and sports events, including the Dino Ciani Festival and the 1953 Miss Italia contest. It has been featured in films like The Pink Panther and For Your Eyes Only. The town has a rich history, including World War I and II events, and is known for its skiing facilities and cultural heritage.

notes.note_text: "Neither Here nor There: Travels in Europe" is a 1991 humorous travelogue by Bill Bryson, documenting his 1990 tour of Europe, with flashbacks to 1972 and 1973 college trips. The 1973 tour included friend Matt Angerer, pseudonymized as Stephen Katz. The journey begins in Hammerfest, Norway, with a goal to see the Northern Lights. Bryson visits numerous European locations, comparing experiences across regions. The book concludes in Istanbul, Turkey, with a view across the Bosphorus to Asia. Key locations include Norway (Hammerfest, Oslo), France (Paris), Belgium (Brussels, Bruges, Antwerp, Spa, Durbuy), Germany (Aachen, Cologne, Hamburg), The Netherlands (Amsterdam, Haarlem), Denmark (Copenhagen), Sweden (Gothenburg, Stockholm), Italy (Rome, Naples, Sorrento, Capri, Florence, Milan, Como), Switzerland (Brig, Geneva, Bern), Liechtenstein, Austria (Innsbruck, Salzburg, Vienna), Yugoslavia (Split, Sarajevo, Belgrade), Bulgaria (Sofia), and Turkey (Istanbul).

Des Moines, Iowa, is the capital and most populous city in Iowa, incorporated on September 22, 1851, as Fort Des Moines, later renamed in 1857. It is located on the Des Moines River, with a 2020 population of 214,133. The city is a major insurance hub, home to companies like Principal Financial Group and Wellmark Blue Cross Blue Shield. It hosts the first U.S. presidential caucuses. The city's economy includes financial services, publishing, and technology, with recent additions from Microsoft and Facebook. Des Moines has a "City Beautiful" project, a skywalk system, and a diverse cultural scene. The metropolitan area has a population of over 700,000. The city has a humid continental climate, with a 2020 median income of $54,843. It operates under a council-manager government and has a public transit system managed by DART. Notable landmarks include the Iowa State Capitol, the Des Moines Art Center, and the Science Center of Iowa. The city has sister cities in Japan, France, China, Russia, Kosovo, Italy, and Malaysia.

- **Title**: *The Life and Times of the Thunderbolt Kid*  
- **Author**: Bill Bryson  
- **Publication Year**: 2006  
- **Publication Details**:  
  - **UK**: September 1, 2006, published by Doubleday  
  - **US/Canada**: October 17, 2006, published by Broadway Books (US) and Doubleday Canada (Canada)

  - Memoir about Bryson's childhood in Des Moines, Iowa, 1950s–early 1960s  
  - Mentions his parents, Bill Sr. and Mary Bryson, and his alter-ego "the Thunderbolt Kid"

Bill Bryson's *African Diary* is a 2002 book by travel writer Bill Bryson. The book chronicles his 2002 trip to Kenya, detailing his experiences, observations on Kenyan culture, geography, and politics, and his visits to poverty-fighting projects run by CARE International. Bryson donated all royalties from the book to CARE International. 

In a Guardian review, Lionel Shriver criticized the book's length, calling it "less a book than a pamphlet" and disliking its tone, which he described as "a po-faced, gee-whizz sincerity ill-suited to a writer who has made his reputation for being light and wry (and even snide) in droll travel books."

"Notes from a Big Country," also known as "I'm a Stranger Here Myself" in the U.S., is a collection of articles by Bill Bryson published in 1998 in Britain and 1999 in paperback. Originally written for The Mail on Sunday's Night and Day supplement between 1996 and 1998, the book explores Bryson's experiences and views on relocating to Hanover, New Hampshire, after living in Britain for two decades. The American and British editions differ in spelling and include audience-specific content, as noted in the introduction. Topics covered in the articles include the death penalty, the war on drugs, gardening, commercials, book tours, inefficiency, Thanksgiving, and air travel. The book reflects Bryson's observations and commentary on American and British culture and life.

Michael G. Bryson (August 22, 1942 – May 22, 2012) was a news and sports reporter and editor from Des Moines, Iowa. He was the elder brother of travel writer Bill Bryson. Bryson co-authored *The Babe Didn't Point: And Other Stories About Iowans and Sports* with his son Michael G. Bryson Jr. in 1989. He also wrote *The Twenty-Four-Inch Home Run* in 1990. He worked as an editor and associate publisher at Sun Press Newspapers in Hawaii from 1979 to 1986. He covered the New York Mets in 1969 as a sports reporter for the Associated Press. Bryson was a news reporter for the Des Moines Register and Tribune from 1970 to 1979. He attended Drake University.

"The Lost Continent: Travels in Small-Town America" is a 1989 book by Bill Bryson. It documents his 13,978-mile road trip across the United States from autumn 1987 to spring 1988. The journey, made largely by car, began in Des Moines, Iowa, his childhood hometown, and included reminiscences about his father. The book is divided into two sections: 'East' and 'West'. The 'East' section covers the Midwest, Deep South, East Coast, and New England, returning to Des Moines. The 'West' section includes the Great Plains, South West, California, and the Rocky Mountains. Bryson aimed to experience everyday America, focusing on small towns and overlooked sites rather than tourist attractions. The book is more observational and humorous than fact-based, reflecting Bryson's personal perspective. It was his first travel book. Published in London by Secker in 1989.

"Mother Tongue" is a 1990 book by Bill Bryson, subtitled "English And How It Got That Way." It explores the history, origins, and quirks of the English language, covering topics such as Indo-European roots, the global status of English, etymology, dialects, spelling reform, prescriptive grammar, and swearing. The book aims to make the subject accessible to general readers but has faced criticism for inaccuracies, including the perpetuation of urban myths. It was published in the UK by Penguin Books under the title "Mother Tongue: The English Language." Bryson later authored "Made in America" as a follow-up to this work.

Bill Bryson Sr. (William Eugene Bryson Sr.), born March 3, 1915, in Winfield, Iowa, was an American sportswriter who worked for The Des Moines Register from 1937 to 1978. He covered 32 consecutive World Series. He began his career at the Winfield Beacon. Bryson was recognized as one of the finest sportswriters in the country and was considered possibly the greatest baseball writer ever by a prominent television sports journalist. His son, Bill Jr., a renowned writer, published a tribute in 2001 describing Bryson's last interview with Babe Ruth in 1948. Bryson married Mary Agnes McGuire (1913-2015), an editor at The Des Moines Register, and they had three children: Michael, Bill Jr., and Mary Elizabeth. Bryson died on January 31, 1986, in Des Moines, Iowa, from a heart attack. His son Michael published "The Babe Didn't Point: And Other Stories About Iowans and Sports."

"Down Under" is a 2000 travelogue by Bill Bryson, titled "In a Sunburned Country" in the U.S. and Canada. It is part of the "Walk About" collection with "A Walk in the Woods." The book details Bryson's travels by train and car across Australia, focusing on the Outback, coastal areas, and remote regions. It includes historical accounts of 19th-century explorers and settlers, as well as cultural and natural aspects of Australia. The book is divided into three parts: "Into the Outback," covering the journey from Sydney to Perth; "Civilized Australia" (The Boomerang Coast), discussing major cities and their development; and "Around the Edges," exploring the Great Barrier Reef, Cairns, Darwin, Alice Springs, Uluru, and Perth. The work is written in a humorous style, similar to "A Walk in the Woods" and "Blue Highways."

notes.note_text: Louisville Thunder was an indoor soccer club based in Louisville, Kentucky, founded as one of the original teams in the American Indoor Soccer Association. Peter Mahlock was President and General Manager, while Keith Tozer served as head coach from 1984–87. Tozer transitioned to player-coach during the 1984–85 season. The team played at Broadbent Arena. Rick Schweizer, the goalkeeper, won Goalkeeper of the Year and was on the All-Star team in 1984–85. The team won the AISA championship in 1987 but disbanded due to ownership issues. Notable players included Zoran Savic, Art Hughes, and Chris Hellenkamp, who were all All-Stars. Savic was Top Points Scorer in 1985–86. The team's existence spanned the 1984–85 to 1986–87 seasons.

Louisville Icehawks were a professional ice hockey team in the East Coast Hockey League, based in Louisville, Kentucky, from 1990 to 1994. Their home venue was Broadbent Arena at the Kentucky Exposition Center. The team's mascot, Tommy Hawk, was banned from the arena for an altercation with a visiting player. The Icehawks were affiliated with the Pittsburgh Penguins NHL team. Trevor Buchanan, a player known for time in the penalty box, had a fan club. The team was renamed and moved to Florida as the Jacksonville Lizard Kings in the 1995–96 season. 

Playoff results: 1990–91: Defeated Knoxville 3–0, lost to Greensboro 4–0. 1991–92: Defeated Toledo 4–1, Cincinnati 3–1, lost to Hampton Roads 4–0. 1992–93: Did not qualify. 1993–94: Defeated Knoxville 2–1, lost to Birmingham 3–0.

The Kentucky Athletic Hall of Fame, established in 1963, is a non-profit organization in Louisville, funded by the Kentucky Lottery and operated by the Louisville Sports Commission. Inductees include Muhammad Ali, Bo McMillin, Pat Riley, Bob Baffert, and Dwane Casey. Notable inductees from recent years include Rachel Komisarz Baugh (2021), Keith Madison (2021), and Kyra Elzy (2016). The 2021 Selection Committee includes media professionals from various outlets. Inductees span multiple sports, with achievements such as Olympic medals, NCAA championships, and Super Bowl rings. The Hall of Fame has honored athletes for 58 years, with inductees from 2016 to 2021. Selections were on hiatus in 1965, 1967-1974, and 1976-1984. Notable facts include Bob Baffert's seven Kentucky Derby wins and Kyra Elzy's role as University of Kentucky's Women's Basketball Head Coach.

Freedom Hall is a multi-purpose arena in Louisville, Kentucky, part of the Kentucky Exposition Center. Completed in 1956, it hosted the Kentucky State Fair World's Championship Horse Show and was named via a statewide contest. It served as the home of the University of Louisville Cardinals (1957–2010) and Bellarmine University Knights (since 2020). The Kentucky Colonels (ABA) played there from 1970–1976. It hosted major events like concerts by Kiss, AC/DC, and The Grateful Dead, as well as Muhammad Ali's first professional fight. The arena's capacity increased to 18,865 after a 1984 renovation. It hosted NCAA tournaments, including six Final Fours (1958–1969), and the Kentucky Boys' High School State Basketball Tournament 23 times. The last Cardinals game was on March 6, 2010. It also hosted the VEX Robotics Competition World Championship Finals (2015–2019) and the Kentucky Stickhorses (2011–2013). The Kentucky Athletic Hall of Fame is located in the

Cleveland City Hall, located at 601 Lakeside Avenue in Downtown Cleveland, Ohio, serves as the seat of government for the city. It opened in 1916 and was designed by architect J. Milton Dyer, marking the first governmental building of its kind for a major U.S. city. The building incorporates Neoclassical elements and was part of Daniel Burnham's 1903 Group Plan. Construction began in 1912 and cost $3 million (equivalent to $81 million in 2022). The rotunda has hosted various events, including the lying in state of U.S. Representative Louis Stokes in 2015. The exterior has remained largely unchanged since 1916, while the City Council Chambers underwent renovations in 1951 and 1977. The building is adjacent to Willard Park and The Mall, and across from Public Hall. It houses several city agencies, including the Mayor's Office, Finance, and Public Safety, though many departments are now located in other downtown buildings.

Louisville RiverFrogs: Professional ice hockey team in the ECHL (mid-level U.S. league with a Canadian team), based in Louisville, Kentucky, 1995–1998. Home venue: Broadbent Arena ("The Swamp"), capacity 6,600. Team mascot: Rowdy River Frog. Known for non-hockey entertainment like a giant frog blimp, hot tubs, and concession booths. Franchise sold after 1997–1998 season, moved to Florida as Miami Matadors (1 year), then to Ohio as Cincinnati Cyclones (2001–present). Cyclones now play at Heritage Bank Center. Cyclones are ECHL team, minor league affiliate of AHL's Rochester Americans and NHL's Buffalo Sabres.

Freedom Hall Civic Center is a multi-purpose arena located in Johnson City, Tennessee. It opened in 1974 on the Liberty Bell Complex adjacent to Science Hill High School. Built by the city, it serves as an entertainment venue and additional space for middle and high schools on the property. Since 2014, it has been the basketball venue for East Tennessee State University. The venue hosts a variety of events, including sporting events, theatrical productions, concerts, ice shows, and rodeos. Notable performers include Van Halen, Bon Jovi, Eric Clapton, Def Leppard, Poison, Ozzy Osbourne, Mötley Crüe, KISS, Bruce Springsteen, Third Day, For King & Country, Chicago, AC/DC, Lynyrd Skynyrd, Metallica, Elvis Presley, Elton John, and Aerosmith.
